Super El Niño could lead to mega CO2 emissions from fires in Indonesia

New Scientist August 21, 2026

Intense wildfires burning in Indonesia have likely been ramped up by the building Super El Niño – and could get much worse if this El Niño event continues to intensify to the record-smashing levels currently forecast.

“The fire emissions that we’re estimating are, for the time of year, comparable to previous really big El Niño years,” says Mark Parrington at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, who tracks wildfire emissions as part of the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service.

Wildfires do normally occur in the region between August to October, but are more intense in El Niño years. “Fire has certainly been greatly enhanced in those previous El Niño years,” says Parrington.

Advertisement

This El Niño will be the hottest by a huge margin

During the strong El Niño in 1997 and 1998, wildfires in Indonesia emitted as much as 2.5 gigatonnes of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere, equivalent to around a third of annual fossil fuel emissions at the time.

That led to a big jump in global CO2 levels – the key driver of global heating – as well as being disastrous for people and wildlife in the region. During another strong El Niño in 2015, wildfires in Indonesia emitted an estimated 1.5 gigatonnes of CO2.

The 2015 and 1997 El Niño are the strongest on record, but the developing Super El Niño could far exceed them.

Free newsletter

“This is an unprecedented event. I have never seen an El Niño signal this intense in our forecasts,” said Adam Scaife at the UK Met Office in a statement released today. “If the forecast is accurate… then 2026 will far exceed our recent experience of El Niño and its worldwide climate influences.”

Definitions vary, but El Niños are generally defined as a sea surface temperature 0.5°C above normal in part of the Pacific. During 1997 and 2015, temperatures in this region were more than 2°C above normal, and the Met Office is forecasting the temperature there could exceed 3°C higher than normal around October.

If the El Niño is as extreme as the Met Office is suggesting, it wouldn’t be a surprise if the wildfires produced emissions totals similar to those that occurred in previous strong El Niños, says Parrington.

Seeding clouds with seawater could prevent a super El Niño

In Indonesia, there have been wildfires on the island of Borneo and in the provinces of West and Central Kalimantan. Smoke pollution has led to school closures and is affecting other countries such as Singapore and Malaysia.

Ground-based sensors in the region are measuring levels of smoke that have previously been detected only in El Niño years, says Parrington. “And we’re still at the start of the season.”

In much of the region, thick layers of peat have built up beneath rainforests over millennia, storing vast amounts of carbon. The clearing of forests leads to peat drying out, making it more likely to catch fire during hot, dry conditions. Peat fires are very difficult to put out, as they can burn underground.

A planet-warming El Niño climate phase has begun, but while the phenomenon can influence Europe’s weather through long-distance atmospheric teleconnections, the effects are often uncertain

Next year, there could be particularly intense fires in the Amazon and parts of North America, says Parrington.

The developing Super El Niño will also have many other impacts on weather around the world, bringing heat and drought to areas such as Australia, and more rainfall and flooding to others. Its impact on Europe is uncertain, but Scaife said there could be increased rainfall and storminess during the autumn in the UK.

It isn’t clear if global heating is making stronger El Niños more likely, but what is clear is that when El Niños occur in a hotter world, their impacts are amplified.

How long could we possibly live? A new estimate is mind-boggling

New Scientist August 21, 2026

A few years ago, I wrote a memorable and quite controversial story about Jeanne Calment, who was then – and remains now – the official holder of the world longevity record. She was born in 1875 and died in 1997, aged 122 years and 164 days. At least that’s the official version of events. According to some doubters, the woman who died as Jeanne Calment was actually her daughter Yvonne, who fraudulently assumed her mother’s identity when Jeanne died in 1934. Yvonne was 23 years Jeanne’s junior. Still a good innings, but not a record-breaking one.

The matter remains unresolved, and so, for now, Calment remains one of the most important data points in biogerontology. When we ask, “how long can a person live?”, the answer is “at least 122 years and 164 days” – assuming Jeanne Calment really did live that long.

Whether a person could live longer has long troubled scientists. It’s an important question in biogerontology because, if we want to achieve life extension, we need to know what we’re aiming for. But it’s surprisingly hard to answer. Calment is an outlier: nobody else has reached 120, which is one reason for the suspicion. The second-longest-lived person was Kane Tanaka, who racked up 119 years and 107 days, and the oldest person today has just turned 117. Aside from a few mavericks, however, everyone agrees that there is a natural limit.

Advertisement

But where is it? There are two main ways of tackling this question. One is by studying demographic data on verified supercentenarians. One such frequently cited analysis produced an estimate of roughly 115, but did not rule out somebody living to 125. Another concluded that Calment’s record is likely to be broken fairly soon.

Another approach is by computer modelling. One such model analysed short-term fluctuations in red and white blood cell counts in adults aged 85 and over, which the researchers converted into a measure of their resilience to terminal age-related disease. At some point, resilience breaks down completely, marking the point of no return. The researchers concluded that this varies from person to person, usually kicking in at about 120. But even for the most resilient individuals there is a hard upper limit of 150.

There’s a big difference between 125 and 150, and we’ll get onto this. But one thing these studies don’t take into account is future advances in medicine. In the 1920s, scientists believed that it was impossible to live past 105, according to biogerontologist Richard Faragher at the University of Brighton, UK. But over the following century, medical breakthroughs steadily added years to people’s life expectancies, helping (along with better nutrition and sanitation) to nudge the longevity record upwards.

What happens if that trend continues? To find out, a team at the Skolkovo Institute of Science and Technology and the Artificial Intelligence Research Institute, both in Moscow, Russia, ran a thought experiment. Imagine, they said, that we manage to cure all the theoretically curable causes of ageing. The only unfixable one is damage to the DNA in our cells, which accumulates remorselessly as we age. In that scenario, the upper limit of a human life soars to 194 years.

I’ll stick my neck out and say it ain’t going to happen in my lifetime, and also point out that the causes of ageing are not yet fully understood. Even so, it suggests there’s quite a lot of room for improvement.

But back to the real world. Why do upper age estimates vary so much? Re-enter Jeanne Calment. When I was reporting that story, I spoke to a longevity researcher called Saul Newman, then at the Australian National University in Canberra. He had just published a paper showing that a small number of errors or fraudulent entries in paper records such as birth certificates can significantly distort longevity data. He told me he suspected the Calments’ alleged identity fraud was just the tip of the iceberg.

Newman, now at the University of Oxford, has just published a book, Morbid: Debunking modern longevity science, revealing the shocking extent of those errors and frauds. In Greece, for example, around 70 per cent of centenarians were found to be dead, kept alive on paper so their relatives could keep on drawing their pensions. Even higher levels of pension fraud were discovered in Japan. People have historically inflated their age for many other reasons, to join (or dodge) military service, get married or get a job. Clerical errors are rife too, especially from the time when today’s centenarians and supercentenarians were born.

Free newsletter

These errors inevitably feed into estimates of the upper limit of human longevity. If the demographic data used as an input is riddled with inflated ages, the output is probably also inflated. Garbage in, garbage out. People used in modelling studies are also tagged with an age, which could well be wrong. When the journal Nature asked Newman where this leaves the debate about a maximum human lifespan, he answered: “in an absolute shambles.”

When I was researching the Calment story, I also came across a 2011 paper that found that, across the whole world, 98 per cent of claims of lifespans over 115 could not be verified. The same paper also found that, in countries with rigorous birth records going back more than 150 years, not one person has been proved to have lived past 115. That, I think, is the best estimate we’ve got. Five score years and fifteen. I’m halfway there.

New Zealand Herald August 21, 2026

Auckland Council CEO Phil Wilson (inset) is appointing an observer to the Manurewa Local Board after allegations of vote rigging and stolen ballot papers.

Auckland Council is appointing an observer to the beleaguered Manurewa Local Board as CEO Phil Wilson concedes some sitting members may have secured their seats by cheating.

“There is that possibility.”

Contact the New Zealand Herald newsroom

Wilson is urging police to determine if the election was rigged and whether criminal offending has occurred.

He also warned more “drastic action” may be required in the form of Crown intervention if the board is unable to carry out its democratic responsibilities.

Wilson took action yesterday amid a growing scandal involving allegations of vote rigging and stolen ballot papers in last year’s local body elections.

He has written to board chairwoman Heather Andrew to advise that an expert external observer will be appointed next week to monitor the board’s operations.

Wilson told the Herald the move was unprecedented for Auckland Council. He was not aware of any such measures being taken across the super city before.

The appointment was necessary because of the fraud allegations and rising relationship tensions on the board, Wilson said.

“There are questions that arose about public confidence and even whether the board can function in terms of making decisions.”

He was concerned at claims teams of people had stolen ballot papers over seven nights last year. It’s alleged the papers were taken to a Manurewa office, opened, ticked in favour of certain candidates, then resealed and posted back to the electoral officer.

Photos purporting to show bundles of stolen papers emerged last week from a whistleblower. They have been forwarded to police and the Serious Fraud Office.

It’s claimed the whistleblower is now in hiding because of threats of a “gang hit”.

Wilson said the allegations risked undermining public confidence in the democratic process and integrity of the voting system.

He urged police to “please, please, please investigate this and get to the bottom of it”.

Asked if it was possible some sitting candidates on the Manurewa board had won their seats by cheating, Wilson said this was a possibility.

“From my perspective that is the very reason for us to take any evidence we are aware of to police.”

He said allegations of impropriety around the election results were unfairly tarring all eight elected members and two local ward councillors, Daniel Newman and Matt Winiata, “with the same brush”.

It was therefore critical that the claims were thoroughly investigated by the appropriate authorities so the matter could be resolved.

Once appointed, Wilson wanted the observer to get an understanding of the board dynamics, then report back in about a month on “whether the board’s ability to function is compromised to the extent that further and more drastic action is needed”.

The next step could involve Local Government Minister Simon Watts putting a Crown observer in place, “and ultimately there’s the question of a commissioner”.

However, Wilson said he didn’t want to “jump too fast” and preferred to give the board a chance to carry out its democratically elected responsibilities on behalf of its community.

The electoral fraud allegations raised questions about the postal voting system, Wilson said. The council’s Governing Body supported a change for future elections because of the perceived level of risk.

Watts told the Herald any issues with the integrity of local government elections were deeply concerning.

“The council has notified me that it has referred the matter to police and the Serious Fraud Office. As inquiries are now being undertaken by the relevant authorities, it would be inappropriate for me to comment further at this time.”

Yesterday, councillor Newman said he was launching a review of candidate selection processes to weed out potential bad eggs from his political ticket.

“People need to be held accountable for their conduct and behaviour,” Newman said.

“The integrity of elections is paramount and non-negotiable.”

Newman said he expected candidates and their volunteers to comply with election laws.

He had “sought assurances” from his own candidates in relation to the claims and “received those assurances”.

An even playing field was essential to ensure the best candidate prevailed rather than someone winning a seat “by cheating”.

Police are leading the investigation but told the Herald inquiries were continuing and there were no updates at this time.

Similar claims emerged last year relating to the Ōtara-Papatoetoe Local Board election in which four members of the Papatoetoe Ōtara Action Team swept to office.

After allegations of widespread theft of voting papers and fraudulent use of stolen ballots, a judge ordered that election to be re-held.

The Papatoetoe allegations were also forwarded to police.

Counties Manukau CIB Detective Inspector Shaun Vickers confirmed to the Herald the investigation had been closed because of a lack of evidence and there were no arrests.

Lane Nichols is Auckland Desk Editor and a senior journalist for the New Zealand Herald with more than 20 years’ experience in the industry.

Forever chemicals found to be reaching Lake Rotorua, calls for urgent PFAS testing

New Zealand Herald August 21, 2026

Lake Rotorua . Photo / NZME

Forever chemicals have been detected in Lake Rotorua, prompting calls for urgent testing and renewed questions about the safety of food gathered from the lake.

Investigators found per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, known as PFAS or forever chemicals, moving through groundwater into the lake from a former firefighting training area on Rotorua Airport land.

The findings prompted tense debate at Tuesday’s Rotorua Te Arawa Lakes Strategy Group meeting, where members expressed frustration that months after contamination was identified, no agency had taken responsibility for further assessment.

Rotorua Airport phased out PFAS-containing firefighting foams in the 2000s as New Zealand moved away from the chemicals.

But PFAS chemicals can remain in soil and water for decades, and some have been linked to cancers, liver damage, reduced fertility and other health effects.

A detailed investigation of the airport site, carried out between late 2025 and April 2026, found PFAS in groundwater, lake water, sediment and soil. The investigation concluded the contamination was consistent with historic firefighting foam use.

Te Arawa Lakes Trust presented the findings at Tuesday’s meeting, calling for urgent testing and public communication around potential risks near the airport site, alongside longer-term monitoring of the wider lake.

The report found PFAS levels near the airport were high enough to warrant urgent investigation into whether chemicals were accumulating in fish, shellfish and other mahinga kai species harvested from the area.

Members were told concentrations recorded around the airport were below the threshold of threat to human health, but the extent of the contamination remained unclear.

The report also recommended communicating potential risks to those who harvest food from the lake. It suggested placing a rāhui on customary harvesting at affected sites while further investigations took place.

Te Arawa Lakes Trust lakes programme co-ordinator Soweeta Fort-D’Ath said the investigation did not yield enough information to determine how safe it was to harvest food from the affected area.

Fort-D’Ath said the trust had been raising concerns for months, but no agency had yet committed to carrying out the next stage of investigation.

“We are saying that needs to happen yesterday,” she said.

She said the airport had made it clear it would not lead any future monitoring or assessment beyond its boundary, while discussions over who should carry out that work continued.

Rotorua Airport chief executive Nicole Brewer said PFAS-containing firefighting foams were considered industry best practice at the time and were widely used internationally.

She said the airport was now investigating “world-leading” remediation options for the site itself.

“While no longer in use, it is important to us to minimise any ongoing impact on the environment,” Brewer said.

Brewer said the airport was continuing to work with iwi, councils and other stakeholders on next steps.

Rotorua Lakes Council infrastructure and assets manager Stavros Michael said the immediate priority should be determining whether PFAS was accumulating in aquatic life around the airport site before assessing the extent of any wider lake issues.

“Just because one site by the airport has identified potential for bioaccumulation does not mean that is the whole lake,” he said.

“The question is, what’s the general picture of the lake?”

Michael said PFAS could enter waterways from a variety of sources, including stormwater, and argued the Bay of Plenty Regional Council should lead a broader assessment.

“The airport are obligated to decontaminate their land, and they are doing so,” he said.

“[The] regional council should lead an assessment on bioaccumulation and based on that assessment, an action plan can follow.”

Regional council chair Matemoana McDonald acknowledged the work done by Te Arawa Lakes Trust and said council staff had heard its concerns.

“I don’t want to leave the room with you frustrated,” she said.

McDonald later said she would make it clear to council staff that the trust needed to be part of the ongoing conversations around PFAS.

The trust’s representative on the strategy group, Nicki Douglas, said communities needed clearer information about risks around the affected site.

“The levels are high enough that we should be warning people not to take kai from that part of the lake.”

Ultimately, the strategy group endorsed the report’s recommendations and delegated the issue to the Rotorua Lakes Programme Steering Group.

It directed staff to progress the proposed investigations and communications work and return with a report on actions taken at the next meeting on September 11.

After an earlier motion that focused on reporting back rather than specific actions, Douglas expressed frustration at the lack of progress.

“Sounds to me like no action again, just more reporting,” she said.

Later, half-joking but clearly frustrated, she added: “Get me a [testing] kit, I’ll do it my bloody self.”

Rotorua Lakes councillor Gregg Brown agreed the focus should now be on action.

“I don’t think that is unreasonable,” he said. “Just get on with it.”

The decision followed repeated concerns that months had passed since contamination was confirmed, but responsibility for further investigation remained unresolved.

“We’re not talking about a long-term assessment,” Fort-D’Ath told members.

“Just the immediate one at the site and that’s the frustration.”

The rise of the robot front line: How Christchurch-made machines are changing security, policing and border protection

New Zealand Herald August 21, 2026

Police using the Christchurch-made robot Cerberus-X. The device was designed and manufactured by Ravi Sanyal's company, Techmatics. Photo / Anna Heath

For decades, when there was a potential threat, a suspicious vehicle or an unknown risk, the answer was simple: send in a person.

Increasingly, that’s no longer the case.

Across border protection, aviation security, policing and critical infrastructure, robots are becoming the first eyes on the scene, gathering intelligence and assessing danger before frontline staff step into harm’s way.

From inspecting the underside of imported vehicles and shipping containers to searching vessel hulls and helping police to assess potentially dangerous situations, machines are being deployed in places where officials would once have had little choice but to send a person.

The result is a growing reliance on technology to go where people once had to.

And many of the machines helping to drive that change are designed and built in Christchurch.

Techmatics Robotics manufactures a range of inspection and surveillance robots used by government agencies and security operators in New Zealand and overseas.

Its technology is used at ports, airports, prisons and other high-security sites where gathering information before deploying personnel can improve both safety and decision-making.

Founder Ravi Sanyal said the company began with a far less dramatic challenge: a building inspector who didn’t want to crawl beneath houses.

Contact our Christchurch newsroom.

“His exact words were, ‘I wish there was a robot that did that.’

“And I just said to him, ‘I’ll make you one,’ and then I went on YouTube to see how to make one and did it ... and fast forward [to] 2026, we have a company, and we have a team of people making them.”

Agencies say the rise of robotic technology is being driven by both safety and increasingly complex security threats.

Customs assistant comptroller of maritime operations Paul Campbell said remotely operated and uncrewed technology had become an important part of its maritime border security arsenal.

“These tools are designed to complement frontline expertise by supporting safer and more informed decisions about when and how officers are deployed,” he told the Herald.

“The main drivers are the scale and complexity of the maritime environment, and the way transnational, serious and organised crime groups continue to exploit international supply chains and conceal drugs on or around vessels.

“It adds to the intelligence, data, partnerships, frontline expertise, X-ray technology, at-sea boarding capability and specialist detection tools already used to protect the border.”

Recent investments for the agency include remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) capable of inspecting hulls below the waterline and uncrewed surface vessels (USVs) used for maritime monitoring and intelligence gathering.

“This technology extends the reach of our officers, allowing them to gather information, monitor activity, and assess risk in environments that can be difficult, complex or difficult to access,” Campbell explained.

“It provides greater visibility and awareness, helping Customs make more informed decisions and target resources where they are needed most.”

Based in Middleton, in the west of Christchurch, Techmatics is made up of Sanyal and six robotics experts. Every part of the design-and-build process is done onsite.

Among the company’s offerings are the Hades range of robots for subfloor, under-vehicle and pipe inspections, and the “throwable” Cerberus-X tactical robot, designed for security operations and tactical surveillance missions.

The gadgets had been used by the Ministry for Primary Industries, the Australian Federal Police and state police in Western Australia and Queensland, the Australian Army, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand and Corrections, Sanyal said.

Police have been using the Cerberus-X, which boasts full voice communication capabilities and can be used as a covert listening and surveillance platform.

It can literally be thrown into a room or building, and officers can scan for offenders and other dangers. It also has a thermal imaging function for trickier environments.

Sanyal revealed that the Australian Army had engaged his company to supply a crawlspace inspection robot; Queensland police used another for “negotiation support and tactical surveillance operations”; and the Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency in Britain was using under-vehicle robots for examining bus and vehicle carriages.

The aim is to identify security threats such as explosives or weapons on vehicles entering secure zones, including the Glastonbury music festival.

In New Zealand, Sanyal said Aviation Security, Corrections and the Reserve Bank had used robots to search under vehicles for contraband such as drugs or weapons because they “provide a safer and more efficient alternative to handheld inspection mirrors”.

Custom inspection robots have also been picked up by both New Zealand and Australian biosecurity authorities, enabling the agencies’ inspectors to examine the underside of vehicles for threats such as snakes, spiders and insects that could endanger biodiversity and agricultural ecosystems.

“These robots inspect incoming vehicles, containers and machinery to prevent harmful organisms from entering the country undetected,” Sanyal said.

Biosecurity New Zealand commissioner Andrew Spelman said Techmatics’ Hades robots had been used since 2019.

“Biosecurity New Zealand is continually looking for innovative ways to improve the detection of biosecurity threats at the border.

“The technology reduces the need to ramp vehicles for inspection, improving staff safety while enabling efficient and thorough inspections.

“The latest generation of robots includes advanced imaging capabilities to help identify biosecurity risks, including pests such as the brown marmorated stink bugs.”

The agency was looking at “other cargo-related inspection uses” for the robot technology.

“For example, since 2025, we have been working with Techmatics to trial the technology for inspecting the undersides of shipping containers.

“The aim is for the robot to operate beneath containers lifted by forklifts or hoists, reducing the need to place containers on hardstands for physical inspection by officers.

“The technology could be particularly beneficial at smaller ports where access to hardstand facilities is limited. We are currently considering a proposal to use similar robotic technology to inspect the sides of shipping containers.”

Sanyal said it was important to him that all the robotic devices were designed, tested and manufactured in Christchurch.

Keeping design, software engineering, electronics and manufacturing under one roof allowed the company to quickly service and adapt products for customers.

There was so much demand for his products that he was looking towards a bigger space and adding more staff to his six-man team.

His ultimate goal was to keep refining his current offerings, rather than add more robots to his menu.

“We just want to make a few more variants – but not too many – and just specialise and be really good at it.

“I’m very proud … very thankful and really amazed at this company. Every day. This is not work for me; this is great. I just have fun, and I’m happy, and we make things, and we make it happen.

“Sometimes it’s difficult because you’ve got challenges to go through, and we’ve got people to satisfy and make them happy with our products. But when you actually see them in operation, finally, it’s just very satisfying.”

Police said the agency used drones, but that was as far as they had gone with any robotic or remote-controlled technology.

“While New Zealand Police’s use of robotics is currently limited, we are always looking to other jurisdictions and organisations to identify developments that may enhance our capabilities and assist us in keeping our communities and staff safe.”

From inspecting cargo containers for invasive pests to helping police gather intelligence before entering a potentially dangerous scene, the robots may perform different jobs.

But the principle is increasingly the same: before sending in a person, agencies are asking whether a machine can go first.

Anna Leask is a senior journalist who covers Christchurch issues and national crime and justice. She joined the Herald in 2008 and has worked as a journalist for more than 20 years with a particular focus on family and gender-based violence, child abuse, sexual violence and homicides. She writes, hosts and produces the award-winning podcast A Moment In Crime, released monthly on nzherald. co. nz.

Motorist takes Auckland Transport to court over mobile camera footage and $85 parking fines

New Zealand Herald August 21, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Auckland Transport (AT) has withdrawn court action after a man challenged the legality of licence plate recognition camera footage used to issue him $85 in parking tickets.

But Auckland man Paul Ryan says material disclosed to him during the court process raises broader questions about whether the mobile camera recordings amount to extended surveillance on unsuspecting residents and ratepayers.

Ryan, who is in his 50s and works in the tech industry, was issued several tickets last year after AT claimed he hadn’t paid to park his vehicle in Parnell.

He disputed the tickets and took the council-controlled organisation to court.

Seeking evidence for a defended hearing, Ryan asked for the raw recording of his alleged parking offences. What he received ran to hours of footage from AT’s mobile camera units, which use automatic licence plate recognition (LPR) to detect infringements.

The footage showed identifiable individuals on streets, inside and outside private premises, church grounds and parks. It also showed cars parked well away from council-controlled spaces such as homes and businesses.

Ryan said he was concerned that all licence plates could be automatically recognised, timestamped and geo-located.

“What I received was video footage of pretty much everything going on in Parnell on those streets at that time of day,” he said.

“It’s a lot more than was needed to, in my view, detect a parking infringement.”

The camera car also filmed people entering a Botox clinic, as well as the entrance of the Green Doctor – “now, I don’t think people want to be surveilled going in and out of a legal cannabis dispensary”, Ryan said.

A privacy watchdog told the Herald any system that recorded people going about their daily lives was inherently “intrusive” and organisations needed clear justification for setting up camera technology.

In a letter to Ryan on July 30, AT’s customer care engagement manager Phil Wratt confirmed the mobile camera units took images other than rule-breaking cars.

AT operated 25 parking camera cars across Auckland, covering all resident parking zones and about 75% of the region’s town and city centres, it told the Herald.

Each vehicle had a suite of cameras and used two-dimensional infrared technology to read registration plates.

Ryan believes the number of cars, hours of filming and geographical spread amounted to extended surveillance.

He questioned whether the collection breached the Privacy Act, Evidence Act or the Bill of Rights Act, and thought the issue should be tested in court.

However, AT said it was confident the footage complied with relevant legislation.

“The footage gathered from camera cars has been presented as evidence in a range of prosecutions Auckland Transport has taken without objection from the courts,” an AT spokesperson said.

Ryan received four parking tickets in Parnell and the central city in late 2025 from AT’s camera units.

Believing he’d paid for parking and the notices were wrong, he sought a defended hearing, hoping the evidence would also legally test AT’s camera fleet’s ticket-issuing methods.

It’s the second time Ryan has questioned AT’s parking notices. A 2022 court challenge was withdrawn by consent after a confidential agreement between both parties.

In the latest case, Ryan asked for raw footage of his alleged parking infringement, the mobile camera cars’ operating manual, data collection and storage policy and any privacy impact assessment.

AT declined the request for a privacy impact assessment, saying it didn’t exist.

Eventually, Ryan received a couriered box of documents and a stack of DVDs holding hours of video footage - not just the period in which his car was allegedly parked illegally.

“I’m not into parking chaos. I’m not challenging Auckland Transport’s responsibility to enforce parking bylaws and regulations.

“What I am saying is that the public should know that these cars are driving around Auckland streets videoing everything they see, in both public streets and in private property.

“I think if we’re going to be surveilled we need to agree.”

On the day of the June defended hearing, AT withdrew all four infringement notices.

Ryan said this denied him the opportunity to legally test the mobile camera cars ticket issuing process.

He is now pursuing costs of $71 incurred preparing his case.

The money was never the focus – “I just think sunlight’s a very good disinfectant”, Ryan told the Herald.

“I think people should know and I think councillors should know since Auckland Transport’s being reabsorbed into council soon.”

AT said it couldn’t comment on specifics as Ryan’s case remained before the court.

However, AT head of transport and parking compliance, Rick Bidgood, said the cars made multiple passes of parking spaces to obtain photographic evidence of offending vehicles.

“We ‘digitally chalk’ the wheels of vehicles and use scene images to confirm that illegal parking has taken place.

“Any footage that is not required for enforcement purposes is deleted.”

Bidgood also confirmed AT may share images with NZ Police in line with legislative requirements.

A spokesperson for the Office of the Privacy Commissioner (OPC) said footage and geolocated plate reading constituted personal information under the Privacy Act.

Agencies with an enforcing role could collect personal information necessary for their functions or activities such as issuing parking tickets.

“However, agencies should not collect more personal information than is required, even if the collection is automated.”

While a privacy impact assessment (PIA) was not a legal requirement, it was good practice, helped organisations address privacy risk and improved public trust, the spokesperson said.

The OPC said it was unable to say whether it had involvement with AT’s programme, citing confidentiality obligations.

Privacy Foundation chair Katrine Evans said camera systems were genuinely useful in protecting people, property and enforcing the law, but they were intrusive.

Agencies needed a very clear justification for setting up a camera system in the first place, she said.

“They then need to design and manage the system in a way that achieves that aim, but also protects against unnecessary intrusions on privacy as much as possible,” Evans said.

This included having proper signs to inform the public they were being filmed and why.

“The Privacy Foundation would expect any agency like Auckland Transport to have a proper PIA in place for its camera systems, particularly for those that use more intrusive technologies such as automatic number plate recognition or facial recognition.”

Recent parking issues are not limited to Auckland, with a Mount Maunganui woman complaining a three-second drop-off captured by a camera and resulting in a $100 fine was an example of “over-the-top” revenue-gathering by the local council.

Tauranga City Council reviewed the matter and considered the infringement notice was justified as double parking was an offence.

Mike Scott is a senior visual journalist at the New Zealand Herald. His work spans writing, photography and video, and he has won numerous journalism awards, including Videographer of the Year and Best Documentary. He has worked in media for more than 25 years, producing stories across New Zealand and internationally.

‘They burned my child alive’: Survivors remember horrors of Myanmar nine years on

Sydney Morning Herald August 22, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

The soldiers threw Rokeiya Begum’s baby into the fire.

“I was crying loudly for my child. As I was crying, they threatened to shoot me. They were pulling me to the village.”

It was August 30, 2017, and soldiers from the Myanmar military had set the village of Tula Toli alight.

Nine years later, Begum, a Rohingya refugee, tells her story from a worker’s cottage in Brisbane’s southern suburbs, where she has been living since arriving in Australia on a humanitarian visa in January.

On that day in Tula Toli, down by the river, Begum said the soldiers picked the men and teenage boys and killed them – shooting them and stabbing them, some of them with long, pointed wooden farming tools called hossa flails.

“Then they would pull them away and make a pile of the dead bodies along the river. As far as I could see, I saw all the dead bodies,” Begum said.

The soldiers pushed the women towards the burning village, and ripped Begum’s child from her arms. “They burned my child alive,” she said.

Mohammed Sadek was 18 months old.

As she cried for her dying child, the soldiers pushed Begum and other women into a hut. Without going into further detail, she said the soldiers “did whatever they wanted to do”.

Then they set the hut on fire too.

The brutality was part of “clearing operations” conducted by Myanmar’s forces in the Rakhine State, on the nation’s western edge bordering Bangladesh.

The aim was to push the Rohingya – an ethnic Muslim minority in a largely Buddhist nation – out.

Conservative estimates say more than 7000 Rohingya were killed in the region in August 2017 alone, with more than 700,000 forced to flee.

As a result of the 2017 operations, and other violence dating back to 1982, more than a million Rohingya have crossed the wide and shallow Naf River into Bangladesh, where they now live in the largest refugee camps in the world.

It was in this river that Saddam Hossain found himself late one night at the height of the attacks.

Nine years later, Hossain sits on the couch in Begum’s house recounting his story.

Along with his wife Rashida Begum and their one-year-old daughter, he had been pushed into the water from an over-crowded boat while fleeing the violence.

Shot three times while trying to free his cattle in the village of Mash Fara, 70 kilometres south of Tula Toli, Hossain could not move himself through the water.

“My body had become white because I had lost a lot of blood,” Saddam said.

Rashida, who was heavily pregnant, was pulling at his body with all her might, but to no avail.

In the dark, all they could see were a few lights twinkling across the water.

“I thought that those were boats, so I told my wife, suppose I am dead, and take the child and take care of yourself. Try to go towards the light,” he said.

He watched his wife and child wade away. When she came ashore, Rashida left a blanket to show where Saddam was.

She was then found by Bangladeshi border guards, who told her they would search for her husband in the morning.

It was a long night, but somehow, he survived.

In the morning, two border guards and two Rohingya men who had made it on boats went to look for him.

“From the water where I got stuck I could see them, they were looking for something,” Saddam said.

“They were looking for me, but they couldn’t see me, but I could see them. I became too weak, I was unable to move.”

Using all his strength, he lifted his arm into the air. They saw him and brought him ashore to Shah Porir Dwip, on the very southern tip of Bangladesh.

It was days before he reached a Médecins Sans Frontières-run hospital in the Kutupalong refugee camp, and a week before he received proper surgery in Chittagong, he said.

In 2026, Hossain lifts his sarong to show the bullet wounds, remembering how pus seeped from the old wound for years while he lived in the camp.

His left thigh is pulled in like a belly button holding back a gut. On his right hip, a scar marks where another bullet ripped straight through him.

Both Hossain and Begum are some of the lucky few who have made it out of the camps on humanitarian visas, landing in Australia this year, almost nine years after the attacks.

For Begum, who only arrived in Australia in March, it is hard to imagine life without those who didn’t make it out.

During the attack on Tula Toli she lost seven family members, including her mother and 10-year-old brother. Now 30, she was 21 at the time of the clearing operations.

After the soldiers set the hut she was in alight, she escaped through the back door.

As violence continued around the region, she walked to the Naf with a group of survivors and was ferried across in a rowboat.

Like Hossain, she was taken to a crowded MSF hospital, where, by chance, she met her surviving brother.

“My brother asked me: ‘Do you know where your husband is?’ I said: ‘No, maybe he was killed by the military.’

“He said: ‘No, he came to Bangladesh with me. He is here in the camp.’

“That’s how I came to learn about my husband after six days of separation.”

Now, their two daughters run around the worker’s cottage as she and Hossain recount their stories.

Mohammed Rofique, Begum’s husband, sits quietly, occasionally reminding her of a detail or taking one of the children into his arms.

Robi Alam, the 26-year-old president of the Rohingya United Youth Network in Brisbane, said Rohingyas had recently been re-added to Australia’s humanitarian intake, leading to a surge in the community’s population.

Alam was born in the Nayapara refugee camp, next to Kutupalong, and was one few Rohingyas allowed in Australia on humanitarian visas in 2009 and 2010.

“Some of us are genuinely scared that our identity [and] our language are at stake,” he said.

“If we don’t do whatever we can within our capacity and whatever means we have, then no one will.”

Along with three other Rohingya groups, Alam and Rohingya United – a football team he helped establish in 2014 – have organised an event on Saturday in Logan, south of Brisbane, to commemorate the victims of the events in 2017.

Over the past 10 years, slightly more than 3000 Rohingya have been resettled in Australia.

In the past two years, Alam said between 500 and 600 settled in Queensland – among them, Begum and Hossain, who will be at the event.

“The diaspora community is very grateful to Australia for that, but we must emphasise that there must be more done,” he said.

Since 2017, Myanmar has only become more volatile, with the military junta officially seizing power from elected leader Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup.

Australian lawyer and former Human Rights Commissioner Christopher Sidoti, who was part of a three-person team tasked by the UN to investigate whether the clearance operations constituted genocide, said between 500,000 and 600,000 Rohingya remain in the Rakhine State.

There have been reports of violence similar to that perpetrated by the military conducted by a local Buddhist militia known as the Arakan Army.

Sidoti said the Arakan army controls much of the state, and there was a burst of Rohingya fleeing to Bangladesh in 2024 when fighting intensified.

“The Rohingya have always faced the problem of being the meat in the sandwich, with the military on one side and the Arakan Army on the other, and neither of them being very supportive or accommodating,” he said.

Sidoti’s work investigating the 2017 killings led to the Gambia accusing military leaders of genocide in the International Court of Justice, from which a ruling is expected later this year.

For Begum, the search for justice is something to hold on to.

“I have lost a lot of family members. I want to live a life like other normal people here in Australia, but I cannot do that. So having the legal proceedings, I feel good about that,” she said.

“In Bangladesh they call us Rohingya because we are Rohingya, but in Myanmar, our own homeland, we cannot introduce ourselves as Rohingya.

“They have made us stateless. We need justice for the crime they have committed.”

‘Anger’s not something that women have been allowed to have’: Why Myf Warhurst is done playing nice

Sydney Morning Herald August 22, 2026

The popular radio and TV personality is known for her warm and engaging style. But turning 50 brought a simmering fury to the surface.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Think of Myf Warhurst and the word “bubbly” might spring to mind. With everything she does – from Spicks and Specks, the Eurovision Song Contest or her documentary The Truth about Menopause – Warhurst is the ray of sunshine; the nice one. But she’s no longer playing nice. She’s taken on the patriarchy in a new book, Middle Rage (out August 25). And she’s mad.

When I heard you’d written a book on rage, I thought maybe it was about you shaking your fist at climate change or losing it over smaller things, like parking tickets. But this book is really serious – about tackling patriarchy head-on. What does the patriarchy mean to you and why did you decide to focus on it?Initially, it was going to be this funny book about all the things in middle age that annoyed me. But because [with menopause] you have this great awakening, you lose your oestrogen, and all of a sudden it’s like you’re overcome with a laser focus. You can see everything clearly. You see the inequality everywhere. And rather than just getting sad about it, I was feeling furious, and then I looked into that and realised, “Oh, anger’s not something that women have really been allowed to have over the years.” Girls are encouraged to play nice, keep it small, don’t be too expressive. There’s all this conditioning that has got us here, and it all leads to one thing, and that is the patriarchy. That’s an easy thing to jump to and say, “Oh, you know, it’s the patriarchy’s fault,” but it’s a system by which we live, and it’s a very clear system that advantages one over the other. It also disadvantages men, because little boys aren’t allowed to become the full human beings that they could become by showing their emotions, and they’re forced into a system that kind of makes them go to work and do shitty jobs for everyone who’s making the money at the top.

I’ve also had a couple of relationship experiences whereby I realised my own conditioning allowed me to put up with certain behaviours that I shouldn’t have ... I’m terrified of [releasing the book] because people aren’t going to expect it from me, but I’m also really proud of it.

What makes you terrified?Girls, especially, learn how to people-please because they realise it makes them safe in an environment. So it’s very hard to strip back all those layers of conditioning and know I might disappoint some people with this book and know that some will think I’ve changed or lost my mind. But this person has always been there. I just hadn’t shown that side of my personality until now.

You also talk directly to men in the book, don’t you?The thing is, I grew up with great men, and maybe that was a luxury and a privilege. My brothers are fantastic; they’re creative, they’re very emotional, they respect me, as do my male friends. But I think it’s probably having had good experiences that led me towards not questioning other men who have come into my world in the same way, because I just trusted a little bit blindly. And I think it’s a Gen X thing, too; the way that generation was brought up. We were brought up on love stories and romances, where the ending was always tied with a neat little bow, and you got married, and then the story stopped.

The book went to some dark places, particularly when discussing one of your exes around the time of COVID-19. You describe it as an unhealthy relationship that left you financially in debt. You wrote that things got so dark that there were nights you went to sleep hoping you didn’t wake up. What was that likeWell, fortunately, it was a long time ago, so now I can talk about it. But also, writing the book allowed me to work through it myself. I haven’t included anything particularly salacious, but I think it was important to note that when you get caught up in relationships that are unhealthy, it can really lead you down a dark path because you feel like there’s no way out, especially if you’ve been manipulated to believe that you’re the problem. But it was also important for me to note that if I don’t say these sorts of things, then other women will be frightened to do so. I never thought it could happen to me because I’m a very well-educated, very privileged white woman who exists in a world full of kind people. How did it happen to me? It does because you’re not looking for it.

What are the top few things you’d recommend to women about recognising controlling behaviour?Just look for patterns, look for repeat behaviours – patterns like denying your reality when you say something happened or how you felt. If they say that’s not how it was, or you’ve remembered it incorrectly, then that’s a huge red flag. Your interpretation of a moment is your interpretation. There is nothing wrong with it. They could also, in the same breath, say they love you, which is confusing and can be quite manipulative. So, look for the patterns, and once you see them, you have every right to just get out in those early days. You don’t have to make it work … Women, especially of my generation, Gen X, were brought up in a culture where we’re taught to believe we are the ones that make it work, regardless of how difficult it is.

How do you reflect on that relationship now? You go through all the emotions. You go through the lows. It wasn’t great and I wasn’t great. For me, it was incredibly educational. It’s taken me until 50 to really see these kinds of behaviours for what they are, and I’m disappointed about that. I wish I’d known [about them beforehand], and I do think younger generations know this stuff a lot earlier than we do, or we did. So, I am genuinely, weirdly grateful because finally it all makes sense, and I’m able to look at this next chapter, whatever the hell it may be – who I can become – without worrying about whether or not I have to have a relationship. I grew up with all those thoughts of feeling “less than” because I never managed to get relationships right. Now, it’s like, “Well, it’s not working now, I can see it. I don’t want that any more.” I see it as fortunate now. I can write a book like this because I’ve got the time. Because I haven’t got kids.

You’ve talked in the book about calling out bad behaviour more now because you’re at this stage of your life. Can you give me an example of that?Look, the theory is real. The practice is harder and I think it’s going to take time to really stand behind everything I’ve written. It’s not like I’m walking around being furious all the time. But I’m a bit more straight-up. I’m not writing those emails any more that say “just checking in”, “no worries if not”. I still do it sometimes, and I check myself … You don’t change inherently as a person. It’s just understanding that you are allowed to be direct, and you are allowed to say what you want or need, and if that disappoints someone, then that’s OK. It doesn’t mean becoming a Karen, either – I use the term in the book, the ladies with the can-I speak-to-the-manager haircuts. Like, that’s entitlement, that is patriarchal behaviour.

It’s interesting there’s no male equivalent to “being a Karen”. There was a news story a couple of years ago where you were in a dispute with a neighbour about a fence. Do you feel like you were depicted as a “Karen” in that situation?That was over legal boundary issues, of which I’m certainly not an expert, and I wasn’t actually involved in that argument – I was in the house at the time. I think the media are always very quick to portray women in a negative light. It gets clicks. It’s the algorithm. I do think there’s this resistance to women speaking up about anything and having an opinion, and that is, again, the last gasp of the patriarchy just trying to put women back in their place. But similarly, for men, they’ve been allowed anger but have had to suppress other emotions. We are allowed as women to cry – I mean, I do it all the time – but men aren’t. And so many men I’ve spoken to while doing this book say that they haven’t cried for years.

What really struck me in the book was the experiences you’ve had with creepy men, like the guy who kept texting you while you were on the radio saying that he was on his way in to see you from the country. How scary was that for you?That’s pretty normal when you’re in the media, though. And my experiences are very similar to most women who are in the public eye. Actually, I’ve probably gotten off pretty lightly compared to women who are very vocal online today and are very vocal in the media. I’ve also realised that what we were taught, which was not to call it out, not to cause a fuss by responding, meant you’re feeding the beast. I actually think maybe staying silent is not the answer.

What would you like people to take away from this book?This book might disappoint some people who pick it up and go, “Oh, that’s not what I was expecting.” But I hope that they can keep an open mind and see it as a way to reconnect with understanding how broader systems work and how that affects all of us, and I think that’s where we need to look right now. Because a lot of women are feeling very frustrated at the moment, and I think it’s important to understand why. How many women were killed by their intimate partner in the last week here in Australia? It was five. A week before that, it was four. Like, what is going on? Things need to change, and I think this book might help people want to change things around them and to help younger generations learn so they can have a safer and more productive time of it, and to make choices that are better for all of them, not just for a system that works against them.

Middle Rage by Myf Warhurst is published by Hachette Australia on September 8.

If you or anyone you know needs support, you can contact the National Sexual Assault, Domestic and Family Violence Counselling Service on 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), Lifeline 131 114, or Beyond Blue 1300 224 636.

Josh Niland has won many accolades for his Sydney restaurant. But it’s on the global stage that he’s really making waves

Sydney Morning Herald August 22, 2026

The Australian chef is making waves on the global stage – and he’s set another audacious goal.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Josh and Julie Niland have a process for working through issues. They talk about them non-stop for weeks until they’ve driven themselves crazy. They then hit on a decision and act on it. It’s been this way since mid-2016, when the then 20-somethings were contemplating opening a fish restaurant on the site of a former sushi train in Oxford Street, Paddington, in Sydney’s east. About 12 months earlier, they’d discussed pursuing just such a dream. “If we ever open anything, I don’t want to own it,” Niland had said firmly.

With this in mind, they’d been planning their Oxford Street restaurant with another chef, who would be their silent backer. The industry wisdom was that fish restaurants don’t work, so the chef was giving them sensible advice on what they’d need to put on the menu to remain busy and, well, stay in business. Some salmon, maybe even a steak. Niland knew the chef had lots of experience. He also knew he didn’t want to compromise his own vision for what the restaurant would be. “Looking around the globe, it was clear the top chefs had a point of view. Mine would be fish.”

It all came to a head the night before the trio were due to sign the lease. “Julie and I were walking around the apartment, looking at each other, going, ‘Argh, I don’t know what we should do,’ ” he tells me. They spoke to Julie’s father, a hand surgeon, who said he could lend them $250,000 to get going on their own.

The couple agreed to write to the chef, saying, essentially, thanks for all your help but we’d like to go it alone. Niland wrote the email, pressed send, then turned and told Julie he’d done it. “She looked at me and was like, ‘WHAT?!’ ”

The would-be chef investor was gracious, wishing them luck. Niland recalls looking at the lease in the lawyer’s office the next day, with the other chef’s name blacked out. When the lawyer went to get him a pen, he vomited into the rubbish bin. “After signing, I sat in my car for about half an hour, heart racing, thinking, ‘What the f--- have I done?’ ”

Ten years on, that fish restaurant, Saint Peter, is one of Australia’s most acclaimed, and Josh Niland among our most revered chefs. Saint Peter was one of only eight Australian restaurants to snare three Good Food Guide hats in 2025, a year in which it was also voted Gourmet Traveller’s restaurant of the year. Indeed, it’s been awarded multiple Australian accolades, both in its original, modest 34-seat Oxford Street digs and after its 2024 move around the corner to the Grand National Hotel. Here it’s evolved into a 40-seat dining room offering $395-a-head 10-course dinners, a 15-room hotel, a private dining space and a 30-seat bar where you might pair your tuna burger with an oyster shell martini or an Archie Rose x Saint Peter G&T.

On top of all that, there’s a Fish Butchery across town in Waterloo, which processes fish for Saint Peter and also sells to the public. Also on offer is a range of merchandise, from fish weights, tongs, fish-oil soaps and fish-bone ceramics through to socks and, now, a Niland-designed fish pan. The Nilands also run a hotel restaurant on Hamilton Island, the Catseye Pool Club.

Perhaps more interesting than all this, however, is that, over the same 10-year period, Josh Niland has become something of a superfish in international waters. The Coachella festival, Dan Barber’s Blue Hill restaurants, Ireland’s Food on the Edge conference: these are just a few of the places he’s been invited to appear. He sits on Spain’s Basque Culinary Centre International Council and, in June, began a relationship with New York’s Culinary Institute of America. The interest revolves around Niland’s particular ways of dealing with fish. Gutting and filleting without water (the extra moisture can spoil the fish faster); dry-ageing to keep it for longer; and treating it as butchers do meat, such that much more than two fillets are used. Eyeballs for ice cream, livers for pâté, scales for granola; you get the drift.

It’s a sustainability story wrapped in an economic one, the whole ethos coming about when Niland realised he’d go broke if he didn’t use more than the standard 40-50 per cent of any fish he bought. “I couldn’t get my costs in place,” he says. “All the drama and anxiety of the worst things to ever happen were running through my head: ‘My business is going to go belly-up, my kids will be on the street, my wife is going to leave me, I’m not going to have a home to live in.’ So, back against the wall, that was when I started thinking I needed to use more of the fish, and when I started looking at all my notes from my training and thinking, ‘Maybe I could treat a fish more like an animal.’ ”

It’s a publishing story wrapped in a culinary one, too. Niland has written three books in which the recipes are more demonstrations of his fish philosophy than home-cooking guides. More than 235,000 copies have gone out into the world, according to publisher Hardie Grant, in 11 languages and across 15 territories, including the US, where they’ve earned four James Beard culinary book awards.

“I travel a lot for work and not infrequently, I’ll be standing in a kitchen in Bangkok or Lima and look on the shelf and there will be a Josh Niland book,” says Pat Nourse, creative director of the Melbourne Food & Wine Festival. “He’s become our best-known chef overseas, certainly in those top-end professional circles.” Nourse agrees the books are less for cooking than learning from: they service Brand Niland and the cooks who want to be like him. “I like his books,” he adds, “but they’re not next to my stove.”

The global acclaim means that about a third of Saint Peter diners are international visitors, and last year it was the only Australian eatery on the World’s 50 Best Restaurants longlist, where it went from 98th to 66th position. Jamie Oliver, Nigella Lawson, Heston Blumenthal, Yotam Ottolenghi and René Redzepi have long sung Niland’s praises. Now, other top names from global gastronomy are partnering with him for a series of dinners to celebrate Saint Peter’s 10th anniversary. For $1250 a head, diners have enjoyed tasting menus designed by Niland in collaboration with the likes of Joan Roca of Spain’s El Celler de Can Roca, Rasmus Munk from Copenhagen’s Alchemist and Virgilio Martinez of Central in Peru, all of whom have also graced the World’s 50 Best lists. You can count on one hand the Australian-based chefs feted like this by the global food elite: Neil Perry, Tetsuya Wakuda, Peter Gilmore, Ben Shewry. That’s about it.

All this makes you wonder what Niland, who is only 37, might do over the next 10 years. Can he keep building his global reputation while ensuring the Sydney mothership, from which everything else flows, stays at its peak, and indeed, afloat, during a cost-of-living crunch? Might he, like Wakuda, capitalise on the offshore interest by moving overseas? Is he chasing further awards or more interested in seeding his fish philosophy into other levels of the food system? And what will he do when the spotlight moves on, as it eventually always does?

There’s a hint as to how he might answer these questions in Saint Peter: Chapter & Verse, a new book to be released on September 1, the restaurant’s actual 10th birthday, detailing the journey from that vomitous lease-signing to today’s global stardom. “The ambition was never to create dishes,” he writes. “It was to create methods and systems that could be developed not just for Saint Peter but for the world.” Niland puts that ambition more succinctly when we speak. “I’ve done it in my 1 per cent, how can I now do that for mass?”

Josh Niland is waiting for me at Paddington’s Grand National, once an English-style corner pub, now the chic centre of his daily life. It’s 9.30am and he’s already had a chat with the hotel manager about bookings and looked in on his kitchen staff. Slim, with brown hair and hazel eyes, Niland is amiable but with a palpable intensity. I feel as if I’ve known him for years although in truth, I barely do. That’s the thing about good hospitality folk: they make it their point to remember you. I was a semi-regular at the original Saint Peter, my dinner-with-friends restaurant of choice in the late 2010s, and while the price point of the current iteration makes it less of a pit stop, when we had American friends in town recently, our treat night out was there.

They were duly wowed by the six temperature-controlled oyster drawers, the coral trout noodles, the yellowfin tuna bone-marrow fudge and the fish charcuterie plate that Good Food national restaurant editor Callan Boys calls the “most singular dish of the decade”. You’d be a grump not to be wowed, not least because, for all Niland’s innovation, his priority remains to make something “yummy”. Not yummy? Try again.

We’ve walked to The Bonython cafe, down a fern-strewn lane a few minutes walk from Saint Peter. Niland comes here after the gym most mornings, where he’ll sit with a long black, writing lists on the yellow notepads he favours and talking footy with his barista mate, Jack. It’s soccer he likes, and not the play per se. “I’m engrossed in the management of those teams,” he says. “I find it fascinating that teams can spend millions of dollars, not only on players but on managers, only then to sack them a week later because they didn’t win their game. How is leadership meant to be instant?”

It’s an instructive hobby for someone who spends most of his waking hours at Saint Peter or thinking about Saint Peter, consumed in between by family life with Julie and their four kids, Georgia, Sophie, Lucy and Ted, aged between four and 12. Niland is at the restaurant five or six nights a week – he reckons Julie would say six – and his fascination with leadership is to ensure that the restaurant, hotel and butchery, which between them employ 60-odd staff, can function well whether he’s there or not. “I’m not trying to be a better leader so I can open 32 restaurants, that’s not my goal.”

That said, Niland likes the idea of testing himself against the best in the world by opening a restaurant one day in, say, New York or London. How that would work with four young kids and a Sydney business, he’s not figured out. “Anybody who likes what they do, would they want to go play in the major leagues? Yeah, of course. But how practical it is, I don’t know.”

For a couple of years he ran a restaurant in Singapore’s Edition hotel, Fysh, but by mutual agreement, that deal was not renewed this year. He enjoyed learning to lead a team whose first language was not always English but in the end, despite having taken up the contract “because we couldn’t afford not to”, it was too taxing on family and Saint Peter to be away six times a year.

More than opening another restaurant, he wants to work out how to scale up his fish philosophy. So when Robert Jones asked him to present at New York’s Culinary Institute of America (CIA), it was a quick yes. Jones, a former fisherman and fisheries executive, now vice-president of strategic partnerships and industry leadership at the CIA, came across Niland via his first and most popular book, The Whole Fish Cookbook. “That book blew my mind,” he says. Niland spoke in June at the Menus of Change summit, a partnership between the CIA and Harvard University, as well as to CIA students. “He broke down a 100-pound [45-kilogram] yellowfin tuna in front of 120 totally enthralled students,” Jones says. “When he’d finished, he didn’t have a spot on his apron.”

It was the start of a relationship Jones hopes will evolve into an advanced fish curriculum for students, as well as programs for CIA alumni. “We’re known for producing top chefs and haute cuisine, but this conversation is much bigger than Michelin stars,” he says. “A huge number of our graduates create meals for millions of American school children, many others work for companies developing food on college and corporate campuses around the world. We’re talking about a fundamental mind-shift, not just influencing fancy restaurant menus.” On this, he and Niland were simpatico. “One of the things he said early on was that he wanted his legacy to be around seafood education and passing on his knowledge to future generations,” Jones says. “He’s not about protecting his IP, he wants to share his knowledge with as many people as possible. The fact that his goal is education, not Michelin stars, says a lot about him.”

The story is similar across the Atlantic, where Joxe Mari Aizega runs the Basque Culinary Centre in northern Spain’s San Sebastián. It, too, wants to develop a curriculum around Niland’s ideas, ideally to start next year. “He’s already done some classes in our master program about his philosophy and practice,” Aizega says. “The students admire how he thinks about fish – his ideas but also his practice, he is so technical and rigorous.”

Niland wants to talk to other cooking schools, too. “You can get a PhD in gastronomy, you can get a masters in fermentation, why can’t we put fish butchery into that?” he says. “Why can’t I have that conversation with [France’s] Le Cordon Bleu?”

Neil Perry was a famous chef before Niland was out of school shorts and runs his own mini-restaurant empire in Sydney’s Double Bay, down the road from Saint Peter’s Paddington. Perry admires what Niland has achieved and also fillets without water, which he’s been doing since his 1980s Blue Water Grill days. “It’s more a case of him agreeing with me on that than me agreeing with him,” he says with a laugh. But dry-ageing is not for him. “I want fish to taste of the sea, to have the unique freshness and verve that can bring.” Perry’s not sure fish should be treated like meat, with primary and secondary cuts and every little bit harvested for use. “Fish has an anatomical variation to land-based animals, which have massive amounts of connective tissue and long muscle holding up a frame that’s moving across the earth,” he says. That combination doesn’t exist “on something that’s moving through the sea”. He doesn’t think he could make up the cost of harvesting everything with the products he’d make, either.

Therein lies one of the big challenges for mainstreaming Niland’s ideas: cost. John Susman, managing director of consultancy Fishtales, agrees with Perry and Niland that fish should never touch water once it’s hauled out of it. He sees Niland’s other practices this way: “Josh’s influence on fish-handling is probably akin to what a Cirque du Soleil performer has on a local Pilates class. He operates at a very exclusive level of high art. That’s pretty hard to translate through to Consumerville.” Susman is glad for the “spotlight Josh has drawn” to fish and says “his craft skills are unmatched” but worries about other cooks trying dry-ageing without Niland’s expertise. Like his mate Perry, Susman prefers fish as fast off the boat as he can get it. “For a crusty old fish bloke like me, it might not be to my taste, but that doesn’t mean it doesn’t have merit.”

Niland stresses his technique is not about pitting dry-ageing against freshness. He serves some fish after one day, others after 15. The practice is all about keeping moisture, and thus the chance for bacteria to grow, off the fish, many of which hang by their tails, not touching, in his cool rooms. The length of stay there depends on variety, size and other factors. “What I’m trying to work out is whether my way of doing things is sustainable on a global scale,” he says. “Can I create a system that’s actually practical, tangible and realistic for everyone to follow?”
