4:40

Fish for dinner? Follow Josh Niland's hot tips

The Sydney chef explains what you should and shouldn't do with seafood.

I find myself worrying: with these big goals, and his regular 12-hour days, how does Niland stay upright? I’d worry for anyone working as hard as he does – taking the family to Hamilton Island so he can cook there is his version of a “holiday”, ditto speaking or cooking overseas. He’s no Anthony Bourdain, rarely drinking or partying, but he’s also got only one kidney, thanks to the childhood cancer he suffered from ages eight to 10.

Niland lights up as he starts telling me about the time he got a “tummy parasite” in Japan, for which he got treated by young doctors at a hospital back home. “They said, ‘We’ve never seen anything like this – where your kidney has come out, your liver has taken up real estate.’ ” What’s more, his remaining kidney had grown to be “the equivalent of two kidneys in one”. His body had been “problem-solving” since the age of eight, he tells me with a smile. The upshot: I need not worry. He’s as healthy as the next small-business-owning workaholic.

I wonder at the role his cancer had on his ambition and he says it definitely acted as an “accelerant”. I tell him about the Netflix documentary on tennis great Rafael Nadal, for whom a degenerative foot bone condition made every year potentially the last he might play. Niland understands how this would have turbocharged Nadal. “When you face your own mortality it’s like, ‘Whatever I want to do, I’m going to try to make sure I do it, in any way I can.’ ” If he hadn’t become a cook, he’d like to have been a professional cricketer, he says, though he’s not sure that he had the talent to match his drive to get to the top.

Monica Brown, the business and PR consultant who helped guide Niland’s global trajectory, says he was always in a hurry. “In the first couple of years, I was more holding him back than pushing him forward,” she says. “When he started to vibrate and make a bit of noise, people came to him looking to invest in the business. I said, ‘Do not sell out for $50,000 when you might be able to sell one day for $50 million. Don’t go too fast.’ I’ve had to unpick some chefs’ careers from their backers, and he was still evolving, his menus were still evolving.” Niland was easy to take on the international circuit, she says, for the simple reason that “he was hugely original and talented.”

That ambition was clear to food publisher Jane Willson, too, when she signed Niland up for his first book at Hardie Grant. They met in October 2018 and he said he’d like his book out the following September. That’s impossible, she said: the manuscript would have to be filed by January and, at the time, Julie was pregnant with the couple’s third child and a busy summer was approaching.

He got the manuscript to Willson by January, writing it (and all subsequent books) before and after his restaurant shifts, on the notes app on his phone. He asked Willson how many sales would make a bestseller; she told him that 20,000-25,000 would be excellent. He was incredulous, she remembers: he thought it would be at least 100,000. She and the publishing team laughed. “I was keen to work with him but didn’t want to overpromise,” says Willson, now at Murdoch Books. “I said, ‘Fish books don’t sell.’ He said, ‘That’s what they said about fish restaurants.’ ” That first book is now on its 23rd print run.

Willson admired Niland’s focus. He really wanted a car sponsorship – he now represents Audi. He subsequently secured a watch deal with Zenith, and an annual slot on Network Ten’s MasterChef. “There are so many in the food world with egos that are fragile,” she says. “He has a big ego but it’s not fragile. He also has the great skill of knowing how to stay in his lane.”

Like others I speak to, not least Niland himself, Brown and Willson both mention Julie as a behind-the-scenes force at Brand Niland, an iron fist in a velvet glove on strategy, negotiations and much else besides. She was sealing the lease on Fish Butchery Waterloo from hospital ahead of delivering their fourth child, Georgia, and only just handed over ordering the toilet paper for their venues.

It’s Julie, too, you can blame if a fish-weight ad is stalking you on Instagram. She recently did a course on social media marketing and sees the online merchandise store as her baby. “I have not learnt as much as an adult, ever, as I did in that course.” She’s just taken the lease on a small shopfront for the merch business. “If you’d asked me two years ago if I’d be selling frying pans, I’d have laughed at you, but I’m having fun.” It’s a smart extra revenue stream at a time when high-end dining is facing economic headwinds.

Saint Peter might be a success story today but the Nilands write candidly in their upcoming book, Chapter & Verse, about the hard, hard grind of getting there. From green 20-somethings with no business experience, no equity investors and no bank loan (they’d paid Julie’s dad back within a year), they detail holding on through cashflow crises, the pandemic and the opening and closing various spin-offs, from their first Fish Butchery in Paddington, to a takeaway fish shop, Charcoal Fish, in nearby Rose Bay, and a second, more suburban restaurant, Petermen, on Sydney’s North Shore.

An early lesson came 90 minutes before their 2016 opening, when they realised the second-hand deep-fryer they’d bought had holes, and oil was pouring onto the floor. At the end of that first night came another thudding realisation: they’d hired the wrong person in a key role. After getting home that night, Julie got into the bath and couldn’t stop shaking. “I was in the foetal position for hours, feeling sick,” she writes. It fell to her to let the staffer go; Niland didn’t have the stomach for it.

In the early years they earned two Good Food hats, only to lose one of them in 2019. Sitting at the event as the hats were read out, and it dawned on him that they’d lost one, was “the most emotionally crippling moment I have ever experienced”, Niland writes.

This is not the kind of content you usually find in a 448-page, gold-embossed coffee-table book with expensive, full-page photography. But the Nilands want Chapter & Verse to tell the real story of what it’s like, behind the glossy facade of a top-end restaurant, to build such a business.

Other lessons came thick and fast. Their decision during the pandemic to renovate the Oxford Street restaurant, replacing the 34-seat table and chairs for an 18-seat long bar, made it difficult for groups of more than two to easily converse. Opening the takeaway, Charcoal Fish, meant they had to learn on the go how to cook at speed (on day one, some waited 45 minutes for their orders), and manage piles of potatoes because they refused to buy frozen fries. The ceiling at Fish Butchery Paddington buckled because of all the Murray cod dry ageing upstairs. They closed Charcoal Fish and Fish Butchery Paddington on the same day.

The opening and closing of spin-off businesses was able to happen quickly because there were only ever two owners in the business. What becomes clear, reading the book, is how much those spin-offs were about solving immediate problems rather than any kind of expansionist mindset. It was truly adapt or die.

Julie reflects on a period after all that expansion when they were losing “huge amounts” of money and had to rely on the Oxford Street restaurant to prop up the other unprofitable parts of the business. “It would get to the point where I couldn’t bear to think about work other than answer emails, pay bills and do what was strictly necessary, then take the kids to the beach or put on a podcast to try to drown out the stress of it all. I didn’t know how to fix the issues.”

While the early 2020s were a brutal time, you can trace the seeds of the eventual upswing back to the morning in 2018 when George Penklis walked into Saint Peter on Oxford Street. Penklis had made a lot of money in private equity, co-founding Quadrant and Odyssey, and had just bought the dilapidated Grand National Hotel. It was a personal rather than finance-led acquisition, he tells me from his summer sojourn in Greece. His dream was to make it the kind of foodie destination Australia should be creating and marketing to the world. He explained this to Niland and asked if he’d like to make a time to come see the premises, with a view to potentially becoming his tenant. “Josh said, ‘Sure, what about right now?’ ”

It took years and a lot of financial stress for that dream to come to fruition. But when Saint Peter finally opened at the Grand National in August 2024, it was with a stunning fitout funded by Penklis to the Nilands’ exacting specifications. It was in this new venue that Saint Peter got its three Good Food hats. The financier laughs when I ask how much he spent on the fitout, or when it will be paid back in rent. “Let’s just say, as we often say in private equity, that it took twice as long and cost twice as much money [as we initially thought]. It cost a bit more than twice [as much], actually. And I couldn’t be happier.”

Penklis is what might be termed a super-fan. He has the Saint Peter fish weight and tongs, dines there more often than his wife would like, and enjoys poring over the cookbooks. “They work very, very hard, I like to support people like that,” he says. “It’s a passion project that’s going well for both of us.” Private equity guys are not known for taking their eyes off the bottom line, though. They’re known for buying and selling. Does he plan to sell the Grand National anytime soon? No, he says. “I envisage doing more down the track with Josh, actually.”

‘Still Kelly country’: Life in Porepunkah after Dezi Freeman, as locals pick up the pieces

Sydney Morning Herald August 22, 2026

A year on from the killing of two police offers, the remote community in Victoria’s idyllic high country is still recovering, but tensions – and deep divisions – linger.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

There is a little hut at the foot of the mountain, just minutes down the road from where Australia’s biggest-ever manhunt began.

It was built more than a century ago in Victoria’s high country, so close to the Buckland River in Porepunkah that you can hear the water rushing past under the wind. Back then, that river still gave up lumps of gold like Easter eggs. But today, you might think the hut long abandoned, if not for the patchwork of solar panels wired along its roof. They were put there – using an elaborate “Batman-style” abseiling rig – by its reclusive yet nimble 73-year-old inhabitant, Ray Kompe.

When we arrive, the former gold prospector has just hoisted a huge new lithium battery onto the roof. It weighs more than he does. “The neighbours did have to check I hadn’t done myself in,” grins Kompe. He emerges from behind his little hut’s screen door with a torch still aglow on his beanie and the sleepy look of a miner stumbling back into the light.

Almost a year ago, on another misty day like this, it was the police who came checking on Kompe. They were looking for a man he once knew well. Kompe first met Desmond Filby down by this river in the 1980s, and began teaching the long-haired teenager bushcraft. Forty years on, Filby was living in his own solar-powered retreat, off-grid, just a few kilometres up the hill, but he had taken a new name: Dezi Freeman.

It was those tactical police, with their big guns, who told Kompe that Freeman had shot and killed two police officers and injured another when they’d gone to his home to serve a warrant in a child sexual abuse investigation. Freeman, 56, had stolen a police pistol and vanished into the trees down by the Buckland River, and he was still on the run.

It would be another seven months before police caught sight of him again – when he emerged, wrapped in a doona, from a shipping container at a remote hideout more than 100 kilometres away near the NSW border. After a three-hour standoff, Freeman dropped the doona to fire that stolen revolver and was shot dead by the tactical snipers calling for his surrender.

“And to think I taught Dezi how to survive out here …” sighs Kompe.

I’ve come to see Kompe because I’m trying to understand how someone could survive in the wild here – or at least how they could be smuggled out of it under the noses of what felt to locals at times like half the state’s police force. But then there’s so much more to understand about what happened in Porepunkah than that, especially for the families still mourning and the remote community still divided by the violence at its door.

Inside Kompe’s hut, we squeeze past a bicycle in the hall and a shower in the kitchen. He apologises for the mess while his white chihuahua Luna darts around our ankles. Kompe watched the police comb through it all a year ago – the start of hundreds of raids on properties across the high country in search of Freeman and those who helped him. They flew a tiny drone “the size of two cigarette packets” straight through his place, politely weaving between towers of books and cassette tapes, into cupboards. Officers even shone a light down into the outside dunny. No Freeman.

“Well, he wouldn’t be welcome here any more,” says Kompe. For decades, he’d put up with his fixations, his rants against the government, as they explored the bush and its hidden mineshafts and waterfalls together. But the idealistic teenager who loved photography and attended hippie festivals had undeniably grown into a bitter and angry man. Even before the pandemic, he’d become a fanatical adherent of the pseudo-law peddled by so-called “sovereign citizens”, those who don’t recognise the authority of government – who drive under fake licence plates and change their names to Freeman (free man).

Well before COVID, though, Kompe had had enough of Dezi. “He fell in with that conspiracy crowd. He was watching these violent WWII videos … of Japanese torture. Sickening stuff. I just thought: ‘Why am I here with this weirdo?’ ”

The night Freeman murdered seasoned local detective Neal Thompson, 59, and 35-year-old rising star, Vadim de Waart-Hottart, snow fell on Mount Buffalo. A battering blizzard of rain and lightning howled down the spine of the tourist road as scores of heavily armed police scoured the forest for the fugitive.

Those who knew the two officers killed – including local police not authorised to speak publicly ahead of an inquest into the deaths – say problems between police and the “cookers” in the hills had been brewing before the shooting. “But we didn’t know what we were walking into,” says an officer who was there when it happened.

Detective Thompson, known as “Thommo”, knew this country well, and how treacherous it can be beyond the tourist bubble of Bright. This is not the Australian bush as seen in dusty, outback noir: stray from the path and the scrub is thick and wet, threaded with blackberries and secret tunnels. Riverbanks can suddenly burst and turn whole clearings into marshlands.

Thompson also knew Freeman. He’d gone along with the other nine officers serving the warrant that day because it was hoped that he might be able to reason with the conspiracy theorist. He’d spoken of Freeman in the weeks prior, Thompson’s best friends Andrew “Crouchy” Crouch and Dirk Wendt tell me over a beer back in Melbourne. “Thommo was thinking: ‘We’ll sort it. I’ll talk him down again,’ ” says Crouch. “I didn’t realise then how big a stronghold that area’s become for them.”

Them meaning the “cookers”, the sovereign citizens – especially the ones who hate being called sovereign citizens. “You know, the nutjobs,” says Wendt.

When I arrive in Bright on the first night of the town’s popular winter festival, my accommodation host explains: “People come here for the peace. But some people come here to hide. Especially out there. Who are you here with again?”

Thommo and Crouchy were supposed to retire together. Two cops working at opposite ends of Victoria, they’d grown up together in Bendigo, and now they’d lined up their final shifts to fall within days of each other. Thommo always had to be first through the door, “like a bull at the gate”, Crouch says, so, of course, Thommo was retiring first, too. A party was planned that Friday, though Thommo was worried his station in Wangaratta would do a guard of honour “or some nonsense”, and had a sly idea to nip off to the pub early.

Secretly, though, he was chuffed. And a little overwhelmed. He’d joined the force barely out of his teens and he liked the swagger it gave him around town. He liked helping people. He still wore the same long, black detective’s coat he’d always worn, chasing crooks through wheatfields, crashing police cars, as if he’d rocketed straight out of a 1980s cop drama. His favourite crook in town called him “The Don”.

“He was finding it harder than I expected, harder than I did, giving it up,” says Crouch. “But we had real adventures planned for retirement.”

Instead, that Tuesday, Crouchy heard news of the Porepunkah killings over the police radios. Thommo, his best friend since he was 12, the cop who was always first through the door, had been shot dead. Crouch’s unit, the dog squad, was called up to the high country to hunt for the killer.

At Wangaratta police station in those early days, there were so many flowers piled in the entryway, the doors could barely close, says Senior Sergeant Luke Vogels. People brought slabs of beer too, though sadly, policy dictated the tinnies had to be turned away. Nothing like this had ever really happened before.

A permanent memorial is now being hewn out of rock outside the station for Thompson alongside de Waart-Hottart – the “gentle giant” from Belgium who had been excited to explore the Alpine wilds on his new secondment from Melbourne. A female officer, who narrowly escaped the shooting herself when the homemade shotgun Freeman turned on her jammed, has been fundraising with her son for a similar memorial outside the Bright station, ahead of Victoria Police commemorations on August 26.

“We’ll have to clear all this out soon,” says Vogels, staring at the photographs of Thompson and de Waart-Hottart still on display on the little white table in the foyer, children’s drawings pinned to the wall behind. “We’re going to do something special for them.”

It rained for days after the Porepunkah murders, every day for nearly a fortnight. But, on September 5, the day of de Waart-Hottart’s funeral, the sun broke through the stained-glass windows of the police academy chapel in Melbourne, as the young constable was being laid to rest. His mother Carolina smiled, raising her hands to the light. She’d told those gathered at the funeral that her son would live on in nature, and now here he was, her Vadim, making everyone smile again.

This March, his parents returned to Australia and to the same police chapel to commemorate the Russell Street bombings that killed another young officer in Melbourne 40 years ago. Beside them was Police Chief Commissioner Mike Bush, as he had been during Vadim’s funeral.

He couldn’t tell them then, but, while they gathered, officers were analysing surprise new intelligence about the whereabouts of their son’s killer. Detectives had thought Freeman already dead – months of searching had failed to turn up a single, useful lead. Now suddenly they had one, and it led to a remote property in the state’s north.

Three days later, when Freeman was found there and shot dead, de Waart-Hottart’s parents were the first people Bush called. Today, police are piecing together how he got there, and who they believe helped him. Multiple people have been raided and arrested. No one has yet been charged.

But “sov-cit” ideas are growing in these hills and beyond, locals say. All elections, from councils to federal parliament, have seen an increase in sov-cit protest votes. Even some of Thommo’s friends, people he got to know out hunting and fishing, would later turn out to be sympathetic to Freeman’s anti-government cause, as conspiracy theorists lionised the fugitive online. They called Freeman the modern-day Ned Kelly. Porepunkah is, after all, they said, just 80 kilometres from Glenrowan, where Kelly made his last stand against police 150-odd years ago.

“This is still Kelly country,” says Freeman’s close friend, Bruce Evans, adjusting a velcro strap on his camouflage pants. It’s a common refrain.

In Bright, where the hills cast shadows of green velvet, the murders split the community. Some rallied around Freeman’s Filipino wife Mali, well-liked but left homeless and adrift with their children after he fled. Others tied blue ribbons to lamp poles to honour the officers shot.

Leanne Boyd, who once employed Mali at her popular cafe and helped fundraise supplies for her, says she fell somewhere in the middle. She was no fan of her friend Mali’s odd husband, but the strain of people pulling in both directions left her exhausted. Either Freeman was a monster or an outlaw hero. Either Mali was his Lady Macbeth accomplice or “a f---ing saint”, as one friend of Freeman’s hisses at me down the phoneline.

It’s the morning rush at Boyd’s cafe and a pen wobbles in her long, blonde hair; a tremulous, load-bearing look about it. These days Mali is rarely seen around town, though prosecutors have dropped talk of charging her over the shootings. “Mali always asks, ‘What’s going on in the outside world?’ ” sighs Boyd. “She just wants peace. I think we’re all sick of thinking about it.”

I understand. Four months ago, when Freeman was shot dead, I’d driven up this mountain and stood on this street and asked the same questions. One in a parade of journalists periodically crashing over the town like the tide and then retreating, with business cards tucked in the crooks of doors and letterboxes. Bright had been all bustling colour then, orange leaves trodden underfoot in the final hours of the Easter weekend. There was hope that, with Freeman gone, the tourism that powered the town would come roaring back to life.

Some businesses are still recovering from the manhunt lockdown that choked off the rare, bumper snow season of 2025, even with government assistance grants. Boyd says she lost $28,000, back when her only customers were the undercover cops in town (“They dressed too well to be locals or ski bunnies”).

Still, today there is fake snow on the air, and fairy-lights overhead and the town is once again heaving with out-of-towners for the winter festival. Over Boyd’s shoulder, I watch a couple struggling to fit armfuls of hire skis – and their gigantic, grinning Samoyed – into the back of a hatchback.

Only the year before the shooting, the property that borders the farm where it happened was taken over by a film crew for production of Netflix movie War Machine. “People with guns were running around then, too, fighting imaginary aliens,” says local Gary Monshing. “So we’ve had a bit on around here.”

Gary’s daughter Georgia and her partner Ben now run the family ski gear shop in Porepunkah. It’s one of many competing ski shops on the tourist road – at least two of them guarded by near-identical border collies – and the Monshings are exactly the kind of genuine, postcard-friendly people that make tourism agencies breathless to remind the public that, yes, Bright really is the same honey-gold snow town it’s always been, thank you very much.

But while many locals are eager not to be defined by the tragedy, others seem just as eager to stress that they don’t believe “the official story”. Some trust police even less than before. And the question of who helped Freeman on the run – and who might have helped turn him in – is still there too, on the air.

When Freeman was killed in March, his eldest son posted a plea online for people not to celebrate. “That’s still my father,” Koah wrote.

Josh Roose, a researcher who advises police and governments on extremism cases, calls the high country “strange country”, where the modern, online phenomenon of sov-cits collides with old bush mythology of the outlaw. You’ll find people in rural poverty, off-grid in makeshift shelters or huts like Kompe – once living rough by the river and still hesitant to use the heating until after dark, until it’s really cold – while, next door, luxury Airbnbs sit empty half the year.

As police hunted Freeman, drones buzzed in the night, but properties were too vast to properly surveil, and phone taps quiet. (“Everyone knew they were listening,” says Boyd.) Some locals even refused to serve police coffee, Roose recalls. “It’s a closed shop up there. They might get tourists but the locals are the locals. That’s their defining borderline between us and them.”

The thing to remember about the Freeman case, Roose tells me, is that “Dezi was not only deeply embedded in a network of anti-government types” – though he was, he was up to his neck in them the way you can find yourself up to your neck in blackberries in the scrub. But Freeman was also “just embedded in his local community in a way most people don’t understand”.

When the sun sets behind the mountain, an underground network of two-way radios crackle to life. Among those listening is Bright blacksmith (and one-time bikie) Stephen Mallett. As the head of Australia’s main “doomsday prepper” Facebook community, he’s met many of those at the other end of the line. Sometimes it’s someone on the roads needing help. Sometimes it’s someone like Freeman. Mallett knew him before the shooting as another local preparing for catastrophe – whatever flavour of civil war, foreign invasion or asteroid collision you preferred. “But the day of the shootings,” says Mallett, “the radio waves all went dead.”

He was one of the first of Freeman’s associates raided (and cleared of helping him). When he opened his door in the howling rain to find red lasers pointed at his chest, he considered racing for his back fence and the forest behind – that forest of old mines, forgotten huts and hidden waterfalls. Mallett is perhaps the 20th local to tell me that police, in their months of searching, didn’t cover even half of it. But Mallett didn’t run.

“Nothing to hide. And I was afraid they’d shoot my dog,” he says as he shows me his camouflage “bug-out bag” or emergency pack. The thing to grab in case of apocalypse. He wouldn’t take the huge knives he makes, custom, for “hippie chicks” online if he was running. He’d pack light. And he’d keep moving, through the pine plantations, the wineries, stealing off fruit trees or going up the waters Freeman used to kayak, which all rush north to the Murray River, near where he was discovered. “They’d never find you.”

Friends remember Freeman pointing out his prepper stashes on the mountain and disappearing into its trees for weeks at a time to hunt. Beth Knights says he knew how to live off the land even back in their 20s, when they met at the hippie festivals in these hills, cooking over campfires and swimming naked in the river. He still went by his family name Filby then, and his hair was long. There was no electricity for a bush-doof rave, but there was a magic idealism on the air; people coming together in little tribes.

Freeman wasn’t like the city folk with whom Knights hitched a ride from Melbourne. He was a local, “with a thick, bogan accent”, but warm and fun and generous then. He knew how to build a fire break, and he’d catch fish with his hands from the river, the water coursing past his legs. Life went rushing on, of course, as it does, and dragged them apart. Knights, today a TV writer in Castlemaine, wonders what dragged Freeman under. A particular conspiracy? A personal tragedy?

She remembers a bitterness in Freeman when she saw him again, at a music festival in the 2000s. “Or maybe it was just sadness. It’s like he couldn’t fit anywhere. He only made sense out there.” Something about him left an impression, though. “I always wanted to know where he ended up. I was just horrified when I realised it was him.”

For the Filbys, Freeman’s ravings had been a problem without a satisfying explanation for years. He lived off welfare support while hating the government; he made fun of “flat-earther” conspiracists, while his own biblical delusions intensified. Freeman had been deeply affected by a series of deaths in his family, though most of the Filbys left were estranged from him by the shootings, including nephews Luke and Joe. Luke remembers his uncle destroying cassettes of Metallica, once his favourite band, because he’d declared them satanic. “Dez was always the oddball uncle,” says Joe. But he was also the uncle who took a young Joe hiking when he was depressed in his teens and offered support. “We never saw anything like this coming. It’s been devastating.”

Around the time of COVID, Freeman’s attempts to arrest a local magistrate and help privately prosecute then-premier Daniel Andrews made him infamous.

But by August 2025, he was facing serious allegations of child sexual abuse, and his brother and wife finally convinced him to see a psychologist. He had an appointment booked on the day of the shooting. He never made it.

Ten minutes out of town, the old, converted bus where the Freemans lived is still there. It sits in one corner of a sprawling chestnut farm, next to the Buckland River. Under the tarp of Freeman’s makeshift kitchen, he hung a sign for the Buckland and a picture of the Virgin Mary.

You can see the property from the hills near the airfield, but it’s easy to miss the turn-off – a narrow gravel track through a tunnel of forest with a metal gate at the end. Exclusion zone, warns a handwritten, cardboard sign. No trespass. There is a strange, fairy-tale feeling to the trees here; lit gold in the sunlight, but, as the sky darkens, they lean too close.

Freeman’s landlords, Andrew and Rebecca Swift, still live behind this gate, in a red-roofed farmhouse with their daughters. Others live here too, “a little community”, according to neighbours and friends. But few people get past the gate.

Freeman made it himself, an elaborate early-warning system of security codes and solar-powered cameras, with more hidden throughout the trees. He always had eyes in the bush, locals say. He’d construct elaborate “hides” from which to watch his neighbours, strap cameras to his chest and don camouflage suits that made him look like Chewbacca. When child services and police surrounded the bus more than once in the years before the shooting – out of concern for the Freeman children – their approach was picked up by this ring of CCTV.

The Swifts aren’t answering the phone, but the gate’s warnings grow more strident the further I read. Offenders will be prosecuted and fined a minimum of ten thousand dollars.

They’re well-liked in town, the Swifts, though fiercely private. Rebecca in particular is known for her anti-government views. The Freemans moved onto their farm four years ago, after a string of fallings-out between Freeman and his former landlords had left them homeless. People speak of Freeman’s terrifying temper, of his obsession with guns and a mysterious marijuana crop that sprung up at one property in Myrtleford. Most of all, Freeman hated female cops. But the shootings in August caught the Swifts by surprise. “They’re peaceful people,” says friend Bruce Evans.

Police had decided a specialist sniper squad wasn’t needed that day to serve the warrant, hoping to keep Freeman calm. Instead, they sent 10 officers, including two of their best: Thompson the veteran and de Waart-Hottart, formerly of the city’s public order response unit.

In Andrew Swift’s own account of what unfolded when Freeman barricaded himself in the bus with Mali and their toddler – as told to a YouTuber who runs wellness festivals, not “the mainstream media” – Swift says he never heard Freeman warn police he had a gun.

Freeman shot Thompson first as the detective climbed in through the bus window. Then de Waart-Hottart.

A preliminary hearing for the upcoming inquest heard that Freeman stole de Waart-Hottart’s gun and used it to shoot Thompson a second time, where he lay on the ground. “Can you hear us Thommo?” called one of the other officers now taking cover. “F---ing scum, die in hell,” said Freeman.

Roose gave expert testimony at the inquest into the 2022 Wieambilla shootings – when Christian extremists murdered two police officers and a neighbour at a remote Queensland property. That should have been a routine missing-person check. But, like Freeman, the Train family hated police, and called them “devils”.

Since the Porepunkah shootings, Freeman’s image has started appearing on posters at far-right rallies throughout Australian cities. Yet, in the regions where these ideologies are also brewing, mental health services and other supports remain painfully thin, says Roose – a knife’s edge. “We have to wake up to this as a serious threat.”

Sunday in Bright, and under the soaring timber beams of the Our Lady of the Snows church, Father Tony Shallue is delivering a sermon on the dangers of misinformation. The Freemans came here most Sundays, including two days before the shooting, though Father Tony worried about Freeman’s strange slide into doomsday fanaticism, his ravings about the Antichrist.

“In this world of information, not all of it is wisdom,” the priest tells his flock now. It’s a sermon so on theme I wonder if my cover is already blown, having just strolled in off the street to find the congregation in a late Mass. The singing had drawn me in. A black dog is tied up out front.

Father Tony briefly pauses his sermon warning of technology coming between people to wrestle with a malfunctioning microphone. But it’s not all bad, he continues, if it brings us together.

We check back on Ray Kompe at his hut, where the only real technology is the solar panels and the gadgets he fashions himself. Kompe apologises again for the mess, but the closer I look, the more I sense an order to the clutter. His dog’s vet records hang, neatly labelled, on one wall. On another are framed drawings from his neighbours’ children, the neighbours who check on him.

People tried to check on Freeman, when they knew something had taken him under. Others seemed happy to draw him deeper and deeper into the whirlpool of pseudo law and conspiracies.

In the past year, Kompe says he’s lost interest in making gadgets entirely, though he’s not sure why. “Everyone’s just on their phones now,” he offers, half-heartedly, but he’s looking across the field, towards the hill where the boy he knew as Desmond Filby shot three men.

“I mean, the world doesn’t ever really go away, does it?”

Manchester United agree deal for Carlos Baleba to continue midfield rebuild

The Guardian Fri, 21 Aug 2026 21:30:45 GMT

Brighton midfielder will join Tielemans and Santos

Club’s most expensive summer signing at initial £65m

Manchester United have agreed a deal worth an initial £65m for Carlos Baleba and the Brighton midfielder will have his medical this weekend in Manchester.

If the 22-year-old is signed he will be the third midfielder added to Michael Carrick’s squad in the window. Baleba, a No 6, will join Youri Tielemans, a No 8, and Andrey Santos, who is also a holding player.

Even before a potential £5m in add-ons Baleba would be United’s most expensive buy of the summer as Tielemans cost £35m and Santos an initial £48m, with a possible £2m of extras. Baleba’s signing would take United’s total spend to £148m.

Privately, United are delighted with the deal after failing to land the Cameroon star last summer. Last year, Brighton were hoping for a price in the region of the £115m they received when they sold Moisés Caicedo to Chelsea in 2023 but Carrick now has his midfield enforcer in a deal which represents value on and off the pitch.

Speaking before the agreement was struck, Carrick outlined the importance of a functioning midfield. “I think it gives you the foundation of the team, you know. I think the foundation of the team is important to be consistent, to be consistent through one game from start to finish, to be consistent over a period of time.

“You need a solid foundation through the middle of the team and trying and putting it together and getting that balance. But certainly, I think if you look at all the top teams over the years, all the great teams over the years, the spine of the team is really strong, you know.

“So we’re conscious of that, and I think we’ve got a good spine of the team right now. We can keep improving as we go in different ways and coaching and helping the boys and developing them, and I think we’re in a good place.”

Wigan sink Wakefield and hit Super League summit with 12th straight win

The Guardian Fri, 21 Aug 2026 21:20:55 GMT

Super League: Wigan 26-12 Wakefield

French leads the way as Warriors break club record

If you are a Wigan Warriors supporter and a keen believer in omens, it may be wise to cancel any plans you had for the first weekend of October.

The Warriors are back on top of Super League, albeit for potentially just 48 hours before Leeds Rhinos get the chance to return serve on Sunday in York. But this was a record-breaking night for one of rugby league’s great clubs, who have now set a club record for most consecutive league wins in the summer era after a 12th straight triumph, this time against Wakefield.

The three previous time they had hit 11 consecutive wins before this season were in 1998, 2013 and 2023. The final outcome in each of those years? Wigan were ultimately crowned Super League champions – and few would back against that becoming a reality again at Old Trafford in October after another impressive display.

Perhaps the biggest compliment you can pay Wigan right now is how rudimentary they are making games of this magnitude look and feel. Wakefield have been magnificent this season and while their own title charge has stuttered with back-to-back defeats of late, Trinity are no mugs these days. Yet Wigan ultimately made this look and feel straightforward.

Wakefield held their own in the early exchanges and underlined why they are not to be written off come the playoffs. They showed that again with a second half effort when the game felt lost. But these crucial matches are defined by big moments and in Bevan French and Jai Field, Wigan arguably have Super League’s two most outstanding players who can decide matches.

French justified that praise when he opened the scoring with a scintillating long-range break after a Wakefield attack broke down. That was the moment that swung it the way of the hosts, with French’s try the first of three in nine minutes that put Wigan in control.

Liam Marshall was the beneficiary of two wonderful pieces of play to score in the corner on two occasions and with Adam Keighran converting both before adding a penalty on the half-time hooter, Wigan had rode out a difficult opening 20 minutes to lead by 20 at the interval. It was a passage of play few, if any, sides could have coped with.

But as mentioned, this Wakefield side are a credible threat come the play-offs, with their place in the top six already assured in all probability. They were much-improved after half-time and Corey Hall’s try to get them on the board was the least they deserved. A period of sustained pressure from the visitors then followed and had they scored again, we could have had a grandstand finale.

However, one of those crucial moments arrived with 15 minutes left. Wakefield spilled the ball while probing the Wigan line and Field collected, nonchalantly stepped around Jack Sinfield and raced the length of the field to put the result beyond doubt. It is a script we have seen so many times before, Field and French starring: but it does not get boring.

There was another consolation for Wakefield with ten minutes left when Ky Rodwell crashed over, and they showed enough to suggest they will be a threat in the play-offs. But Wigan, without being on optimal form, showed right now, there is only one team really to beat.

The Wigan coach, Matt Peet said: “The run is going to end at some point, but hopefully it’s not the next game. I’ve got a group I love working with. There’s a lot left in us but some of the good stuff comes through the imperfection. We can certainly be slicker but we were very hard to break down against a good team.”

“It was a tough game we were in all the way through,” Wakefield’s coach, Daryl Powell, admitted. “We talked about their speed and what happens if you give them loose ball and we gave them two tries when we had the ball. Ultimately that was the difference, but we should be proud of our effort.”

Arsenal sweep Coventry aside to start Premier League title defence in style

The Guardian Fri, 21 Aug 2026 21:07:53 GMT

What a difference a title makes. The last time Arsenal played in front of their own supporters, you could cut the nervous tension with a knife as Mikel Arteta’s side scraped to a 1-0 victory over already relegated Burnley. Ninety five days on and having ended their long wait to be crowned champions the following night when Manchester City slipped up against Bournemouth, Arsenal gave Coventry a rude awakening in their first Premier League game for 25 years.

It’s now 46 matches since Arsenal lost at home to a newly promoted side and there was never any doubt about this result as soon as Kai Havertz – who scored the only goal against Burnley that turned out to be priceless – picked up where he left off by giving Arsenal the lead in the 15th minute. A tap-in from Bukayo Saka and captain Martin Ødegaard matching his Premier League tally from last season just after half-time made it almost the perfect start for the reigning champions.

Arteta had warned beforehand that his players were hungry for more silverware this season and as well as assembling one of the deepest squads, they now have the vital experience of having actually done it. It was telling that with 15 minutes still to play and his side cruising towards victory, the Arsenal manager had the luxury of replacing the outstanding Ødegaard and Declan Rice with two World Cup winners in Mikel Merino and Martín Zubimendi.

It could have been much worse for Coventry had Arsenal not taken their foot off the accelerator by then. But Frank Lampard will know that their chances of survival will not rest on this result and next week’s homecoming against Hull should provide more of a barometer of their prospects.

In another show of their considerable strength, Arsenal had paraded their new signing Ezri Konsa before kick-off after the England defender completed his £51m move from Aston Villa. But they were without Bruno Guimarães after the £75m midfielder picked up an injury on his debut in Sunday’s convincing Community Shield victory over City.

• Mikel Arteta recorded his 150th Premier League victory in charge of Arsenal, and is now one of only five managers to reach 150 wins in fewer than 250 games (249), after Pep Guardiola (204), José Mourinho (231), Jürgen Klopp (237), and Alex Ferguson (247).

• Arsenal are unbeaten in 46 Premier League home games against promoted sides, extending the longest such run by any team in the competition’s history (W41 D5). Within this run, they have won the most recent 17 matches by an aggregate score of 47-9.

• Frank Lampard (pictured) has won only one of his last 18 games as a manager in the Premier League (D4 L13), while his side have failed to keep a clean sheet in each of the last 17. Opta

Coventry’s line-up contained five new signings including the Ghana midfielder Caleb Yirenkyi and it showed. At least they managed to avoid a repeat of their only two previous visits to this stadium when they conceded 10 goals in FA and League Cup ties at a time they were in the third tier. But while not many of the supporters who made the journey to north London will remember Micky Quinn’s hat-trick in Coventry’s win on the opening day of the 1993-94 season at the old Highbury, Lampard had urged his players to show belief that they belong at this level.

Sadly for him, Arsenal were in no mood for sentimentality. Christos Tzolis was not the most eye-catching arrival of the summer but the Greece forward was a lively presence from the start and could have given them the lead twice in the first 10 minutes before Havertz eventually did. Tzolis and Riccardo Calafiori teamed up on the left flank to dispossess Milan van Ewijk and the Italian rolled a pass perfectly on to the onrushing Havertz to finish.

Before Coventry knew what had hit them they were two behind. A flowing move started by Rice involving a clever one-two with Ødegaard saw Carl Rushworth play a cross from Tzolis straight to the grateful Saka. Yirenkyi went into the book for hauling down Myles Lewis-Skelly as Coventry struggled to keep their heads above water. It was no surprise that Lampard looked so concerned as he watched on with his arms folded firmly across his chest. Only four of his squad have previous Premier League experience that amounts to little more than 200 games in total. They will need to learn quickly.

Loum Tchaouna almost caught David Raya napping with a speculative lob just before half-time but Yirenkyi was perhaps fortunate not to be shown a second yellow card after catching Tzolis with a late challenge.

Coventry’s luck didn’t last long. A scuffed finish from Ødegaard after he was set up by Ben White only four minutes after the restart extinguished any hopes of mounting a comeback. Rushworth’s face said it all as the ball trickled over the line.

From then on it was damage limitation. Rushworth was at full stretch to tip over a powerful drive from Lewis-Skelly before Ødegaard had a goalbound effort deflected wide. But the departures of Rice and Saka with little more than 20 minutes to play was an indication that Arteta was more than satisfied with the scoreline. The substitute Jack Rudoni came closest to grabbing a consolation for the visitors in the dying minutes but Coventry can console themselves with the realisation that it doesn’t get any harder than this.

In a rare kind of attack, a bear killed a man in Crystal, New Mexico, on Thursday, local police said.

The police department for the Navajo Nation said officers within its Window Rock district received a call at about 1pm that a bear had attacked a man.

Authorities shot the bear, and the creature fled into woods near the scene of the attack. They said they ultimately found the bear and “neutralized” the animal.

“Our thoughts and prayers are with the victim’s family at this time,” the Navajo police department said in a Facebook post.

The Native American reservation’s police department said its criminal investigations department as well as its fish and wildlife department also responded to the scene of the fatal attack.

They neither identified the victim nor said what type of bear had killed him.

The police department said it “urges the public to stay away from potentially dangerous wildlife. If a bear is spotted, please call your nearest [police] District.”

Thursday’s fatal bear attack appeared to be the first such case in New Mexico since 2001, according to a comprehensive list with information about bear attacks. That 2001 case, meanwhile, was the first fatal New Mexico bear attack in a century, the Associated Press reported.

The victim in that case was Adelia Trujillo, who was killed by a 250lb male bear that broke into her house.

In 2020, a bear attacked a woman in Los Alamos, New Mexico. The 37-year-old woman and her husband were sitting on the deck at a ski lodge when it approached them.

The bear came within a foot of the couple and started chasing her and then attacked in the parking lot. Her injuries included “several broken bones, a collapsed lung, bite marks and scratches”, New Mexico wildlife authorities said at the time.

The woman in that case survived, according to KRQE, and authorities reportedly killed the bear.

North America generally has only a handful of fatal bear attacks annually. According to the North American Bear Center, a person’s chances of being murdered by a fellow human is 60,000 times greater than dying at the hands of a black bear.

National park service statistics indicate that the chances of being injured by a bear is exceedingly rare at one in 2.1m.

The Dutch data protection authority has fined ⁠Uber €825m ($966m) for deactivating driver ⁠accounts through automated systems without ​adequately informing them, according to a 17 August decision.

The penalty would be the second-largest issued yet under Europe’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).

It is behind only a €1.2bn ($1.4bn) fine ⁠imposed on Meta by Ireland in 2023 for unlawfully transferring European Facebook users’ data to the United States. Meta is appealing.

Uber said it would also appeal.

“We strongly disagree with this decision and disproportionate fine,” a spokesperson ⁠said, adding that the company takes drivers’ rights seriously and its policies include both human reviews and opportunities for drivers to dispute platform suspensions.

The Dutch ​authority confirmed the decision later on Friday.

“Uber has committed ‌serious infringements” by deactivating driver accounts without ‌warning or human involvement, the organization’s deputy chair Monique Verdier said in a statement.

“From one moment to the next they no longer ‌had any income … A computer should not make decisions on its own that have (such) major consequences.”

European regulators have imposed billions of euros in penalties on large US technology companies in recent years under privacy, competition and digital market rules. The EU fined Google €890m ($1.04bn) for anti-competitive actions last month.

Meta, Google, Apple and Amazon all face multiple fines, though headline fines are often reduced or reversed after years-long appeals processes. Donald Trump has criticized such fines. In April, a US state department official said they were the “biggest ‌single source of friction” in US-EU economic relations.

GDPR rules ban decisions made solely by computer algorithms when they have a significant impact on people’s lives, such as on employment, saying such decisions require meaningful human review and a way to challenge a ​decision.

The case against Uber concerns European incidents from 2018 to 2022, stemming initially from a French complaint. It was handled by the Dutch regulator because Uber’s European headquarters are in the Netherlands.

Pull. Breathe. Kick. Glide … the cautionary tale of the first cross-Channel swimmer

The Guardian Fri, 21 Aug 2026 20:06:59 GMT

In this content-driven age, we consume sport as fleeting entertainment – but the fate of Captain Matthew Webb suggests we always have

Pull. Breathe. Kick. Glide. Three decades since my last swimming lesson, I found myself sitting in a lecture theatre chanting these words with a few dozen strangers, all of us trying not to take anyone’s eye out as we matched them to the actions.

Pull. Breathe. Kick. Glide. I’ve been to enough Edinburgh fringe shows to inure myself to the embarrassment of audience participation. And, to be honest, this one was a pretty euphoric communal experience. It turns out you don’t need to be near water to marvel at a swimming feat, especially one that’s more than 150 years old.

The comedian Adam Riches previously created a one-man show out of Jimmy Connors’ 1991 US Open run, a theatrical effort that involved a lot of leaping, smashing and two-handed backhands. The Captain, which runs through August, evokes a less explosive kind of sporting endurance. It’s named for Matthew Webb, the first man to swim the Channel unaided, although we never meet the hero himself. Instead, Riches narrates his story in the person of Fred Beckwith, the promoter who helped Webb train for his feat at Lambeth Baths.

Pull. Breathe. Kick. Glide. Today, we probably think of breaststroke as the least flashy of all the competitive swimming disciplines. It’s hard to imagine people packing Victorian music halls to watch live demonstrations of it, but then, for the previous millennium, there hadn’t been much of a European tradition of swimming at all. Consider Leonardo da Vinci’s 16th-century notebooks, where, among his thoughts on flying machines, gunpowder, and steam-powered cannon, he mused on “how it is that all other animals which have feet with toes, know by nature how to swim, excepting man” and “in what way man ought to learn to swim”.

In Riches’ show, Beckwith tells us that “swimming, pre-Captain Webb, wasn’t an act in itself – it was merely a counterpoint to drowning”. Not entirely true, because in 1810 Lord Byron had already channelled his Main Character Energy into crossing the Hellespont – which we know today as the Dardanelles in Turkey – to prove a point. The mad, bad aristocrat managed the dangerous four-mile stretch of straits in just over an hour – with a club foot, no less – and immediately wrote a poem about his achievement. Within a couple of decades, the types of races that had been held in lakes for informal wagers were gradually being organised into something formal by the National Swimming Society, and artificial pools were being opened in London.

Still, Webb’s heroics did significantly popularise the pastime, not least because his aquatic adventure had gone almost fatally wrong. What should have been a 21-mile distance turned into nearly 39 as tides and weather threw him off course. Even then, his actions inspired plenty of others to emulate him, including Agnes Beckwith, Fred’s daughter, who set her own long-distance records, swimming 20 miles of the Thames from Westminster to Richmond and back to Mortlake.

Olympic swimming owes him its own debt: the races at the first modern Games in 1896 were held in the Mediterranean Sea, where athletes contended with frigid temperatures and 13ft waves. (After winning gold in the 1200m, 18-year-old Alfréd Hajós stated that “my will to live completely overcame my desire to win”.) The Channel has had a share in Webb’s glory, too. For decades that treacherous, traffic-lined stretch of water became (and in some ways remains) the ultimate marker of endurance swimming.

Gertrude Ederle’s 1926 crossing – the fastest in its day and the first by a woman – became as well known as Webb’s. And it was Ederle’s memory that inspired the legendary Lynne Cox on her own record-breaking swims: the first woman to cross the Cook Strait between New Zealand’s North and South islands, then the first human to traverse the Bering Strait between the US and the Soviet Union. A cold war effort indeed, in waters that literally froze around her.

For me, it has been impossible to contemplate Webb without following an imaginary current to a more recent legend of the breaststroke. Admittedly, Adam Ramsay-Peaty doesn’t have to swim further than 100m at a time, and it usually takes him under a minute, as opposed to the 21 hours and 45 minutes that Webb struggled between Dover and Calais. Still, there’s something in the obstinate ambition of each man that echoes down the centuries, that calls across the 30 miles between their Shropshire and Staffordshire birthplaces. Ramsay-Peaty has been, like Webb, the greatest breaststroke swimmer that ever breathed, kicked, glided. He’s also learning that even the lushest of laurel wreaths don’t stay green for ever.

Webb’s own tale was, tragically, a cautionary one: he died at 35, chasing the fame and fortune that never lasted long enough. We’re equally minded, in this content-driven age, to consume sport as any other fleeting entertainment. And perhaps that’s how it should be. It was, after all, conceived and marshalled under its new 19th-century codes as a byproduct of the burgeoning middle classes’ appetite for leisure and recreation.

But there’s something in the nature of sport – its sense of a physical science, a way of measuring human progress – that will always speak to us at a deeper level. Sabastian Sawe and Yomif Kejelcha breaking the two-hour barrier at the London Marathon. Josh Kerr running the fastest ever mile. Katie Ledecky becoming the greatest distance swimmer in history. And Captain Matthew Webb – whose ghost John Betjeman would decades later write a poem about – doing a thing that everyone but him believed humanly impossible.

You’re Killing Me review – did an AI monkey write this terrible Brooke Shields crime caper?

The Guardian Fri, 21 Aug 2026 20:00:43 GMT

I desperately wanted this show to be Gilmore Girls meets Murder, She Wrote – but the story of a novelist turned amateur sleuth is just so lazy. And yet, I still have high hopes for the confirmed second season

Look, we all want Brooke Shields to be in gainful employment. We all want her to have a fabulous third act to her career. God knows, the child model turned star of prurient fever dreams Pretty Baby and The Blue Lagoon (and the “Nothing comes between me and my Calvins” jeans ad campaign when she was 15) has earned it. Plus, she did a fine turn in Friends and a number of us remember Suddenly Susan very fondly.

But she’s terrible in the terrible new thing she’s in, which is a six-part comedy drama called You’re Killing Me. Shields plays successful cosy mystery novelist Allison Chandler, who lives in the picturesque town of Founder’s Cove, Maine. It’s Murder, She Wrote vibes all right, but please lower your expectations.

Allison’s publishers are beginning to make noises about the need to attract a younger demographic to her books. Allison – who is less a character than a loose assemblage of simple responses to stimulants, though things improve slightly after the pilot – is outraged. She is also incredibly rude to young true crime podcaster Andi (Amalia Williamson), who comes to her book signing, because she knows Andi has called her work “outdated and inaccurate”. But when her sleazebag pal Nash Gilbert (Matthew MacFadzean) suggests that her latest book maybe isn’t her best work, she executes her reflection-response instead. Could the times actually be a-changing and leaving her behind? If only there was a young person around to ask and maybe learn from, however antagonistic she might be.

Alas, before Nash can guide her further on this voyage of self-discovery, he has plummeted to his death from a balcony. An apparent suicide – or is it? Soon, whichever AI monkey is in charge of storyboarding has contrived to bring Andi and Allison together to investigate what they believe to be murder. Soon the police, led by new county detective Coppy McCopface – sorry, I mean Jack Kerrigan (Tom Cavanagh) – agree. Plot is added (a blackmail setup, a naive stepdaughter, impromptu gift shop closures become pivotal, people are flung into car boots when the monkey realises nothing as happened for a while). Murder suspects duly emerge, are given a grilling by Allison and/or Andi, establish their alibis and then are banished to the wings until it is time for one of them to re-emerge and drop himself in it.

Repeat with one new murder a week (adulterated EpiPen at a wedding, electrocution in a hot tub, and so on) set against the background of Andi and Allison learning to live, laugh, love and write a book together. It’s not the publishing deal you get that matters, of course – it’s the intergenerational bickering you are scripted along the way.

There needs to be a moratorium on boomers/gen Xers watching in horror as young ’uns give their lengthy coffee orders to baristas. And on the latter explaining basic mobile phone functions to them. And on the former reacting like Victorian dowagers when they hear a word like “chatbot” or “Zoom”. I don’t know what the average age of the writers on You’re Killing Me is, but someone needs to tell them that Allison/Shields is 61, not 106. She would know what cancelling someone means and that it is not done by an annoyed woman shouting “I cancel you!” at another. Come on.

The whole thing is thin, lazy and so disappointing. It could have been fine – maybe even good. The setup has perfectly legitimate dramedy potential, with each of the two main characters having what the other lacks in terms of skills, experience and attitude. With a little effort, a little genuine wit, intergenerational stuff can be fun, funny and occasionally even illuminating. Someone somewhere should have thought to try it. Shields can do comedy, but here is thrown back on shrillness and interminably hamming it up to try to make things stick. Williamson is clearly capable of much more, too, but Andi is written mostly as an arrogant brat and there is nowhere really to take her.

All that said – and I could say more – it has just enough charm (and honestly, if I could work out how, I would bottle it, sell it and retire to a picturesque cove of my own) and enough goodwill attached to Shields that I greet the news that it has been commissioned for a second series with hope rather than despair. I want it to work. I want it to improve, like it did – slightly – between pilot and subsequent episodes, and to become the Gilmore Girls-inflected, Murder, She Wrote homage it once flickeringly promised to be. But they do say that it’s the hope, at least as often as poisoned EpiPens, that kills you.

Deselected candidate claims Lib Dems’ religious discrimination cost him £790,000

The Guardian Fri, 21 Aug 2026 19:16:26 GMT

David Campanale seeks damages after what he says was organised campaign against his faith in Sutton and Cheam

How much is a career in politics worth? The Liberal Democrats, despite admitting claims of religious discrimination, say about £22,800. A former Lib Dem candidate claims £790,000.

It is a question before the Central London county court after David Campanale argued that discrimination against his Christianity cost him his political career in a civil case against the party.

Campanale, a former BBC journalist, was selected in 2021 as the party’s candidate for Sutton and Cheam, but was removed in August 2023.

The Liberal Democrats have admitted claims of direct and indirect discrimination on grounds of religion or belief under the Equality Act and their failure to deal with complaints Campanale made about his treatment, leaving the amount of damages to be determined by the court.

Campanale’s schedule of loss, seen by the Guardian, puts his claim at £788,740.75, including interest. It seeks compensation for injury to feelings, aggravated damages, past and future earnings, the loss of an MP’s pension, counselling costs and the “loss of a chance”, or “loss of political capital”.

But in a counter-schedule filed on Friday, the Lib Dems described Campanale’s claim as “grossly inflated and egregious”. Their lawyers say £14,000 should be awarded for injury to feelings, and as a volunteer political party member, Campanale could have been expected to withstand “rigorous political debate and criticism”. They put aggravated damages, past and future loss of earnings, an MP’s pension and the loss of political capital at £0.

Campanale says he was mocked and abused over his Christian beliefs and faced an organised campaign to remove him, while some activists refused to campaign for him.

In his claim Campanale said that at a meeting in January 2022, he was questioned about his Christianity by about 30 people and asked whether he was enjoying his “martyrdom just like Jesus did”. He also claims he was excluded from election leaflets and told not to campaign in certain wards because activists disagreed with his beliefs.

His claim also referred to a phone call in March 2022 in which he said Luke Taylor, his replacement, told him that he had no right to a conscience based on his faith and that a “secular party” was being built with no place for Christians.

After Campanale was removed, Taylor won the seat with a majority of 3,801. The seat has since become safer territory for the Lib Dems with recent polls putting them well ahead of the Conservatives.

The case has prompted criticism from senior Liberal Democrat figures inside and outside the party. The former leader Tim Farron and former deputy leader Simon Hughes have backed calls for an independent inquiry. Farron has urged the party to apologise, saying there had been “manifest discrimination” against Campanale and party figures at all levels of the party failed to intervene.

Britain’s railway prepares for more extreme weather as intense El Niño develops

The Guardian Fri, 21 Aug 2026 18:07:51 GMT

Experts say more must be done to adapt to changing climate, after two trains derailed within 24 hours during a recent heatwave

Railway companies are racing to prepare for another brutal summer next year, as a developing El Niño could see 2027 break more heat-related records.

Britain’s railway system has already been under stress from extreme heat this summer, with several operators reducing timetables and train speeds.

Two trains derailed within 24 hours during the UK’s fifth heatwave in August, in what Network Rail said had “presented exceptional challenges to the railway”.

“Traditionally, our railway system hasn’t been designed for hot weather. So that puts our railway system under stress but also our overhead lines as well. That can also cause trouble for the whole [railway] system, not just the ground infrastructure,” said Xueyu Geng, a professor of ground engineering at the University of Warwick.

The Met Office has said that the El Niño event developing over the Pacific Ocean is likely to be the strongest for more than 100 years, with the UK forecast to experience increased rainfall and stormy weather this autumn due to the “unprecedented” weather pattern.

In 2024, Network Rail increased their projected five-year spending on climate, earthworks and drainage by five times the amount allocated from 2019.

“I believe Network Rail has done a great job to maintain our railway network, but we still need to be able to adapt more in order to cope with this changing climate,” Geng said.

She warned Britain must begin to factor in higher temperatures as part of the design standards for its railways. “We need to look at how the hot countries are managing their railway systems. For example, in Spain, their rail system is managing between 0C and 45C. Saudi Arabia is 10C to 55C. The track is pre-stressed. We need to manufacture the pre-stress level in order to cope [with extreme heat].”

Geng explained that Britain’s railways can typically handle temperatures as low as -10C, and this will need to be maintained. “We might have extreme cold as well. But, in the meantime, we need to look at the upper boundary temperature, and to actually manufacture our rail to cope with both kinds of extreme temperatures.”

Prof Adam Scaife, the Met Office’s head of long-range forecasting, said the scale of the growing El Niño is unprecedented. “We’re expecting the biggest El Niño for over a century, [with Pacific sea temperatures] peaking at something over 3C. That is unheard of in modern climate records.”

Rail operators need to be prepared in the coming year for both “potentially prolonged periods of hot dry weather and more intense rainfall and storminess,” said William Powrie, professor of geotechnical engineering at the University of Southampton.

“There will need to be a serious look at parts of the network where past decisions have compromised the infrastructure, such as the extensive singling on the Salisbury to Exeter line, and reducing the train speed to account for poor track quality as a result of soil moisture deficit destroys the timetable,” Powrie said.

“The most important consideration is that we should now distinguish between maintenance and adaptation. Clearing a drain prepares us for the next storm, [but] redesigning or increasing the capacity of that drainage system prepares us for the next 30 years. We need to be doing both.”

The most recent disclosures include £858 worth of tickets to a Harry Styles concert at Wembley from the PRS for Music industry group, which was accepted by Powell, the deputy leader and education secretary. And Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, accepted tickets to the Chelsea flower show from Lloyds Banking Group worth £1,839.

Haigh also accepted a £1,314 ticket to the Ivor Novello awards, while Anneliese Midgley, the chief whip, enjoyed Brit Awards hospitality for two worth £3,432, hospitality at Cheltenham festival horse racing from the betting company Flutter worth £350, and tickets to the Grand National valued at £560. All were backbench MPs while accepting the hospitality and have now been elevated to cabinet jobs under Andy Burnham.

Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, accepted £1,480 of tickets to the men’s Wimbledon singles final while in her cabinet job, while Ellie Reeves, the attorney general, accepted a £1,314 ticket to the Ivors while solicitor general.

Burnham declared hospitality worth about £6,000 this year – mostly relating to his former role as the mayor of Greater Manchester, such as £3,800 tickets to the Brit Awards in Manchester, but also £500 worth of tickets to Ladies’ Day at the Grand National in Aintree.

The acceptance of free hospitality by MPs appeared to fall after mid-2024 when the spotlight fell on Starmer’s string of free tickets to watch Arsenal football games. In March 2025, Rachel Reeves, the then chancellor, said she would not accept free concert tickets again after she was criticised for using free tickets to take a family member to see Sabrina Carpenter at the O2 arena. She defended the decision on security grounds but said she would not do it again because she understood “how people feel about it”.

At the time, another government minister, Matthew Pennycock, said he had accepted “zero” free concert tickets as he personally did not think it was appropriate. “If I want to go to a concert at the O2, I’ll pay for it. But individual MPs, individual ministers, make their own decisions,” he said.

The value of free tickets being accepted by MPs was at about £300,000 a year in 2025, according to the Times last December. But this appears to have increased, with almost £400,000 of complimentary tickets, hospitality and other gifts having been declared between January and July this year – not including foreign trips.

Sue Hawley, the director of Spotlight on Corruption, suggested MPs should consider whether they should accept free tickets. “Some ministers and MPs appear to have short memories of the freebie-gate scandal that engulfed the first few months of Starmer’s time in No 10,” she said.

“Showering MPs and ministers with gifts and hospitality is a tried and tested lobbying tactic by big business and foreign governments. There is no good reason why elected officials should be accepting jaunts and tickets to events that have nothing to do with their parliamentary or constituency business.”

Duncan Hames, the director of policy at Transparency International UK, added: “Just because something is permitted it is not necessarily appropriate.

“MPs should be clear-eyed about why these invitations are really being offered. Before accepting hospitality, they should stop to consider what the company might be hoping to gain and what the public will make of it.”

The scale of the declared hospitality may have gone up partly because ministers have become more consistent about declaring hospitality on the MPs’ register, after Starmer changed the rules around transparency. Previously, some ministers declared the value of their free tickets on the MPs’ register and some only put it on the quarterly ministerial register without showing a value if they could argue it was connected to their government job.

Now both registers are updated at least monthly and have to show how much the hospitality or gifts were worth. Ticket prices have also risen, with many consumers complaining about the unaffordable costs of going to events.

Under the updated ministerial code, the last government set out a “well-established and recognised rule that ministers should not accept any gifts, hospitality or service which would, or might reasonably appear to, compromise their judgment or place them under an obligation to people or organisations that might try inappropriately to influence their work in government”.

It points out that ministers have a responsibility to represent the government, and their duties will sometimes require them to attend events where hospitality may be offered, and adds that it is “primarily a matter of judgment for ministers who are personally responsible for deciding how to act” in relation to accepting gifts.

The acceptance of free tickets is not limited to Labour. The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, accepted tickets to Wimbledon worth £1,360 from the All England Club, while her shadow chancellor, Mel Stride, took £1,839 of hospitality from Lloyds Banking Group to visit the Chelsea flower show. The shadow business secretary, Andrew Griffith, also took tickets worth £919.50 to go to the Chelsea flower show, and £1,800 of tickets to the Formula One grand prix from Silverstone.

Hundreds of backbench MPs were also wined and dined by corporations, including Google and Diageo, the drinks company. Many free tickets were provided by sports hosts and concert promoters, and some of them related to constituency interests, such as Powell, the Manchester Central MP, accepting tickets to Manchester City football matches and the first hosting of the Brit Awards in Manchester.

After cabinet ministers who accepted hospitality were asked why they took free tickets and whether they would do so again while in office, a Labour party spokesperson said: “After Labour entered office, the ministerial code was strengthened to include new transparency requirements and clear principles governing the acceptance of gifts and hospitality. All declarations have been made in line with ministerial and parliamentary rules.”

A Conservative source said: “All hospitality was properly declared in line with the rules. Transparency matters and we would expect the same standards and scrutiny to be applied consistently to politicians of all parties.”

A PRS for Music spokesperson said: “PRS for Music advocates to policymakers on behalf of our songwriter, composer and music publisher members to protect the rights of creators and promote the vital contribution of the music industry to the UK economy.

“Our public affairs initiatives create opportunities for stakeholders to engage directly with creators, experience how our industry works, see first‑hand the challenges they face, such as the impact of AI and post‑Brexit EU touring barriers, and understand the real world implications of policy decisions on music creators’ livelihoods.”

The result made it seven consecutive Test victories at Headingley for England, a run that began with an innings win against Pakistan in 2018. It will be some time before they build on it, with the ground not hosting men’s Test cricket in 2027 and 2028.

“I’d love to play as many games as possible here,” said Root of his home venue. “It’s a surface that provides brilliant Test cricket and one that we’ve had quite a lot of success in recently. So it’s a shame that we don’t get to play here next year. But I’m sure we’ll see many, many more brilliant Test matches here.”
