The many tragedies of the Jason Arday case

The Guardian Fri, 21 Aug 2026 16:43:22 GMT

Readers respond to Guardian reports and commentary about the academic, who was found dead at his home last weekend

Hugh Muir is right to muse on the tragic nature of the Jason Arday case (A rightwing witch-hunt focused on Jason Arday – but so did legitimate journalism, 19 August). For it’s a tragedy in so many, many ways. It’s a tragedy that a man has died, leaving a grieving family and friends behind. And it’s a tragedy that the real and necessary objectives of diversity, equity and inclusion have been done a gross disservice by Cambridge University’s cynical tokenism.

It’s a tragedy that this lamentable affair may set back the vital pursuit of equality of opportunity. And it’s a tragedy that in place of moderate voices who understand the need for better representation but with caveats, we have bad actors who see things only through the heated lens of ideology, be that from left or right.

It’s a tragedy that the latter tendency would encourage some on the left, through anger in the wake of Arday’s death, to double down on circling the wagons for their side. And it’s a tragedy that in doing so, they risk becoming entrenched participants in a destructive culture war – and to hell with truth, integrity and decency.

And finally, it is, as Muir points out, a tragedy that in pursuit of a noble cause, some would go as far as attacking the many honourable journalists who were simply doing their job to report this story, in what is still a free press. Colin MontgomeryEdinburgh

Hugh Muir’s article identifies what has been too peripheral in media coverage of the Jason Arday tragedy so far: that this situation has been the product of a ruthless campaign by the extreme right.

The Arday case is evidence of the extreme right’s obsession with academia as a key battleground, and the extent to which the views of a tiny number of highly marginal figures are hugely amplified by the mainstream media.

Much of the coverage of Arday’s position ignored the fact that the campaign against him had been led by Nathan Cofnas, a self-defined “race realist” with racist views who was dismissed from Emmanuel College, Cambridge. He and his like represent a minority within academia, but this summer has shown how the powerful resources of the extreme-right media machine can overpower scholarly standards.

This should be a wake-up call for all academics and universities to take seriously the power of these extreme groups and the need to hold their views to account. Eleanor NewbiginCambridge

I agree with your editorial (17 August) concerning the role of racism in press coverage concerning Jason Arday and that journalists seeking to act responsibly should not be subjected to an onslaught of abuse any more than he was. But there is something missing from the editorial that our institutions, including our media, need to reflect on. You refer to Arday as an autistic child. That autistic child became an autistic adult, and I am not aware of the implications of this being considered in media reporting. Carol AdamsBallarat East, Victoria, Australia

The Guardian’s coverage of the Jason Arday story was badly misjudged. Not so much the content as the prominence given to it. For at least two days the headline piece on the website was devoted to someone I had never heard of and concerned events I had little interest in. This at a time when the world is at war and on fire.

The events leading up to the resignation of a Cambridge professor had a place in the UK news section of the website, but not as the lead story on successive days. Your self-serving editorial simply compounds this mistake. It justifies the content but makes no mention of the massive misjudgment in the prominence given to the story. Stephen TompsettWinchester

I appreciated the Guardian’s self-examination following the very sad death of Jason Arday as I have been reflecting on your coverage as well as that of other media. I would, however, urge you to expand the final sentence of your editorial, adding the words in italic here: “A society committed to equality must allow black people the same freedom as everyone else: to achieve, to excel, to teach and to lead, but also to be flawed, to make mistakes, and even to fail, without their failure becoming an indictment of their race.”Annie GristHebden Bridge, West Yorkshire

A straightforward mea culpa from Cambridge University would be more appropriate than expressions of sorrow over the tragedy of Jason Arday’s death.

The proper way to address the underrepresentation of black academics is to commit sustained time, effort and resources to the pipeline – from GCSE and A-level through undergraduate and graduate education to research fellowships and academic appointments.

Instead, Cambridge chose to make Jason Arday’s appointment into a highly public symbol of its commitment to diversity.

In doing so, the university inevitably focused exceptional attention on one individual and created circumstances in which both his record and his subsequent difficulties would receive exceptional scrutiny. Whatever the rights and wrongs of the allegations subsequently made against him, the immense pressure that followed was surely foreseeable.

Universities should address structural inequalities structurally, rather than place the burden of representing institutional progress upon individuals. Prof John EllisGonville and Caius College, Cambridge

I am deeply saddened to hear of the death of Jason Arday (Report, 14 August). I didn’t know him well enough to comment on the allegations he faced (which at the time of writing remain just that). But far from being a self-serving ladder-climber, he was a deeply thoughtful and generous colleague who cared for those he worked with and taught.

He took the decision early in his career to speak out about prejudice and reduce barriers for those who come after him, and the legacy of his work will live on. Far from Black scholars receiving preferential treatment, solid and repeated quantitative and qualitative evidence show that systematic biases are baked deep into the academic system, from postgraduate research onwards.

Yet it is so easy for us not to see racism, or not to acknowledge it. Over three decades in higher education, I have seen countless instances of plagiarism, lies on CVs and job applications, sexual misconduct and bullying by white academics; too often there has been little action taken, the academics in question have been promoted, and sometimes those raising these problems are victimised.

What can we do to honour Jason’s memory? Recognise the organised campaign of intimidation that Black and Brown students and academics are now facing in the UK, and our complicity in this tragedy; educate about the realities of prejudice; and continue Jason’s work to dismantle the barriers to higher education. Prof Rachel PainNewcastle University

Douglas Hurd didn’t say ‘prison is an expensive way of making bad people worse’

The Guardian Fri, 21 Aug 2026 16:43:14 GMT

Jon Silverman says that the often misattributed line was probably written by the civil servant David Faulker, but with one crucial difference

In his letter about ever-lengthier prison sentences (18 August), Nik Wood makes two familiar mistakes in attributing the quote “prison is an expensive way of making bad people worse” to Douglas Hurd.

In fact, the line appeared in a white paper published in 1990 by Hurd’s successor, David Waddington. And there is no declaratory “is”. Instead, it warns that “prison can be an expensive way of making bad people worse” unless other rehabilitative measures are taken.

Wood suggests that Hurd was “an unlikely figure” to author such a thought. Waddington, a hardliner who supported the return of capital punishment, was far unlikelier. The true originator of the much misquoted line was probably the civil servant David Faulkner, a liberal on penal matters, whose influence on crime and punishment ended with the arrival of Michael Howard as home secretary. Jon SilvermanFormer BBC home affairs correspondent

The Guardian view on Andy Burnham’s buses: a blueprint for governing Britain

The Guardian Fri, 21 Aug 2026 16:25:08 GMT

The prime minister is right to think that taking Manchester’s model national could widen opportunity, clean the air and rebuild state capacity. Other public services could be next

Barely a month into his premiership, Andy Burnham is already taking the lessons of Manchester’s buses national. This week his government backed the West Midlands mayor Richard Parker’s move to bring the region’s main bus operation into public control. In July, he announced that he would reinstate a £2 national bus fare cap from January 2027. He’s also expanding free bus travel for disabled people to all hours. Transport affordability is clearly part of Mr Burnham’s cost of living programme. That is to be applauded, as is the emphasis on public transport, which – importantly for Labour – reduces social exclusion, boosts local economies, and is better for the environment. Yet buses may matter to Mr Burnham for another reason: they offer a blueprint for how he wants to govern.

This is because Mr Burnham seems to have a worked-out model. He told the Times this week that the prescription for services such as water, housing and energy isn’t yet clear, “with the exception of buses”. Public control, Mr Burnham reasons, gives government the power to make provision cheaper and more reliable – and to shape it around the public interest. For buses, that means the government determining the shape of the network even where private companies run the services. Municipal ownership this is not.

Despite that, more money will be needed. Austerity slashed public transport budgets, and consequently bus journeys fell. Outside London, buses clock up about 736m miles a year, nearly a third below 2005. Getting back to a decent service would cost a paltry sum. For £300m a year, England could get buses back into its worst-served communities. For about £1bn, the Campaign for Better Transport calculated, ministers could provide decent, frequent services in towns and rural areas. In 2021, the Campaign to Protect Rural England put the price of a Swiss-style bus network – an hourly service from 6am to midnight for every village of more than 300 people – at £2.7bn a year. Accounting for inflation, that would be £3.4bn today, just 1.5% of the NHS budget.

Public transport isn’t only about moving people around. London’s extensive tube, rail and bus network gave Sir Sadiq Khan the room to introduce Ulez. The scheme charged drivers of older, more polluting vehicles and brought measurable health benefits. A study has shown that children’s lungs grew bigger and stronger after Ulez was introduced. It is worth noting that Mr Burnham abandoned Manchester’s clean-air charging zone when the post-pandemic cost of replacing dirty vehicles threatened to fall heavily on businesses. He instead pressed ahead with the Bee Network, giving Manchester a more affordable public-transport alternative, while simultaneously spending public money cleaning up the city’s bus fleet. It was a politically shrewd sequence: improve the alternative so that you could persuade people to use their cars less.

Both Theresa May and Sir John Major have tried to diminish Mr Burnham’s mayoral experience by contrasting “running Manchester” and “dealing with buses” with being in Downing Street. Yet the prime minister appears to regard buses not as an incidental part of his record but as an exemplar for his government. The Centre for Cities thinktank argues that poor transport makes big English urban centres outside London effectively smaller in economic terms, by cutting workers off from opportunities. Perhaps his critics have it backwards: buses are not a distraction from governing Britain; connecting people to cities is part of the job.

The Guardian view on the export of fossils: they deserve national treasure status

The Guardian Fri, 21 Aug 2026 16:22:47 GMT

Scientific specimens are being sold to foreign museums or snapped up by the super-rich. They should have the same legal protections as works of art

As Sir David Attenborough has observed, “there’s nothing more magical than finding a shiny shell and knowing you’re the first person to have seen it for 150 million years”. Senior museum figures are campaigning for fossils to be classed as national treasures, according to the Waverley criteria, which control the export of objects considered culturally important to the nation. But the rules only cover natural treasures that are “made”, excluding fossils.

These calls come after a private collection from the Jurassic Coast was sold to the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi for a reported eight-figure sum. Both the Natural History Museum in London and Amgueddfa Cymru (Museum Wales) were offered the 318 fossils, but they didn’t have the funds. Unlike countries such as Brazil and Mongolia, where fossils belong to the state, Britain relies largely on a voluntary code of conduct.

The line between fossils as scientific specimens and fossils as aesthetic objects is becoming increasingly blurred – and their value is rocketing accordingly. Where once Damien Hirst’s shark made waves on the contemporary art scene, a dinosaur fossil appeared at London’s Frieze Masters in 2023. Last month, a 67m-year-old Tyrannosaurus rex fossil called Gus broke records at a Sotheby’s auction in New York. He toppled Apex, a stegosaurus bought by an American hedge fund manager in 2024, now on loan to the American Museum of Natural History in New York, and Stan, another T rex, was also acquired by the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi in 2022.

Big beasts of Hollywood have also got in on the act, with Nicolas Cage and Leonardo DiCaprio battling it out for a fossil. Today’s dinomania has everyone from tech giants to TikTokers in its grip. But there is nothing new about fossil collecting. Mary Anning, a cabinetmaker’s daughter born in Lyme Regis in 1799, was one the UK’s greatest palaeontologists, although, as a woman, she was not allowed to join the Geological Society of London. Her life story inspired Tracy Chevalier’s 2009 novel Remarkable Creatures and the 2020 film Ammonite.

The Victorian passion for palaeontology provides the backdrop to the clandestine love stories in John Fowles’s French Lieutenant’s Woman (also set in Lyme Regis) and AS Byatt’s Possession. Fossils have provided a rich seam for writers and film‑makers from Tennyson (an enthusiastic collector on the Isle of Wight) to Noel Streatfeild’s 1936 children’s classic Ballet Shoes starring the foundling Fossil sisters, to Steven Spielberg’s Jurassic Park blockbusters. Last year’s Jurassic World Reborn has been credited with contributing to the recent collecting boom.

Fossils and dinosaurs are a source of childhood wonder. These long-dead specimens speak to us across millions of years. But they also hold important clues to the future, recording changing ecosystems, climate and biodiversity, providing vital evidence in the environmental emergency.

Without private hunters, many of these discoveries would not be made, especially in rapidly eroding landscapes like the Jurassic Coast. These collections are better in a museum, even if it is abroad. And the UK has no shortage of fossils from other countries. But measures to protect them are overdue. Important fossils should not be allowed to disappear into the collections of the super-rich. They should be accessible for scientists to study and the public to enjoy for hundreds of years to come. They are national treasures and deserve to be treated as such.

David Harbour has blown Tony Stark’s cover in Avengers: Doomsday. It might just be what Marvel needs

The Guardian Fri, 21 Aug 2026 15:37:53 GMT

The actor, who plays Red Guardian in the film, made a cryptic comment to Variety that raised more Robert Downey Jr-shaped questions than answers. But was it a clanger, or expert trolling?

Nobody knows exactly what solemn blood oaths Marvel uses to prevent spoilers. But we do know that Andrew Garfield spent most of the run-up to 2021’s Spider-Man: No Way Home – in which he would eventually turn up as one of two secret Spideys – behaving as if Kevin Feige was standing behind him, holding up a giant card saying: YOU HAVE NEVER MET TOBEY MAGUIRE. So we can imagine it’s pretty full on. Why, then, has Avengers: Doomsday star David Harbour this week apparently blurted out the biggest Marvel secret since Ben Kingsley’s Mandarin in Iron Man 3?

Invited by Variety magazine to offer up a line from Doomsday “completely out of context”, Harbour thought for a moment, adopted the Russian accent of his Red Guardian character and came out with: “You … are Tony Stark.” Which is quite a thing to say about a film whose entire marketing campaign so far has depended on us accepting that Iron Man remains dead, and that the actor who used to play him, Robert Downey Jr, is playing Victor von Doom instead.

So what’s going on? The simplest and most likely explanation is that Harbour is trolling us, that Stark is not in the movie at all, and we’re all just fools. The new trailer for Doomsday, premiered last weekend at Disney’s D23 event in Anaheim, leans heavily into the prevailing wisdom that the film’s villain will be the tyrannical, unstoppable baddie of spurious eastern European extraction that Stan Lee and Jack Kirby dreamed up in 1962.

We even get to hear more of Doom’s heavily accented voice, and there is no suggestion that it belongs to anyone but Downey Jr beneath the mask. The footage talks repeatedly about “Victor”, hints at the supervillain’s tragic history and seems determined to establish him as a fully fledged character in his own right. If Marvel is planning a rug-pull here, it is certainly doing an impressively thorough job.

Not that this has stopped anyone. Some fans have already noticed that one closeup of the masked villain in the new footage appears to show a pair of blue eyes, rather than Downey Jr’s brown ones. Others noticed that the costume Marvel displayed at D23, on mannequins, was subtly different from the version shown at San Diego Comic-Con in July. From this slender collection of ocular and tailoring evidence has emerged the theory that there may actually be two incarnations of the character: Downey Jr’s version, perhaps initially presented as an ally; and a nastier variant who eventually replaces or kills him.

Naturally, because Cillian Murphy has blue eyes and has spent years being fancast as Victor von Doom, the internet has decided that the second man behind the mask must therefore be Cillian Murphy. If it’s correct, this may be the first big Hollywood casting decision achieved entirely through collective wishful thinking – at least since Marvel rewarded years of online fancasting by briefly turning John Krasinski into a variant Reed Richards in Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness.

The irony is that Harbour’s line sounds plausible because Marvel has spent the past two years – ever since Downey Jr was unveiled beneath Doom’s mask at San Diego Comic-Con – slyly hinting that if you watch the next two Avengers films, you may just find out what the hell is going on. Now it has to actually make good on that promise, even though this is a universe in which umpteen superheroes (and enough filmgoers to rack up the best part of $3bn at the global box office) watched Stark save all existence by snapping his fingers and expiring in front of them in Avengers: Endgame.

Perhaps Harbour’s line is genuine, and it is only our interpretation of it that is wrong. Red Guardian is hardly the MCU’s leading authority on interdimensional metaphysics: confronted by a man with Stark’s face, “You are Tony Stark” would be a perfectly reasonable thing for Alexei to say even if the answer is simply: “No, actually, I’m Victor von Doom.” This would allow Marvel to acknowledge the elephant in the room without turning its new villain into Iron Man gone bad, and still leave Downey Jr free to be exactly who the studio keeps insisting he is.

Either way, the genuinely strange possibility now seems to be that Downey Jr’s return really does have absolutely nothing to do with Tony Stark. And yet, you do not bring back the actor who spent 11 years as the face of the MCU, put another metal mask over that same face and then expect audiences to regard the resemblance as an administrative coincidence. Harbour may have leaked the biggest secret in Doomsday, or he may simply have made up the most obvious line imaginable for a laugh.

Neutrogena responds to criticism over how brand deal with Hayden Panettiere ended

The beauty brand Neutrogena has acknowledged making its former ambassador Hayden Panettiere “feel unsupported during a very difficult time” – alluding to when the late Hollywood actor said the company severed ties with her after she spoke about enduring postpartum depression (PPD).

Neutrogena issued a statement addressing the situation four days after Panettiere, 36, was found dead on Sunday at an apartment complex in Greenville, South Carolina.

The aftermath of the Heroes and Nashville star’s unexpected death had seen her fans circulate a podcast interview from May in which she recounted how Neutrogena cut off its relationship with her after she had detailed her experiences with PPD.

Some of her supporters also published comments criticizing Neutrogena on social media, including calls to boycott the brand over its treatment of Panettiere, who is seen by many as only the latest victim of an industry with a history of letting its younger stars down.

Neutrogena’s statement on Thursday then said it was “deeply saddened by Hayden Panettiere’s passing” and referred to her as a “valued member of our … community” after she was affiliated with the company for a decade beginning in 2005.

“We are proud to have partnered with her and understand that we made her feel unsupported during this difficult time,” Neutrogena’s statement continued. “This is not what Neutrogena stands for or who we want to be.”

The skincare products manufacturer did not elaborate. But in an interview three months earlier with podcaster Jay Shetty, Panettiere explained how she had once made impromptu remarks about having faced PPD during a live interview in 2015 with talkshow hosts Kelly Ripa and Michael Strahan.

“When they tell you about postpartum depression, you think about – ‘OK, I feel negative feelings towards my child. I want to injure my child. I want to hurt my child,’” Panettiere said back then. “I’ve never, ever had those feelings. But you … don’t realize [how] broad of a spectrum you can really experience that on, and it’s something I think that needs to be talked about. And women need to know that they’re not alone.”

She later learned that “Neutrogena wanted to fire me over that”, she said to Shetty.

“I had no intention of or plan to talk about postpartum depression,” Panettiere said. “It just came up, and I was just being honest. And never for a second did I think that anyone – or care that anyone – would have a bad reaction to it. It was my truth.”

Panettiere added: “I had the morals clauses. They caught absolutely everything. And of all the things … that they would fire me over, this was the last thing that I thought they would ever fire me over.”

She said her representative “saved the day that year” by replying to Neutrogena with something to the effect of: “That’s illegal. You can’t do that.” Nonetheless, Panettiere said Neutrogena declined to renew her contract when it expired.

“I had worked with these people for 10 years,” Panettiere recalled to Shetty. “And I remember not hearing a word from anybody.

“Not a ‘great working with you for 10 years’. Not a nice … ‘hope you’re good. We wish you well.’ And I remember that really breaking my heart.”

In her memoir, This Is Me, which also came out in May, Panettiere documented scars from a full-time acting career that began when she was five, preceding alcohol addiction and mental health struggles.

The book said she grappled with PPD after the birth in 2014 of her daughter, Kaya, with then lineal heavyweight boxing champion Wladimir Klitschko, Panettiere’s fiance at the time. Kaya, who is now 11, began living with Klitschko full-time in his native Ukraine when she was two.

PPD can affect up to 14% of people who give birth, according to the Cleveland Clinic. The clinic says PPD can be characterized by “feeling sad, worthless, hopeless or guilty” or “worrying excessively or feeling on edge”, among other symptoms.

“You may also feel that you can’t care for your baby or for yourself,” according to the Cleveland Clinic.

Panettiere, who entered rehab in 2015 while filming Nashville, told Shetty: “I think there’s been this very common misconception that I just gave up my child. That could not be farther from the truth.”

The Greenville coroner’s office completed an autopsy of Panettiere on Monday. The agency said her cause of death was pending further investigation. She would have turned 37 on Friday.

Neutrogena, meanwhile, said it initially waited on releasing its statement about Panettiere “out of respect for Hayden’s family and loved ones”.

Without elaborating, Neutrogena also promised to make “a significant investment to a longstanding community health partner to help give more women access to the support they need, including care for postpartum depression”.

“Hayden’s courage in sharing her challenges helped inspire important conversations and awareness,” the company said.

Britain, Australia and Canada have called the decision of the Israeli military authorities not to open a criminal investigation into the April 2024 airstrikes that hit a convoy of aid vehicles in Gaza “shameful”. The strikes killed seven humanitarian workers from the US-based World Central Kitchen (WCK) organisation.

WCK staff from the three countries were among the casualties of the attack, which prompted global outrage.

“This decision is both too little, and too late. The victims of this incident and their families deserve justice and accountability, and we will continue to seek answers on their behalf. The World Central Kitchen attack is one of countless incidents in Gaza where there has been no accountability,” the countries’ joint statement said.

It continued: “In Gaza, humanitarian workers continue to work tirelessly to support civilians in desperate need, risking their lives whilst working in the most perilous conditions. Yet despite the fragile ceasefire, Gaza remains the deadliest place to deliver aid, with 186 humanitarian workers killed in 2025.”

On Thursday, Australia’s government expressed “outrage” over the decision, while relatives said that Zomi Frankcom, the Australian among those killed, deserved more than an “internal, opaque process that ends with a short statement by the Israeli military absolving their soldiers of criminal wrongdoing.”

Israel’s ambassador to Australia, Hillel Newman, defended the decision.

The Polish government said on Thursday it was “very disappointed” and called for Israeli authorities to cooperate with Polish investigations into the incident. Damian Soból, a volunteer from Przemyśl, was also among the casualties.

In London, the Foreign Office said the UK was “appalled and angry” for the families of John Chapman, James Henderson and James Kirby, three British citizens who were killed in the attack.

WCK, which distributed food in Gaza throughout the war, said immediately after the lethal attack that it had coordinated with the military over the movement of its cars, which had the group’s logo on their roofs visible from the air.

“There has never been any excuse or justification for the attacks, and there is nothing in this account that does so. The decision is inconsistent with the full truth and deeply offensive,” it said in a statement.

The IDF said on Wednesday that it had mistaken several individuals in the vehicles for armed Hamas military operatives, and that the WCK convoy had deviated from the previously coordinated route. But it concluded that “the decisions of the commanders did not raise reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct”. Two officers were removed from their positions at the time and three others reprimanded.

One of the officers who was dismissed had reportedly signed an open letter earlier that year calling for Gaza to be deprived of aid. Israel imposed strict restrictions on the entry of humanitarian assistance during the conflict in Gaza, where experts declared a famine in August 2025.

The Israeli military admitted on Wednesday that its troops had opened fire on a car carrying five-year-old Hind Rajab and six family members in Gaza in 2024, saying it had ordered a criminal investigation into the killing, as well as into the fatal shooting of 15 paramedics in 2025.

Hind Rajab died after a desperate three-hour phone call to the Palestinian Red Crescent on 29 January 2024 in which she pleaded for rescue. The family’s Kia Picanto car had been hit as they sought to flee a new Israeli offensive into Gaza City. All the other passengers were also killed.

The IDF repeatedly denied its troops had been in the area near the incident, but investigations by media and others found evidence that strongly suggested nearby Israeli tanks were responsible.

The IDF said that as part of the its obligations under international law and Israeli domestic law it examined “exceptional incidents that occurred during combat”, but experts said criminal misconduct investigations into Israeli troops over the killing of Palestinians very rarely lead to convictions.

Germany seeking to extradite suspect from Romania over guns it is feared could have been used ⁠in assassinations

Germany is seeking to extradite a suspect from Romania over the discovery of an underground stash of weapons in a forest near Berlin that German media reports have linked to Russian intelligence.

Two weeks after German authorities found a drone carrying explosives at Leipzig airport, the interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, confirmed federal prosecutors had opened an investigation related to the secret cache of guns “on suspicion of preparing a serious act of violence that threatens national security”.

“This case demonstrates that ‌we are operating under a high threat level,” he told reporters. As with the Leipzig incident, Dobrindt said he could not rule out the involvement of “foreign powers”.

Earlier, local media had reported that German authorities had unearthed two handguns and ammunition about a year ago in a wooded area outside the German capital after agents of the domestic intelligence service received a tip.

The find has been the focus of covert investigations by state security and counterespionage services on suspicion Russian intelligence was plotting assassinations on German soil, according to separate reports by Der Spiegel magazine and an investigative team led by Süddeutsche Zeitung.

Rather than removing the arms, German authorities left them on site after rendering them unusable in the hope they would lead to clues during a months-long electronic surveillance operation, Dobrindt said.

No one was observed trying to collect the weapons, leading investigators to believe the agent or agents had learned of the cache’s discovery and it was now “dead”.

Dobrindt described the suspect in Romania, whose nationality was not disclosed, as a “low-level agent” and noted several other such operatives had ‌been detained so far this year.

Although the investigation into the Berlin stash has been long-running, the revelations apparently led Dobrindt to hastily call the news conference on Friday.

Sinan Selen, the head of the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution, Germany’s domestic intelligence agency, has warned for months of more aggressive tactics by Russian secret services, including plans for targeted attacks on German soil.

Moscow’s potential hit list is believed to include weapons contractor executives, opposition figures in exile and other prominent Ukraine supporters, according to the report by Süddeutsche and the public broadcasters NDR and WDR.

The federal prosecutor’s office and the Russian embassy declined to comment. A BfV spokesperson said: “As a matter of principle, we don’t comment on matters relating to any specific intelligence activities.”

Spiegel said German authorities were looking into possible links between the arms cache – a familiar Soviet tactic during the cold war – and a sabotage campaign against Ukrainian logistics routes blamed on Russia.

Last year Polish security officials arrested several people allegedly planning to mail parcels containing incendiary devices or detonators, some of them reportedly posted from Romania.

Investigators believe the packages could have been remotely ignited or set off using timers during transit to do serious damage to vehicles, cargo planes or logistics centres and spread fear in the EU.

In 2024, a firebomb in a parcel posted via DHL exploded in a freight container on the tarmac at Leipzig airport. Only a delayed flight kept it from going off in the air.

Ukraine has been using the facility in Leipzig as an alternate location for the transport of military goods since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, according to official records.

This month the German newspaper Die Zeit reported that Russian secret services were plotting an attack against Stefan Thumann, the head of German drone manufacturer Donaustahl.

The report said German investigators were tipped off by a foreign intelligence service at the end of last year and arrested a Ukrainian man and a Romanian woman this spring.

Thumann is said to be under police protection. The case recalled reports in 2024 that US intelligence services had foiled a Russian plot to assassinate the chief executive of Germany’s leading arms manufacturer, in an apparent attempt to retaliate over the company’s role in providing armaments for Ukraine.

The plan to murder Armin Papperger, the chief executive of Rheinmetall, was reportedly one of several Russian government schemes to kill defence industry executives in several countries in Europe that have been supporting Ukraine’s war effort. The plot against Papperger was believed to be the most advanced.

Russia has repeatedly denied any involvement in sabotage, disruption or intimidation against EU member states.

Palestine Action ‘Barclays five’ will not be sentenced as terrorists

The Guardian Fri, 21 Aug 2026 14:30:26 GMT

Activists who targeted bank in Burnley were found guilty in June of causing damage exceeding £200,000

Five Palestine Action activists who vandalised a Barclays branch in Burnley will not be sentenced as terrorists, a judge has ruled.

Dubbed the Barclays five, Brendon O’Hagan, 28; Amanda Kelly, 31; Hmeera Atiqnisar, 31; Mohammed Malik, 28; and Alma Yaniv, 70, were all found guilty in June of causing damage exceeding £200,000, after breaking windows and throwing red paint at a branch of Barclays Bank in Lancashire in August 2024.

The group targeted the site in protest at Barclays because it held shares in the Israeli weapons company Elbit Systems.

Judge Altham, the recorder of Preston, ruled on Friday that while the damage was substantial, it was not of the size of other attacks or against a sensitive property, such as an arms company, as has happened in previous Palestine Action incidents, and thus did not meet the high threshold for a terrorist sentencing.

All five will still be sentenced next month for criminal damage, but will face shorter jail terms as a result of the ruling.

After the five activists were found guilty in June, the trial judge, Philip Parry, told the prosecution and the defence he intended to consider a “terrorist connection” to the offending. It is understood this was a result of new information coming to light during the trial.

Neither the five activists nor the jury that found them guilty of criminal charges were aware that the case would be considered as terrorism until after they were found guilty.

During the hearings that took place at Preston crown court on Friday, legal representatives for the activists stated that four of them, excluding Yaniv, had admitted to being members of Palestine Action during the trial, but that this was irrelevant, because Palestine Action was not proscribed as a terrorist group until a year after the act of vandalism.

In a statement put out by the five after the ruling, the group said they were “extremely relieved that the court has seen sense” but said a terrorism sentencing “should never have been an option” and accused the state of “attempting to equate property damage to the Israeli war machine with terrorism”.

They said: “A terrorism sentence would not only aggravate our sentence significantly, it would mean we would be imprisoned as terrorists and subject to notification requirements for 15-plus years upon release. Those requirements include notifying police of any new address, bank account, phone number, email address, relationship and more. If we failed to do so, even by accident, we would face an additional five years in prison.

“The proscription of Palestine Action, the arrests of over 3,500 people under the Terrorism Act for holding signs and the sentencing of direct action activists as terrorists, are all tools being used by the state to protect the Israeli weapons industry and continue its role in the ongoing genocide in Gaza.

“The use of counter-terror powers against direct action for Palestine came after extensive lobbying by the Israeli government, Elbit Systems, pro-Israel lobby groups and politicians with vested interests.”

It was reported in October 2024 that Barclays had sold all its Elbit shares. The bank had previously said it held them only in relation to client-driven transactions, being neither an investor nor shareholder in the arms company.

Commenting on the ruling, Kerry Moscogiuri, the chief executive of Amnesty International UK, said: “The fact that the defendants in today’s case were not sentenced as terrorists is welcome. No one should be treated more harshly under the law because their crimes were part of a protest against genocide or any other issue, and the misuse of terrorism powers in this way should never have even been considered.

“We now need to see the proscription against Palestine Action lifted and an end to the misuse of sweeping counter-terror powers against direct action protesters. The government should begin the process of reversing the years of attacks on our right to protest, one of the most effective tools we have to hold our leaders to account.”

A party, 101 princesses and an eccentric millionaire: Jon Ronson on a mysterious castle – and what it taught him about masculinity in crisis

The Guardian Fri, 21 Aug 2026 14:00:37 GMT

When my son texted me from a Connecticut fortress in the middle of the night with an alarming message, it set me on a quest to understand the bizarre lifestyle of its owner

I awoke one morning in the summer of 2023 to discover that, while I’d slept, my son Joel had been texting my wife and me a series of unnerving messages about a perilous situation he had found himself in, in Connecticut.

From what I could tell, as I frantically tried to piece together the night’s events, one of Joel’s friends had been invited to a party being held by a stranger she’d met that week on Tinder. So Joel and two others went along for the ride. But when they arrived, they found the man’s home so bizarre that Joel did something he’d never done before – he sent me the coordinates of his location and a photograph, just in case.

The photograph was of a vast medieval castle with a drawbridge, gargoyles and many – I couldn’t shake the sense that there were too many – spires, towers and turrets, reaching like skeletal fingers to the looming clouds above.

“I honestly have no clue what is going on,” read Joel’s second text. “This is very weird.” Then: “You drive down a road in the middle of a forest and then there’s this gate and it’s just a huge, massive castle.”

It was a few days later and Joel and his friends were sitting in my office, recounting for me the disquieting events that had occurred that night. It began with an invitation to one of Joel’s female friends: “Castle party Saturday! 3:00pm to whenever. Dress code: Formal. Tell your friends. 18+ to come, 21+ to drink.”

It was a three-hour drive from New York City to the pleasant town of Woodstock, Connecticut (160 miles from the more famous Woodstock, New York, of festival fame). Then their GPS took them out of town, on to a winding forest road, and finally to a set of imposing iron gates. They stared at the menacing castle that loomed beyond, urgently discussed turning around, but then the gates swung open and they found themselves entering.

Standing on the drawbridge were a man, a woman and a large black dog. The man was the castle’s owner, Chris Mark. He was in his early 60s.

“He had sharp blue eyes,” Joel’s friend Delaney said, “but glazed over.”

“And he had a cut above one of his eyes,” said Joel.

The dog was called Cerberus, named after the multi‑headed hound that guards the gates of Hades. The woman was blond and much younger.

Mark beckoned them inside. They crossed the drawbridge and entered the grand banqueting hall to discover … there was no party. The room was completely empty, all except for a small number of equally bewildered young people standing around awkwardly.

“I’m sorry, but where’s the party?” someone asked.

“Oh no,” Mark replied. “I’ve invited you here for a different reason.” The room fell silent.

“Which is?” someone asked.

“I’d like you all to take part in my reality show,” Mark replied.

“What’s the name of your reality show?” Joel asked.

“101 Princesses,” he replied.

“What’s the core concept?” Joel asked.

“I’m the lord,” Mark replied. “I’m looking for my queen and I’ve got 101 princesses to choose from.”

He turned to Joel’s female friends. “Are you ready to get into your princess costumes? Come downstairs to my costume room.”

Which they did.

I found this part of their story especially melancholy, that these young people were prepared to follow him to the bowels of his castle to dress as princesses.

Mark’s costume room was located near his hot tub grotto room, which doubled as his botanical gardens. Whirlpool baths nestled among subterranean plants illuminated by purple lamps. In the next room was his pole-dancing nightclub. There were mannequins and, one of Joel’s female friends said, “a whole collection of extravagant princess attire, racks of medieval gowns and a glass display case of tiaras. He told me to choose a dress and pick a tiara to match.”

Mark seemed far more interested in the young women than in Joel and his male friend Cement, but he gave them tuxedos to change into all the same.

After the women re-emerged, wearing princess outfits and tiaras, a videographer appeared. They were assured that while 101 Princesses hadn’t yet been set up with a network, it would end up on Netflix. Then filming began. Mark walked in and a woman who apparently lived at the castle curtseyed and said: “Yes, my lord?”

Yet Mark seemed increasingly on edge, irritated that Joel and his friends were observing rather than participating in 101 Princesses.

(It isn’t entirely clear what participating would have entailed. But they were told it was “a collaborative project” and the makers would be open to ideas. Joel later surmised that along with dance skits and other castle-themed vignettes, the princesses would have been encouraged to make out with each other on camera, while Joel and Cement would have appeared in scenes in which they were rejected by the princesses in favour of Mark.)

Finally, seemingly exasperated by their lack of interest, Mark sent his videographer to inform them that: “Chris wants everyone to leave. Everyone has to leave now.” And that was the end of their story. I stood up to thank them for telling it to me, then I let out a scream.

In terms of them finding themselves in unsettling situations with older men, Joel and his friends were, I have to admit, somewhat out of the frying pan and into the fire. Six days earlier, I had been in surgery, having a foot of my colon removed due to diverticulitis. I was still in pain, which was causing me to let out sudden, unexpected shrieks.

I’d been recuperating partly by sitting on park benches, staring out at nothing, trying to think up ideas for stories. But after about 10 minutes, I’d invariably find myself overwhelmed by a dreadful thought: I’m just a man sitting on a bench. It’s a terrible feeling, that sense of purposelessness, which is why I spent the following days not sensibly convalescing but instead learning whatever I could about Mark and his castle.

The castle, although you’d never know it from the photographs, is newly built. Construction began in 2003 and was completed in 2010. Mark’s money was inherited. His great-grandfather Clayton had been a gilded age steel tycoon – the owner of the Clayton Mark & Company.

Back during construction, when rumours were circulating around Woodstock that a wealthy scion was building an ostentatious castle on the edge of town, journalists managed to unearth fragments of strange stories about the place. Like how it had been claimed during Mark’s 2010 divorce hearing that one of the couple’s pet camels had starved to death due to neglect. Mark blamed his estranged wife; she blamed him – but given that camels can last for several months without food, that sounded like a lot of neglect.

Sixteen days after my surgery, I drove three hours to Mark’s castle. Each time my car hit a bump it tore at the still-raw scar, causing me to yell out. Still, I had no regrets. I was embarking on a story, one that had crashed into my life unannounced. It’s always nerve-racking to be driving into the unknown – and this journey did feel like it might be dangerous – but the sense of purpose I get from following strange stories like this is more powerful than any painkiller.

Mark was waiting for me on his drawbridge. He knew I was coming. I’d texted him to say I was a nonfiction writer and that “my son and his friends were invited to take part in 101 Princesses, and they told me about the extraordinary world you’ve created for yourself at the castle. I’d love to come and write about it.”

“OK,” he’d replied.

He beckoned me inside. I passed an Egyptian sarcophagus and a suit of armour, its helmet tilted forlornly towards the ground. Perhaps because of my proximity to these privately owned relics of war and death, I found myself brooding over my surgery; how while under anaesthetic I must have resembled, for a moment at least, a medieval drawing of a heretic being tortured, intestines spilling out – a drawing that wouldn’t have looked out of place inside this remarkable but disquieting castle.

Guarding this great fortress had clearly gone to Cerberus’s head, because he repeatedly lurched at me and bit my foot – too hard to be considered playful, not hard enough to be deemed an assault.

“Hey, pal,” I said tentatively. And, “Hey, buddy.” Finally, I tried to engage Mark. “Your dog does like biting my foot,” I said.

“For some reason it’s not a negative thing,” he replied. “It means he likes you or something.”

“Oh, OK,” I said.

“How do you convince people to visit the castle and take part in 101 Princesses?” I asked him.

“I go on dating apps,” he replied, “and I make some kind of relationship. Then I have them come here and I adapt them to this lifestyle.”

I asked how he “adapts them”, and he explained that some of them have never had sex with other women so he has to coax them into trying it: “I always thought it would be amazing if I had living here six, eight girls, but the only way it works is if the girls love girls. That’s how the princessing works.”

“Princessing?” I thought.

“We go out and find more girls,” Mark continued, “because they’re looking for themselves. And I just benefit from it.”

So it was fortunate, he said, that once he brings them round to the idea of sex with other women, “they actually really like it”.

I noticed several young women padding silently around in the darkness. Some looked away when they saw me glancing in their direction; others eyed me with suspicion.

I continued to pepper him with questions about his life inside the castle. Eventually, it evidently dawned on him that he was saying unwise things to a journalist, because he suddenly stood up, walked to a kitchen drawer and retrieved a document from a pile of identical documents. It was a non-disclosure agreement.

“I need you to sign,” he said.

“I don’t feel comfortable signing an NDA,” I said.

He looked sharply at me. But he relented. He put the paperwork back in the drawer. But the atmosphere had changed, and soon afterwards I thanked him for allowing me to visit and left.

I had many questions. For instance: who comes up with a word like “princessing”? Also, why was he trying to control me with an NDA? Moreover, why did he have a whole pile of NDAs? Who else was he asking to sign them, and why?

Several weeks later, I was driving Joel from upstate New York to Manhattan when Mark began sending me a series of texts – 42 of them during the three‑hour journey. I asked Joel to read them out to me. He picked up my phone, his eyes darting, and read out an increasingly disturbing sample.

“I’m meeting with my lawyers tonight,” he read. “I’ll spend whatever it takes to protect my family. I’m having the largest international investigation company learn everything about you. I want to get to know you really well.”

I flinched. The car swerved.

There were more pings. This time, as Joel looked at the texts, I saw his eyes widen in shock.

“What?” I asked.

“I’m going to be sending you some of my friends that were in prison for killing somebody,” Joel read. “Maybe you could help them write something good so they can turn their lives around … One of my good friends who got out of prison is on his way to New York today … Do not ever mention anything negative about the castle because this guy will get really upset. He thinks I’m like a god, and you don’t want to see him angry. He just got out of jail like a week ago and has been in there for, like, 15 years … To be honest, I’m even a little bit afraid of some of these people … Carlos and Brandon are on their way to New York right now.”

Joel fell silent. “Meet them,” he said.

“You want me to meet Carlos and Brandon?” I said.

“Yes,” he said. “But take security with you. Take five security guards.”

“I’m not going to take five security guards to meet Carlos and Brandon,” I said. “You want me to escalate this to gang warfare?”

Joel looked frustrated by my reluctance to hit back harder, but the truth was those last texts had brightened my mood. Libel courts surely don’t respond well to plaintiffs threatening journalists with visits from murderers – especially not when the threats were read out to the journalist by his own son, who was arguably emotionally harmed by them.

“Yes,” I thought. “This is good.”

Mark’s volley of texts continued. I was surprised by how uninhibited they were. He was saying the worst things he could think of: “Everything is a mirror. You destroy someone and someone destroys you.” But he’d intersperse these ominous messages with positive character references from friends and colleagues: “I am Shaolin kung fu grandmaster Tyrone Bullock. Chris Mark is an amazing and remarkable person with such a wonderful heart.”

The only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.

after newsletter promotion

To be honest, I felt the threats were rendering the character references somewhat redundant, but on rereading the messages I was pleased to notice him dialling back the eeriness regarding Carlos and Brandon, even offering to cover my costs.

“If you take my murder friends out,” he texted, “I’ll Venmo you the money.”

The next day, I received an email out of the blue:

Hi Jon,

I am a friend and advisor to Chris Mark and handle a number of business matters for him. Somehow, someway, you really got under his skin and it’s driving him crazy … I’d love for some feedback so I can get a sense of what is happening. Thanks, Charles Cady

Eleven days later, I sat on Cady’s terrace, overlooking his woodland and stream, five miles from Mark’s castle. He was in his late 60s, and with his kindly demeanour he reminded me of a favourite grandfather from a Frank Capra film.

“Chris and I were doing 15, 20 phone calls and texts a day about you,” he told me.

“Oh God,” I said. “He says he has two murderers on his staff?”

Cady chuckled.

“I assume those people don’t exist,” I said.

“They do exist,” he said.

But he assured me Mark was “completely harmless”, and that he only had ex-convicts on his staff to give them a second chance in life.

But I must have hit a nerve, because at the end of our two-hour conversation, Cady glanced out over his quiet, rolling land and suddenly said: “If I suspected in the least there was something creepy going on, I’d drop it like a hot potato. I have no desire to see a police car pull into the yard. I don’t have any room for that in my world.”

Before Joel and his friends were kicked out that night, they’d swapped numbers with two other young women who’d arrived under similar pretences. Now, I was on the phone to one of them. I’ll call her Ari. She filled me in on what had happened next – how they’d all piled into Mark’s Rolls-Royce to go clubbing in Boston, and how Mark kept “asking if we’d be down to film a shower scene or a hot tub scene with a bunch of women. At that point we figured maybe this wasn’t actually a Netflix show.”

“By the way,” I asked her, “did he ever happen to mention Hugh Hefner to you?”

“Yes!” she exclaimed. “He said how much he loved Playboy, and that 101 Princesses was based on the whole Playboy situation. He said Hugh Hefner was one of his idols.”

It struck me that Mark was trying to be Hugh Hefner during surely the worst period in human history to be Hugh Hefner. Unless you’re the creme de la creme of manosphere influencers, you can’t lord it over princesses in your castle like it’s the 1970s any more.

And so, despite there being nothing immediately relatable about his story, being a tale about the complexities of luring women to your castle in the post‑#MeToo age, I could see a resonance. It was a story about men out of time, men failing to adjust to a world that was moving away from them. The world had changed shape and all kinds of men were discovering there were things they’d once done that they couldn’t do any more.

Mark’s situation was, of course, bizarre and extreme. He had the resources to construct a fantasy bubble within which he could pretend his lifestyle wasn’t dated and weird and damaging, but aspirational. However, I was picturing less empowered and more sympathetic men than him – men who used to derive structure and meaning from, say, office or factory life, and were now struggling to adjust to a society that had reorganised itself without them in such a central position.

Some were instead scratching a living as YouTubers, “personal brands”, content creators with no job protections, while others were withdrawing, folding in on themselves. There’s data to prove it. By 2022, one in six US men aged between 25 and 54 wasn’t working. But within that statistic was a more startling one: two‑thirds of those men weren’t even looking for jobs. That’s 6.7 million US men, and countless more around the world, who’ve just … bowed out.

I was aghast. Why had those men opted out of society? What havoc was that purposelessness wreaking on their inner lives, and on the lives of their loved ones – partners, parents, children? And given that some of them would inevitably grow sick of a life in the shadows – of a life of male nothingness – what might happen next?

While many traditionally male sectors, such as factory work, are dying, I’ve noticed one role for men that’s flourishing: actors who can play doofuses in television ads. Modern TV commercials, certainly, are an orgy of male buffoonery, of men who can’t do anything right and have to be constantly bailed out by their exasperated wives. I’ve watched men falling off lawnmowers, driving off cliffs (1st for Women insurance), accidentally abandoning their babies on restaurant conveyer belts (Philadelphia cream cheese) and being terrible at sex (Domino’s pizza).

“Hey, honey,” says the man in the Domino’s ad, “the Domino’s lady just said we’ve got 30 minutes. Are you thinking what I’m thinking?”

His partner looks at him. “What are we going to do with the other 28 minutes?” she says.

I wondered about the actors who play the doofuses. Are there particular go-to men who invariably snag the parts? I messaged the veteran casting director Zita Zutic Konak, and she emailed back: “Hi Jon, meet Ed – a wonderful actor who we’ve cast in these types of roles previously.”

Ed has played a man in a Specsavers ad who misses his plane because everything goes wrong at the airport due to his own ineptitude and the general frustrations of modernity. He can’t scan his boarding pass. The barcode won’t work. He refuses to give up his water at security so he guzzles it down, drenching his Hawaiian shirt. He loses his hand luggage on the moving walkway. He can’t find the gate. The ad ends with his wife, who’s already through security, looking long-suffering and irritated.

“I did one for Scholl insoles where I had to gallop like a horse,” Ed said. “I’m a regular guy walking to work, but then I put on these really comfortable insoles and I start galloping like a horse down the street. I had to look quite doofusy for that.”

“Fifty years ago,” I said, “there was the Marlboro man being stoical and masculine on a horse, whereas nowadays you have to be the horse.”

“Yeah,” said Ed. He thought about it. “But when you look at those old ads, do you relate to those men on any level?”

“You’re right,” I said. “I don’t relate to the Marlboro Man at all. I relate far more to the man who can’t make it through the airport.”

As the old structures collapse – across both office and factory life – men who feel cut adrift have had no shortage of advice about how to re-anchor themselves. Some men’s health influencers advocate stoicism, while others encourage the opposite: vulnerability, that “once we finally reveal what’s under our ‘manly masks’ we can start to live authentically”.

Then there’s all those doofus men blundering around the culture. Clearly, all this reimagining of what it means to be “male” has been disorienting or irritating for some men, leaving them feeling tossed around in a sea of conflicting ideologies about what being a man actually means.

Perhaps that’s in part why yet another male archetype has emerged – the Manosphere Man.

Take influencer and virulent antisemite Dan Bilzerian, whose 28.7 million Instagram followers get to watch him sit on thrones next to lions, walk through forests with assault rifles, and dine on private yachts with near-naked women and, in his pre‑incarceration days, with Andrew Tate.

“I had sex nine times in one day. I was so proud of myself,” he told Joe Rogan in 2016, sounding a lot like Mark. And “I couldn’t fuck all the girls if I had five dicks … I’m not bragging.”

“I salute you, sir,” Rogan said at one point. “You’re living a life that doesn’t even seem real.”

Several months had passed since I’d been in contact with Mark. Finally, though, my curiosity got the better of me and I texted him: “How are things at the castle?” “Everything at the castle’s good,” he replied. He was working on new reality show proposals. He sent me one. It was called Queen to Fraud, and, per its synopsis, it would document Mark’s “battle for justice against Anya and Sasha [not their real names], two women who manipulated his wealth and engaged in deception on a massive scale. Tagline: She was supposed to be the queen. But she became the queen of fraud.”

Both Anya and Sasha had, at one time or another, lived at the castle. Mark had already told me about Anya – how she’d reported him to the police for trying to throw her into his moat, “but they looked at my surveillance videos and saw she was lying”.

I didn’t know Sasha, but the Queen to Fraud pitch document outlined his complaints against her – how he’d showered her with “endless luxuries”, but then she was disloyal to him in Bangkok. Episode three, “Betrayal in Thailand”, would recreate “the shocking moment Sasha disappears to buy drugs, leaving Christopher stranded and sick”. But by episode 10, “The Maximum Sentence”, he’d get his restitution. He’d collaborate “with law enforcement to ensure the harshest penalties” for the women’s treacheries.

I suppose that answered my question about how things were going – evidently, not well. In the short time I’d known Mark he’d gone from developing a reality show where he’d meet and woo his queen to one where he’d have her imprisoned – a similar arc, it struck me, as Henry VIII’s.

He sent me ChatGPT’s assessment of Queen to Fraud. It called it “the most compelling entertainment project ever created”.

“AI likes you a lot!” I texted him.

“That’s who I talk to most of my time,” he replied.

We continued to correspond and I met him in Fort Lauderdale, in the lobby of a beachfront hotel called Ocean Manor. He was in Florida, he said, because he was planning to build another castle and was scouting for locations. There, he outlined for me another new plan – to construct in his Connecticut castle’s grounds an orphanage called Ark of Light.

“Is Charles helping you out with this?” I asked. Mark shook his head. “I don’t know what happened to him,” he replied, looking genuinely baffled. “We talked almost every day up until a few weeks ago.”

Cady – Mark’s friend, spokesman and business adviser for 20 years – was suddenly no longer returning his calls? It had always been Cady’s job to handle Mark’s permit applications, on occasions when Mark had, for instance, tried to turn the castle into a bed and breakfast or a wedding venue. Now that the responsibility had presumably fallen to Mark, was he concerned that the town of Woodstock might not grant him a zone variance for a campus of orphaned prodigies?

He shrugged it off. “They’d look bad if they go against me,” he said.

This was Mark falling for ChatGPT’s sycophancy again. The chatbot had assured him that should Woodstock choose to “fight a billionaire humanitarian trying to help people, headlines would be brutal: Town of Woodstock opposes billionaire’s plan to feed millions.”

Mark’s devotion to ChatGPT was far from uncommon by this point. Millions were falling for its obsequiousness. It felt like a ripple from the downfall of the old structures. People fall apart, people become directionless, and the tech companies swoop in with new ways to monetise our feeling of purposelessness – our desire to be of use – by telling us we aren’t worthless. Far from it. We’re creating “the most compelling entertainment project ever”.

A breakup can be good news for a journalist, and so, after I left Florida, I messaged Cady to let him know I’d just interviewed Mark again.

“Lucky you, spending quality time with Chris,” he replied.

There was a distinct and, I thought, intriguing change in his tone. We arranged to meet. I arrived at the restaurant early. Cady was already there, looking grave, tapping his fingers on the table. I sat down. We ordered lunch. And then Cady told me the news.

Mark, he’d learned, was under investigation for a number of alleged sex-related crimes. It was at a federal level, with several agencies involved, including the Department of Homeland Security.

“My head exploded after I met with the feds,” Cady said. “I am angry and upset. And I started thinking, ‘Oh my God, what was I involved in as an unsuspecting individual?’ I feel incredibly, incredibly naive.”

At this time of writing, August 2026, the investigation into Mark is ongoing. Of course, an investigation is not evidence of criminal wrongdoing – and he has not been charged in the US. Maybe he never will be. I don’t know where Mark is. I’ve heard he’s abroad, perhaps in south‑east Asia. Maybe he’s anxious about returning to the US due to the police investigation, and the publication of my book, which tells the stories of many unravelling men, including him. But after I left Cady that day, I dug and dug and I finally feel I’ve learned the truth of what was really going on inside his castle.

I think that, like many men, Mark was trying to create a fantasy life within which he didn’t have to live or interact with other people except on his own terms. It’s a growing phenomenon – men responding to the collapse of the old structures, and a shift in power, by becoming like separatists, succumbing to uninhibited behaviour, trying to create false utopias where they can behave however they want. But it feels like the experiment is failing. As Mark is presumably learning, sometimes when you push boundaries, reality bites back.

When approached by the Guardian for comment on this article, Chris Mark said that Jon Ronson had “presented me and events involving me in a profoundly misleading manner”. In relation to 101 Princesses, Mark denied deliberately deceiving people into coming to the castle, adding that “the gathering related to a proposed creative project … that also had a genuine charitable purpose”. He added: “I strongly dispute any characterisation suggesting that I groomed, conditioned or manipulated women into sexual activity.” He denied that the text messages referencing Carlos and Brandon in any way constituted a genuine threat: “I did not intend to instruct anyone to physically harm Jon Ronson.” In reference to the allegation from his 2010 divorce hearing about mistreatment of a pet camel, he said: “I dispute any implication that I intentionally starved or neglected an animal.”

The Castle: Adventures in a World of Unravelling Men by Jon Ronson is published by Viking (£20). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop. com. Delivery charges may apply.

Ditch the giant handbag, don’t overdo the botox and 16 other ways to extend your ‘hotspan’

The Guardian Fri, 21 Aug 2026 14:00:36 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

If ‘lifespan’ is the time you’re alive and ‘healthspan’ the years you’re disease-free, then ‘hotspan’ is the period you’re attractive and vibrant. Want to increase yours? Experts share their tips

Forget 12-step skincare routines, red light therapy and injectables – the single most important thing you can do for your skin is wear UV protection. “Not just sun protection, but UV protection, every single day, regardless of weather or season,” says Dr Jennifer Owens, resident aesthetic expert at the Reborne Longevity clinic in London. “Up to 90% of visible skin ageing is caused by UV exposure – nothing else comes close in terms of impact.”

Beware the misguided logo, warns Guardian fashion columnist Jess Cartner-Morley: “Never, ever wear a sweatshirt or, worse, carry a basket with a slogan that includes the words ‘dance’ or ‘love’. Be cautious of words in French. These are the style equivalent of having a ‘Live, laugh, prosecco’ poster in your kitchen. Sorry, but you cannot buy youthful insouciance at M&S.”

Want to look instantly better without spending a penny? Standing up straight makes you look younger – and thinner – says Nick Finney, personal trainer to celebrities including Jennifer Lopez: “Our posture suffers with age, due to a combination of weakness, atrophying muscles and tightness. The solution is to strengthen all the muscles in your posterior chain [the rear of your body] while making sure that the muscles at the front have enough mobility to allow them to pull your back upright – tight pectorals will pull your shoulders forward.” Strengthen your posterior chain in the gym by perfecting Romanian deadlifts and horizontal rows.

People get hung up on wrinkles and middle-age spread, but dodgy teeth are far more ageing, says Sali Hughes, the Guardian Saturday magazine’s resident beauty expert: “Teeth that are discoloured, significantly crooked or even missing are very ageing and so, conversely, a well cared-for mouth can take years off.”

According to Ten Dental’s Dr Jenni Rawes: “As we age, enamel naturally wears down, revealing more of the dentine underneath, which is a darker, creamier colour. It’s also more porous than enamel, so absorbs staining from food and drink far more readily, making teeth look darker still over time. Brightening the smile has a huge effect on how youthful and well someone appears.” Rawes says that visiting the hygienist for a scale and polish, and whitening the teeth using custom-made at-home trays are the fastest, lowest-effort ways to upgrade your smile. Expect to pay about £375 for whitening.

Still operating on the presumption that a pressed outfit signals that you have your shi(r)t together? Keep up. “Youth culture treats ironing like a hobby from the 50s, which means creased natural fabrics have become the ultimate modern Prada-esque symbol of chicness,” says the Guardian’s fashion and lifestyle editor, Morwenna Ferrier. “Looking kempt means looking corporate.” Also: “Don’t tuck things in. Modern fashion is all about the drape.”

“Why are so many men of a certain age walking around wearing hideous chinos, which sag at the knee and taper at the ankle?” bemoans fashion consultant Simon Chilvers. “A pair of trousers in a flattering cut and decent fabric are the linchpin of great style as we age. Equally, a pair of well-made and well-kept shoes are central to the stylishness of any male wardrobe – and, yes, that can include sneakers, as long as they’re not too desperately trendy.”

Thought middle age comes with a compulsory mum cut? Think again. “Longer hair is absolutely not the preserve of the young,” says Hughes. “Healthy hair of any colour (including grey and silver) that falls at the shoulder and beyond actually looks brilliant and sexy on women over 50.”

Hairdresser George Northwood – whose clients include Alexa Chung, Gwyneth Paltrow and the Duchess of Sussex – agrees: “Hair condition and texture are more important than your age when thinking about your hairstyle. The important thing to consider is: ‘Does my hair look relevant?’, rather than subscribing to a particular length for your age, which feels a bit outdated.”

“Everyone fixates on lines and wrinkles, but uneven skin tone is more ageing,” says Owens. “It’s also more fixable – home care, UV protection and treatments like peels or microneedling can reverse existing sun damage. There’s decades of evidence behind microneedling as a technique.” A course of three sessions can boost collagen for months afterwards, and you can repeat that course once a year. “It’s one of the few treatments that’s genuinely within most people’s reach, and paired with good home care and daily UV protection, the results are transformative.”

“Get a smaller handbag,” commands Cartner-Morley. “Look around you: young people have really small bags. You can basically do everything with a phone now, after all. You don’t need to carry around a wad of second-class stamps. Nor do you need two packs of tissues or spare tights. Live life on the edge!”

“Ditch the wallet-style phone case – you know, the one with the flip cover,” says the Guardian’s deputy fashion and lifestyle editor, Chloe Mac Donnell. “Instead, buy a thin screen protector and a slim case. Casetify does fun collaborations if you’re into prints.”

Good news, men – you don’t have to ditch your favourite hoodie and jorts, post 40. “I personally don’t think that men have to dress according to their age,” says fashion commentator Derek Guy, AKA the menswear guy. “I like it when people break expectations, such as an older man who adopts youthful fashions. To me, seeing people use clothes to express themselves outside the narrow boundaries set by class, sexuality, gender and age is what makes fashion so rich and interesting.”

“Next season’s ‘visible boxer shorts’ look has the potential to come off as a wardrobe malfunction at a certain point in life,” cautions Chilvers.

What worked in the 90s may not land today. “I meet so many people who are wearing the same makeup they wore 15 or 20 years ago – when their lifestyle, budget, skin and tastes were very different,” says Hughes. “Swapping out a heavy matt foundation for a sheerer, glowier skin tint is a fast way to look modern and more confident, and switching a complicated, dated eyeshadow palette for one cream or liquid shadow and a liner looks instantly carefree and chic.”

Ferrier adds: “It’s not that a little flick or cat eye will age you, but it does betray you as someone born before 1990.”

There are no prizes for ageing naturally. “I don’t care whether people want Botox or not,” says Hughes. “There are many very valid reasons for not wanting to engage in ‘longevity treatments’, from the political to the financial. What I find baffling is that I’m asked every single day about other non-surgical treatments, from Juläine to Morpheus 8, by people that I know would find what they are looking for more quickly and more cheaply in Botox, but who – through some misplaced and wildly inconsistent guilt – can’t bear to be that person. Get it or don’t get it – but life is too short for such hand-wringing.”

“Overtreating with Botox is one of the most common mistakes I see,” says Owens. “As we age, brows naturally drop, and the frontalis is the only muscle doing the work of holding them up. Weaken it too much with Botox and it stops ‘exercising’ – it can atrophy, and brows drop lower, earlier than they otherwise would. That’s part of why heavily treated faces can end up looking older, not younger. Botox absolutely has a place, but restraint is what keeps it looking natural.”

In an Ozempic-obsessed world, it’s easier than ever to lose weight – but looking frail is ageing. “As we get older, our skin loses its tautness at the same time that our muscle mass declines,” says Finney. “This combination exacerbates the soft and baggy appearance people dislike.” Instead of worrying about losing weight, consider getting stronger through resistance training in the gym. “As your muscles strengthen they’ll push closer to the skin, causing a shrink-wrapped, more taut appearance.”

“If you’re going bald, just go bald,” advises Mac Donnell. “A shaved head will make you look more confident than a receding hairline. And it’s cheaper than a hair transplant.”

As for greys? According to Northwood, they can also be embraced. “I think men look great with silver hair,” he says. “I might bleach my hair for a statement, but I don’t think men should be trying to cover their greys – often it can end up with a red or khaki tone, which looks strange. As we age, our skin lightens and it looks washed out when men have a pale face and dark hair. It’s different for women, who dye their hair, as chances are they will also wear makeup.”

“Don’t bang on about ‘being old’,” says Mac Donnell. “Referring to yourself as ‘ancient’ when you’re 43 is an ick. You don’t hear Madonna doing it, and she’s a pensioner.”
