What is salmonella, how does it spread and are eggs safe to eat?

The Guardian Fri, 21 Aug 2026 13:46:05 GMT

UKHSA says imported eggs eaten in restaurants are source of outbreak that has infected more than 200 people

Contaminated eggs have infected 207 people with salmonella across the UK, killing one and hospitalising 34.

Eggs imported into Britain and eaten in cafes and restaurants were the source, the UK Health Security Agency has said. The outbreak has prompted public concern. But what is salmonella, and are eggs safe to eat?

“Salmonella isn’t a single ‘bug’ but the name we give to a whole group of bacteria that can cause infection in humans. There are over 2,500 different types of salmonella bacteria,” said Dr Malick Gibani, a clinical associate professor at Imperial College London.

Most disease in the UK is caused by just a few of those 2,500 types. They are usually found in contaminated animal products such as meat, dairy and eggs. But chocolate, peanut butter and cucumbers have also been at the centre of previous UK outbreaks.

Salmonella can be spread by contaminated drinking water, contact with animals, person-to-person spread or poor food hygiene and preparation, “particularly when cooked food comes into contact with contaminated and undercooked or raw foods”, said Gibani. Storing food poorly, which allows the bacteria to replicate, and not cooking contaminated foods thoroughly are also risks.

Salmonella causes an infection of the gut – gastroenteritis – and that leads to food poisoning. Symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhoea, vomiting and a fever, though some people also feel very tired and suffer sore muscles and joints. Symptoms can appear within a few hours to a few days.

Gibani said: “Salmonella can be unpleasant for a few days. In most cases, people will get better without any treatment, but in some instances antibiotics might be needed, particularly in vulnerable groups. Antibiotics are usually only needed when there’s a severe bloodstream infection, but thankfully this is pretty rare in healthy adults in the UK.”

Children and older adults, people whose immune systems are suppressed, perhaps because they are taking chemotherapy drugs for cancer, and those with underlying health conditions can be more severely affected.

Scientists aren’t sure why. But, Gibani said, the fact that such groups are hit more severely shows that “there’s definitely an immune component which influences severity”.

“In some people, instead of just causing an infection inside the gut, salmonella bacteria can spread into the blood, which can be very dangerous. When this happens it can cause a severe sepsis-like illness,” he said.

“We often consider salmonella as a disease with an ‘image problem’. It can be dismissed as ‘just food poisoning’ and a bit of diarrhoea. But severe and invasive cases kill thousands of people a year around the world.”

Severe infection is a big problem in parts of sub-Saharan Africa, which has high rates of salmonella bloodstream infections, including in children who have recently had malaria, are malnourished or have advanced or untreated HIV.

No. But you should choose the eggs you buy carefully, experts say.

Kimberly Coffin, the technical director of supply chain assurance at LRQA, a global risk management firm based in Birmingham, said: “The safest choice for consumers is to buy eggs produced in the UK which carry the red lion mark. These eggs come from hens that have been vaccinated against salmonella.”

She offered other tips to avoid catching salmonella. “Cooking eggs and egg-containing dishes until both yolk and white are firm, or to a temperature of 71C, is the best way to provide consumer safety from salmonella.

“It’s also important not to use any cracked or broken eggs, nor eggs that have external evidence of wet or dry residues due to the potential for ingress of potential microbiological contaminates on the surface into the egg. Washing dirty eggs before use does not reduce this risk and, in fact, increases the risk.”

Gibani said: “It’s understandable that people might be worried about salmonella and what and where they ‘should’ eat. The public should be aware and informed but not alarmed.”

He and Coffin both stressed that the UK has robust systems of protection against salmonella, brought in after previous outbreaks, such as the vaccination programme and strong food standards and controls, especially for eggs. But no regime is failsafe, as this new outbreak shows.

The UKHSA website is a useful source of information about salmonella.

‘I could have put a deposit on a house or do this crazy experiment’: the British musician playing 365 gigs this year

The Guardian Fri, 21 Aug 2026 13:37:51 GMT

Isaac Neilson is burning through his savings to play a gig every day in 2026 in a bold bid to break through – and champion Britain’s struggling grassroots music scene

In a lively pub in Oxford this week, Isaac Neilson picked up his guitar and performed live for the 231st day in a row.

The singer-songwriter’s performance at the Old Bookbinders is part of a marathon effort to play a gig every day this year. The challenge has seen him put nearly 20,000 miles on the clock of his Peugeot 208 and cost him the best part of his life savings. “I was in a position where I could maybe put a deposit on a house or I could do this crazy experiment,” says Neilson, 26. “I chose to go all in on the music.”

Neilson plays punchy indie rock (albeit acoustically on these dates), and describes the mission as “insanely ballsy, borderline insane” – but the kind of big play he feels he needs to break into an industry where “nepotism and other invisible barriers” shut out many independent and working-class artists.

Over a drink before his show, Neilson says he is determined to make it as a solo artist while also highlighting the UK’s grassroots music scene and testing the “old industry myth that if you work really hard then you can get somewhere”.

So far, he has performed in more than 60 UK towns and cities including 28 gigs in his native Derby. He performed for more than 500 people supporting Cast in Barnsley and, unsurprisingly, completely empty rooms during the World Cup. He thinks he has gone through “two major mental breakdowns and six minor ones” but says his voice has “never been better”.

Often performing more than once a day, he is on course to log more than 400 performances by the end of 2026, an undertaking that takes a daily average of three hours on the road. He is often accompanied by his girlfriend, Ashlea, who manages his social media, while a manager came on board after learning about his goal.

Neilson has been booking gigs through relationships with promoters, and by scouring Facebook and Instagram for venues with stage time. He has set just two rules. He must perform every single day, and “no busking”. A promoter in Georgia in the US has promised to fly him out should he maintain his streak until September. “Christmas Day is going to be difficult but I have a plan,” he says.

Neilson describes himself as “frugal” and knows what he is doing makes little financial sense. He went into the year with just over £30,000 in savings and expects to end it with about £3,000. He estimates it is costing him about £400 a week to keep going, with fuel as his biggest expense. Friends’ sofas and long drives home help save on accommodation costs.

Breaking new artists is an increasingly difficult proposition in a music industry where executives value social media followers and streaming numbers over untapped talent at open mic nights.

There was outrage last month when the longstanding BBC Introducing stage at Reading and Leeds festivals was axed. Organiser Festival Republic promised to offer a “much wider pool of emerging talent”, with performances from the children of David Beckham and Liam Gallagher.

Neilson is proud of his “anti-algorithmic, anti-AI approach”, though he is also pleased that his streaming figures and follower numbers – both between 3,000 and 4,000 – have increased this year. “Virality is overrated,” he says. “People are yearning for community and looking for a connection. Numbers on a screen don’t represent the impact you can make in the world if you actually go out and meet people. My marketing budget is the time I spend in a room with you.”

Neilson’s mission wouldn’t be possible without the pubs, clubs and small venues in which he has performed, sites also facing their own challenges. Recently published figures by the British Beer and Pub Association (BBPA) suggest British pubs are in trouble. A total of 161, or two a day, closed in the first quarter of 2026 amid spiralling costs.

“Hospitality is an experience economy now,” says Bruno King of the Temple pub in Doncaster, where Neilson performed in May. “You have to offer something different and we have live music three times a week. It’s one of the most popular aspects of our venue. People really do appreciate being able to support grassroots musicians.”

Conversely, last year the number of grassroots music venues in the UK showed the lowest rate of annual decline since 2018, suggesting that the sector is stabilising five years on from the pandemic. Andy Burnham’s recent announcement that pubs, clubs and live music venues will receive a 20% cut to their business rates bills next year was further welcome news.

Live Trust CEO Jon Collins says the positive figures are “testimony to the commitment and passion of the people who are running the venues” but warns that challenges are still there. “It’s more expensive than ever to put shows on. Customers are still facing cost of living challenges while promoters having a bad night can lose a couple of thousand pounds.”

Collins praises Neilson’s commitment and shares his belief that new talent can still be discovered on stage. “Nobody arrives fully formed on [Glastonbury’s] Pyramid stage,” he says. “You learn your trade, you find your voice and you build your audience from those earliest gigs onwards.”

In Oxford, Neilson earns big cheers from a packed room of early evening drinkers, most of whom he manages to add to his ever-growing mailing list. After he steps off stage he is relaxed about where his undertaking will take him. “Regardless of the outcome of this year, I can die knowing I threw everything at it,” he says. And with that he is off to his next gig.

Neilson plays Frome (21 August), Cwmbran (22 August), Bristol (23 August) and Mexborough (24 August), among others. Find more tour dates on his Instagram.

Prince Harry and others ordered to pay interim £9.5m to Daily Mail publisher

The Guardian Fri, 21 Aug 2026 13:06:27 GMT

Judge orders payment within seven days towards legal costs in failed case over alleged unlawful information gathering

The Duke of Sussex and six other high-profile claimants must make a £9.54m interim payment within seven days towards the Daily Mail publisher’s legal costs after losing their high court case over allegations of unlawful information gathering, a judge has ruled.

Associated Newspapers Ltd strongly denied the claims made by Prince Harry and co-claimants including Doreen Lawrence and Elton John.

Mr Justice Nicklin dismissed all the claims last month after an 11-week trial in London earlier this year. The court had been told that ANL’s legal costs were £34.5m.

Lawyers for the claimants, who also include John’s husband, David Furnish, the actors Sadie Frost and Liz Hurley and the former Liberal Democrat minister Simon Hughes, had argued the interim payment should be just over £7.9m. The £9.54m must be paid by 4pm on 28 August.

In the costs ruling on Friday, Nicklin also said that, aside from where orders had already been made, ANL’s costs should be determined on an indemnity basis. This means that, as the losing party, the prince and the others must pay towards ANL’s costs without the publisher needing to show these were reasonable and proportionate.

An indemnity basis is more unusual than a standard basis, and there must be conduct or circumstances “outside of the norm”.

Nicklin said in the ruling that it was “was not simply a case in which serious allegations were made and failed”, nor “merely a hard-fought piece of litigation in which, after a lengthy trial, the court preferred the evidence and submissions of one side over the other.

“The claims, and the manner in which they were brought, pleaded, pursued, maintained and publicly advanced, involved a combination of circumstances and conduct which took the litigation outside the ordinary and reasonable conduct of civil proceedings.”

He said in the 44-page ruling that he was granting costs on this stricter basis for several reasons, including “the speculative and substantially inferential character of the claims at their origin”, the “exceptional breadth” of the cases, “and the public presentation of allegations of serious criminality and impropriety which were not ultimately established”.

He said the group were criticised for “the making and maintenance of very serious allegations against many individuals, the failure to reassess those allegations when the evidence required reassessment, and the continued pursuit of allegations which were unsupported or had ceased to be realistically maintainable”.

“In my judgment, that conduct was unreasonable to a high degree,” he added.

Nicklin refused to cap the costs.

In a statement, ANL said the ruling “is a devastating critique of an attempt to destroy a newspaper and the reputations of its journalists, editors and executives”.

It added that despite the “collapse in evidence to support the extremely serious allegations of ‘abhorrent criminal activity, crimes and terrible and reprehensible covert acts’ by the Mail,” the allegations were “not withdrawn, and were pursued until the bitter end of the trial”.

“The truth is that these outrageous claims should never have been brought. That they were pursued raises disturbing questions about the conduct of elements of the legal profession.”

Hughes said he was “disappointed and surprised” the judge had declined to limit the costs.

The ruling does not mean ANL is entitled to recover all the costs it incurred. Any incurred unreasonably will be disallowed and if the parties cannot agree, the costs will be assessed by a costs judge.

The parties have been given until 2 October to lodge permission to appeal in respect of the trial judgment or the costs ruling.

Friday’s ruling means the claimants may have to pay millions out of their own pockets to cover the costs, with the court having previously been told there was a shortfall between ANL’s total costs and the group’s insurance cover of a combined £16.2m.

The judge described the £34m costs claim from ANL as “excessive”, “striking” and “largely unexplained”, but said imposing a ceiling “would risk unfairness and be vulnerable to the charge that it was arbitrary”.

The court did not make any findings that any of the claimants had acted dishonestly.

David Bailey-Vella, the chair of the Association of Costs Lawyers, said: “This could not have gone much worse for Prince Harry and the other claimants. The only chink of light is the judge’s comments about the £34m costs claim appearing ‘excessive’ and his ‘real concerns’ about how much of it would meet that test before a costs judge.”

The judgment comes after it was made public that Harry and Meghan are moving back to the UK this month. According to the Australian news website News. com. au, Meghan is said to have been offered a role in an upcoming project based in the UK, though no further details have been confirmed. A source close to the duchess did not deny the report, according to the BBC. The former Suits star quit acting when she and Harry got married in 2018.

Nigel Farage called us ‘nobodies’ in the Clacton byelection. He seems to treat the town in much the same way

The Guardian Fri, 21 Aug 2026 13:00:34 GMT

I had few resources as a candidate, but the contest allowed me to speak to local people about their lives and their MP. They deserve so much better

In the early hours of last Friday morning, a video was posted. It showed Nigel Farage among his team of volunteers, before the votes had been counted, celebrating his victory and saying that he was not going to humiliate himself by sharing a platform at the count next to “nobodies”.

He was referring to the 33 other candidates who had taken part in what was effectively an unnecessary election, one Farage himself had instigated just a few weeks earlier to send one message: that the people of Clacton were backing him, despite parliamentary investigations into his receipt of an undeclared £5m donation. The election is over, but it’s worth thinking about Clacton and those candidates, of whom I was one.

I migrated to Britain from Iran 27 years ago, and have not been back there for 24 years because my Christian faith and my political activities put me at risk of persecution. Iran’s Islamic regime has massacred thousands of innocent people who want the democracy and freedom we have in Britain and it continues to execute protesters. Perhaps that’s why I felt so passionately about defending our democratic system in Britain from being abused.

Some in the British-Iranian community had high respect for Farage as it was not long ago that he met and embraced protesters outside the Iranian embassy in London after the Islamic regime’s massacres. Many of them were puzzled as to why I was standing against him and why I had left the Conservatives, for whom I had previously stood as a candidate in local elections, to do so. I remember Reform supporters in Surrey asking me: if Farage could not save the country, who could? My decision to stand was not a personal vendetta however. Having closely followed Reform’s campaigns on immigration, borders and security, I had seen the deep divides they created in communities.

Throughout the election, Farage did his best to keep his distance from the other candidates. He refused to engage with us, to attend hustings and ultimately to share a platform on the night of the count.

The campaign itself was revealing, as I met voters who had become disillusioned with Farage. Some were frustrated that he had never visited them or replied to their constituency emails. Others were concerned about his undeclared multimillion pound funds and connections with crypto billionaires. Some felt he had done almost nothing for Clacton, or that he had put Clacton “on the map for the wrong reasons”. Others were angry that he had triggered a byelection, wasting about £250,000 of taxpayers’ money.

Interestingly, some who had previously voted for Reform because they were concerned about immigration changed their minds when they learned more.

As an expert in immigration law, I was able to explain why the small boat crossings were happening. Leaving the EU meant that the UK was no longer part of the Dublin III regulation and could therefore no longer return asylum seekers to the first safe country in which they had arrived. When the UK left the EU, it created a legal void in relation to returning asylum seekers to EU countries.

They also learned how some of our laws do not make sense. An asylum seeker has to be physically present in the UK before making a claim, rather than being able to make a claim from overseas and have their identity and background checked before arrival.

Did they know that Farage had criticised the Rwanda scheme as a “con”? No. Did they know that he said it was “a political impossibility” to deport all illegal migrants? No.

Were they aware that he was planning to take the UK out of the Refugee Convention, which allows those being persecuted by regimes such as those in North Korea and Iran to seek protection in another country? No. Did they agree with protecting genuine asylum seekers? Yes.

Did they know that leaving the European convention on human rights without replacing it with a British bill of rights could affect British citizens and their rights relating to privacy and freedom of expression? No.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

Having only two weeks to knock on doors, and a few hours each day on my feet to talk to those who were willing to listen was hard, but 126 residents backed my campaign. I have since received messages of support from some of them, telling me that if I stand again, they would help. I am honoured.

One fact became clear. People want the Clacton MP to tackle crime in his constituency, to address its infrastructure weaknesses, and to create more opportunities for its young people and families. Farage isn’t doing any of these things, so how likely is it that he can renew Britain?

Given all these issues, it was unsurprising that so much of the electorate did not support him. He won, but Nigel Farage MP has some serious work to do in Clacton.

Attieh Fard is a lawyer who was an independent candidate in the Clacton parliamentary byelection

With ICC sanctions, Trump wants to make the world safe for war criminals

The Guardian Fri, 21 Aug 2026 12:00:35 GMT

The US is engaged in a lawless quest to protect American and Israeli officials

The Trump administration has taken another step in its crusade against the international criminal court by imposing sanctions on two more senior ICC officials. The growing number of sanctioned jurists – now 13 – does not change the lawless nature of this quest.

Donald Trump and his henchman, Marco Rubio, want to make the world safe for US and Israeli war criminals. No one should let them.

The latest victims of Trump’s vendetta are the ICC president – its chief judge, Tomoko Akane of Japan – and Abdoulaye Seye of Senegal, a senior ICC trial lawyer, evidently for his role advancing the prosecution of Israeli officials. Yet the real victims are not these particular individuals, but people worldwide who look to the court as one of the few avenues of recourse against unscrupulous leaders who commit mass atrocities such as fighting wars by targeting civilians.

We should never let Trump normalize these sanctions. Their main effect is to deprive the target of the ability to use the international financial system – no credit cards, no access to banks, extreme difficulty navigating a modern economy. That is a tool once reserved for corrupt or violent officials who were otherwise beyond the law. Trump is using them to attack the public officials who would bring such heinous individuals to justice.

Rubio, the secretary of state, dressed up the sanctions with high-sounding rhetoric about the ICC threatening “America sovereignty”. That is true only if Americans (and Israelis) have a sovereign right to commit war crimes wherever they want. Even Rubio cannot get himself to spell out what King Trump’s campaign is really about.

Rubio’s main articulated complaint is that the ICC can “investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute officials whose government has not consented to ICC jurisdiction”. That is true, but it is wrong only if one adopts a conveniently (for Washington and the Israeli government) narrow sense of how the court should obtain jurisdiction for a crime.

On the one hand, when a country joins the ICC, it accepts the court’s jurisdiction over its citizens. That might be called jurisdiction by virtue of nationality. The US government accepts that route to jurisdiction because it never joined the court.

But when a country becomes a court member, it also confers jurisdiction over crimes on its territory, even when committed by a foreigner. That is hardly controversial. A hallmark of sovereignty is the ability to enforce the law on a country’s own territory. Even the Trump administration would not dare object to, say, the British government prosecuting an American for a crime committed in London.

But the administration claims it is somehow an outrage if a country confers that same territorial jurisdiction on the ICC for war crimes and similar atrocities committed by foreigners on its territory – a major purpose of the court. The US government objected to such territorial jurisdiction when the court’s treaty was adopted at a major diplomatic conference in Rome in 1998 – and lost overwhelmingly, by a vote of 120 to seven.

Since then, even the US government has accepted territorial jurisdiction when convenient. After the ICC used it to prosecute Vladimir Putin (Russia never joined the court) for the kidnapping of children from Ukraine (a member), Joe Biden called the prosecution “justified”. The late senator Lindsey Graham, a Republican leader on foreign policy, orchestrated a unanimous Senate resolution in support.

But for Trump, territorial jurisdiction suddenly became toxic again when it was used to charge Benjamin Netanyahu and the former Israeli defense minister Yoav Gallant with deliberately starving and depriving Palestinian civilians in Gaza. Israel is not a member of the ICC, but Palestine, where the alleged crimes took place, is.

Territorial jurisdiction can also be used to charge foreigners from non-member states with aiding and abetting crimes in a state where the ICC has jurisdiction. For example, the court might charge United Arab Emirates officials with aiding and abetting genocide in the Darfur region of Sudan by sending arms and mercenaries to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, Rwandan officials with aiding and abetting war crimes in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo by arming and supporting the M23 rebel group, or US officials (Trump’s real concern) with aiding and abetting Israel’s genocide in Gaza by supplying arms and military aid.

Indeed, territorial jurisdiction means that the sanctions themselves could lead to prosecution of Trump and Rubio. Article 70 of the Rome Statute, the ICC’s founding treaty, codifies the crime of obstructing justice when someone retaliates “against an official of the Court on account of duties performed”. That’s exactly what the Trump-Rubio sanctions do. The court would have jurisdiction because the sanctions relate to the prosecution of Israeli officials for crimes committed on Palestinian territory.

Rubio has vowed to dismantle the ICC “brick by brick, if necessary”, announcing: “We expect more countries to join our campaign by ending their funding and participation in this politicized and unaccountable court.” Yet that bombast so far has produced few results among the court’s 125 members.

Venezuela, which has become a US vassal state since Trump’s seizure of Nicolás Maduro, has announced its withdrawal. So has Chad, which announced its departure after a call from a state department official. But Chadian officials have their own reasons to worry about the court because they allowed their territory to be used by the UAE to arm the RSF in Sudan.

(Separately from Trump’s campaign, three military juntas in the Sahel have also announced their exit from the ICC: Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso.)

Yet if the response to the Trump administration’s call to leave the court so far has been tepid, the defense of the court by its supposed closest defenders has not exactly been vigorous. The European Union has what is known as a “blocking statute”, legislation designed to negate the application of US sanctions in Europe by prohibiting European banks from complying. But while the EU says it “deeply regrets” these new sanctions on the ICC, it has not invoked the blocking statute to protect court personnel.

One reason appears to be fear among banks, particularly in the Netherlands, of retaliation from Trump. The ICC is located in the Hague, also the Dutch seat of government.

In other words, as European officials see it, fighting genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity is important. Trump’s efforts to allow Americans and Israelis to commit these crimes with impunity is disgraceful. But if defending the rule of law might put Dutch banks in Trump’s crosshairs, justice can wait.

The EU can do better than that.

Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale University and a former executive director of Human Rights Watch. He is the author of Righting Wrongs: Three Decades on the Front Lines Battling Abusive Governments

‘It could only have been one person’: top ex-detective says system failed murdered journalist Lyra McKee

The Guardian Fri, 21 Aug 2026 12:00:34 GMT

Jason Murphy believes he knows who killed McKee in Derry, but culture of silence and mistrust of police is denying her family justice

When Lyra McKee was shot and killed on the night of 18 April 2019, approximately 150 people were in her vicinity. The 29-year-old journalist had watched in a crowd as rioting broke out in Derry, Northern Ireland. Police footage captured the grainy outline of a man firing a handgun.

“Someone’s fucking shot,” a bystander could be heard crying in mobile phone footage shown as evidence in court. “There’s a fucking kid shot in the head.”

The New IRA has claimed responsibility for her death.

This July, more than seven years after McKee was killed, a Belfast judge delivered a verdict after a 25-month trial. Three men were found not guilty of her murder among a series of mostly failed prosecutions.

The judgment criticised the prosecution’s case, in particular the lack of evidence identifying the defendants as those depicted, often masked, in video footage. None of the many onlookers on the street that night came forward as a witness to the murder.

Jason Murphy was head of major investigations for the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) when McKee was killed. The former detective superintendent oversaw homicide investigations across Northern Ireland’s six counties while running his own caseload, including McKee’s murder. Next week Channel 4 will air a three-part documentary on his investigation.

Murphy is confident that he successfully identified the shooter, who he believes “could only have been one person”. But while the suspect was arrested, they were not charged. The prosecuting barrister felt that based on the evidence they could present in court, a guilty verdict was not likely. No eyewitness would confirm their identity. Within days of the killing, the New IRA offered its “full and sincere apologies” to McKee’s family, but no individual was held responsible.

Murphy believes that a culture of silence within this tight-knit community – partly owing to a severe mistrust of the police, and partly out of fear of violent repercussions from allies of those implicated – is denying the McKee family justice for Lyra.

“She was an innocent bystander,” he says. “Quickly it was clear this was an attack on the police.”

It was a challenging investigation. McKee, who was from a Catholic background, was shot on the Creggan estate, one of Northern Ireland’s last IRA hotbeds. During the Troubles, the mostly Catholic area was a violent battleground, and it remains hostile territory for the PSNI.

People here were reluctant to help “find someone within their own community who killed one of their own”, Murphy says. After McKee’s death, threatening graffiti appeared across Derry and placards were tied to lamp-posts warning of repercussions for providing information to the police. “Informers will be shot. IRA,” read one, illustrated with a rat in crosshairs.

Simple tasks were resource intensive, with two public order units enlisted to support each house search. The murder weapon wasn’t initially recovered from the scene, meaning “there were firearms circulating in the community, uncontrolled”.

Acquiring bystander mobile phone footage required “court warrants to do searches and seize mobile phones from teenagers”. This was out of necessity, but also to ensure that children weren’t targeted in revenge, Murphy says.

Early on in the investigation, he learned that the TV presenter Reggie Yates had been filming in Derry the night McKee was shot. A group of young men were showing Yates around the Creggan area for an MTV documentary about the impact of Brexit, though in her judgment, Mrs Justice Smyth stated it appeared Yates had been “making a documentary about Saoradh”, widely understood to be the political wing of the New IRA.

In the footage, Yates is told by one man, Patrick Gallagher, that there “could be a number of people gathered” outside a property being searched by police, including “those that are more than capable of carrying out acts of resistance”.

One of the last moments filmed is a woman pleading with Yates: “The rioting is going on because of the camera crew … it’s all set up for youse.”

The cameras are switched off before McKee is shot.

Days later the BBC interviewed Gallagher for a Newsnight segment. He was asked if he was surprised nobody had been charged with McKee’s murder. “Not really,” he replied. “People have called for members of this community to inform … but the people of this community know the life of an informer. Judging by history, they know exactly what would happen.”

Originally from Belfast, McKee had moved to Derry to live with her partner. Her book Angels with Blue Faces, about a Troubles-era murder, was published soon after her death.

She rose to prominence in 2014 after a blog post titled “Letter to my 14-year-old self”, in which she spoke about the struggle of growing up gay in Belfast. The letter was later turned into a short film.

While McKee was not the intended target of the New IRA, which said she was “tragically killed while standing beside enemy forces”, the prosecution’s case was still “that Lyra had been killed in a coordinated attack by members of the New IRA”, Murphy says.

It also argued that “connectivity between mobile phones showed a direct relationship between the riot and known New IRA leadership. Therefore, the riot and shooting of Lyra were one continuous event.”

In total, 10 men were charged with 52 offences. Gallagher was one of them. Three were charged with joint enterprise murder. None were alleged to have fired the gun, but to have intentionally encouraged or assisted the shooter. Separately, Niall Sheerin was sentenced to seven years in prison for possessing the murder weapon.

Of the nine men ultimately prosecuted (the 10th died last year), seven were acquitted on all counts by the judge, including the three charged with murder and Gallagher.

Kieran McCool was found guilty of common assault, and Christopher Gillen of possessing and throwing petrol bombs, and riot. Due to the risk of paramilitary interference, there was no jury.

Murphy and his team “fully expected” to secure the “vast majority” of prosecutions, including the murder charges.

The defence called no witnesses and presented a small amount of evidence. The prosecution faced further difficulty when some of the little identification evidence presented was dismissed by the court after police errors. A firewall was constructed between Murphy’s team and other PSNI officers tasked with identifying suspects.

“Unbeknown to me, one of my team had visited the office of some of [these] officers,” says Murphy. “Those conversations should never have taken place.”

Had that evidence been considered, Murphy concedes case outcomes “could have been” different against some defendants, though there were “multiple strands the judge didn’t agree with”.

He believes McKee’s family are likely to feel let down by the police and prosecution. “I felt ashamed to be part of a system that failed this family and community,” Murphy says. “I hoped the judgment would be the start of the grieving processes for Lyra’s family.”

He says the case raises uncomfortable questions for the Northern Irish authorities. “How do we bring terrorist cases before the courts, with a realistic chance of conviction?” he asks. “If we can’t convict on the basis of five hours of documentary footage that has almost the totality of events, what else can we do?”

He believes the outcome risks reinforcing “fears from the public: ‘Why put my head above the parapet, give evidence in court, to have them found not guilty?’”

Nichola Corner, Lyra’s sister, says she feels “really, really let down”. She adds: “Some people have evidence that would assist us and are choosing to withhold it.”

The Murder Detective starts on 26 August at 9pm on Channel 4

Mike D: ‘After Yauch died I couldn’t make music. I’d open a computer file and just feel sadness’

The Guardian Fri, 21 Aug 2026 12:00:34 GMT

As part of the Beastie Boys, the rapper shot to fame and notoriety in the 80s, before bandmate Adam Yauch’s death saw him withdraw from the spotlight. He returns with a solo album that sees him reckon with greed, mortality – and his past

‘It’s funny how far a joke will get you,” Michael Diamond grins. This time 40 years ago, the New York rapper known as Mike D was working with schoolfriends Adam “MCA” Yauch and Adam “Ad-Rock” Horovitz on Licensed to Ill, their 1986 debut album as the Beastie Boys.

The “joke” in question is that record’s cartoonish send-up of frat-bro culture, set to fusions of hard rock riffs and hip-hop beats. As for how far it got them: destinations included global stardom, a page in the history books with rap’s first US chart-topping album, and the crosshairs of British tabloids as they roused a generation to “fight for your right to party”.

The Beastie Boys would evolve into one of the most musically and socially progressive acts of their generation, with a run of boundary-pushing albums touching on politics and spirituality until they disbanded in 2012 after Yauch’s death from cancer. Diamond has since focused his creative energies on producing records for Soft Play and the Hives, while his sons, Skyler and Davis, took up performing as musicians themselves with the indie pop duo Very Nice Person.

Sitting in the lounge of his London hotel, happily munching cereal between questions, the wiry, thoughtful 60-year-old seems content in this quieter chapter of his career. But after jamming with his sons reignited his passion for writing, he is returning to the mic with his dizzyingly creative debut solo album Thank You.

The Beastie Boys formed in New York City in 1981; all three members hailed from artsy, middle-class backgrounds – Diamond’s father was an art dealer, and his mother an interior decorator. The group quickly decided “we had to have our own personas that were distinct and separate”, and took inspiration from teen comedies such as 1979’s Meatballs. The results were the beer-crushing, school-hating louts heard on Licensed to Ill. “When you’re 19,” Diamond says, “you’re just spewing out whatever, like: ‘This is going to be hilarious.’ You haven’t faced a major reaction yet.”

In the UK, they faced the strongest reaction of all. With an album strewn with sexist and homophobic jokes, shows featuring a giant inflatable penis and go-go dancers in cages, and tabloids circulating (instantly denied) rumours about them mocking sick children at Montreux pop festival, their 1987 UK tour stirred a Sex Pistols-style moral panic. MPs issued calls to ban them from performing. “Get Lost Beasties” ran one headline in the Mirror. Their Liverpool show was cut short after just 12 minutes and ended in a riot. “Britain was this lightbulb moment of: ‘Wait, what we say does actually impact people,’” Diamond says, calling the experience “terrifying, humbling, alienating and surreal”.

They nearly split that year largely due to the fallout. The joke wasn’t funny any more; they also left their record label Def Jam after a dispute over royalties, then Horovitz moved to Los Angeles. But the group were creatively reinvigorated by Horovitz’s new west coast friends, the Dust Brothers, who were masters of digital sampling.

“It was like our dream come true. We could have an old blues guitarist with a funk drumbeat and a jazz trumpet,” he says. “We could create these endless possibilities, this musical collage.” That collage was made into their second album, 1989’s Paul’s Boutique, a left turn that received a muted critical reception but has since been hailed as an experimental masterpiece.

Even more striking is how the trio who once delivered punchlines such as “You like men and we like beers” (Hold It Now, Hit It) became beacons of positive social messaging. As mainstream rap largely grew more toxic through the 1990s, the band went the other way and apologised for past lyrics, declaring “the disrespect to women has got to be through”, (Sure Shot); “homophobics ain’t all right” (Alive); and “love can conquer hate in every situation” (Bodhisattva Vow).

“In the same way we felt shame after some of the reaction to Licensed to Ill, we felt this nice, enriched feeling,” he says of the later albums. “I don’t want to get too ambitious here, as we are just a rap group, but maybe it changed how some people thought a little bit.” But across their albums, comedy and music remained partners. “They’re both things humanity desperately needs.”

Diamond’s new record is also experimental and socially conscious. There’s plenty of his old band’s fun-loving eclecticism, with nods to industrial music, psych and dream-pop, while the lyrics take in self-reflection – the need, he says, to “look under the hood, check inside”. But this time the backdrop of laughter was replaced by grief. “After Yauch died, I couldn’t make music for quite a while. I’d open a computer file, and I’d just feel sadness.”

Sign up to The Guide

Get our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every Friday

after newsletter promotion

His return to rapping emerged from free-wheeling home-studio jams with his sons, whose brand of vivid indie pop is stamped all over Thank You. “When we first started playing, everybody just picked up something we’d basically never played before,” Diamond says. He began to loosen up, scribbling ideas in notebooks as they came to him, and dipping back into them during sessions. “When I started actually being open to writing lyrics that were more genuinely working around how I was feeling, it started to feel good,” he says. “It was this liberating thing.”

Reflections on mortality loom large in Thank You; in It’s Time, he raps about “all these things that I want to get done”. For Diamond, Yauch’s death stirred up unresolved feelings. “In the New York we grew up in, there was a high mortality rate. We grew up in a club scene that was filled with drugs. Aids was brand new, and gay figures we knew from clubs started to drop dead. My dad died when I was 15. There was all this emotion I’d never dealt with,” he says. “Part of ageing is this thing of your own mortality. You can push it away and ignore it, or acknowledge it and feel what you’re feeling.”

An acquaintance of his sons, who was getting rich from cryptocurrency at 19, inspired Thank You’s most overtly political track, Crypto. “I was just taken aback to see that’s the reality of the world we’re in,” Diamond says of its reflections on greed and capitalism. “You just get sucked so quickly into this vacuum.” I ask how his own experiences around that age may have shaped his attitudes on greed, given the Beastie Boys’ financial disputes with their label. “It was a great lesson that everything comes with a price.”

Rather than money, Diamond feels “time is the most valuable commodity”, and returning to making and releasing his own music is time well spent. “I’m the most whole version of myself when I’m creatively completely engulfed and engaged.” There’s another note of contentment when he reflects on hip-hop generally, which the Beasties helped propel into the mainstream. He praises two artists who released their debut albums just as the Beastie Boys ended: Death Grips (“a real influence” on much current music) and Tyler, the Creator. “When I first saw Odd Future come out, I felt kind of happy inside – it felt like a continuation of an energy we brought.”

Thank You’s closing title track is an impressionistic look at his early years, filled with fleeting images of partying with his friends at 16 (“We were just kids freaking out,” he sings). It strikes me as a possible parting tribute to the Beasties, but Diamond explains it’s universal. “It’s for everyone. This combination of your social group, your passion, coming of age, and music all stirred up together.” The title of the album, meanwhile, was inspired by a visit to a Buddhist monastery (the religion practised by his old friend Yauch) which prompted him to reflect on “who I get to make music with, who I’ve made music with”. A smile spreads across his face: “I’m so grateful for all of this.”

Thank You by Mike D is out on 28 August.

When TV turns sour: the shows we simply can’t stomach any more

The Guardian Fri, 21 Aug 2026 12:00:34 GMT

They were once the hottest shows on television – gripping, sexy, hilarious, zeitgeisty. But for our writers, the likes of America’s Next Top Model, House of Cards and The Office are now part of their viewing history they feel tainted by

When I think of the summer holidays when I was a teenager, I think of watching America’s Next Top Model for hours on end, critiquing each contestant with my sister. The makeover episode was always my favourite: girls sobbing as their hair was cropped short, or even shaved off. At the time, Tyra Banks seemed like a big sister, giving the contestants the tough love they’d need to succeed in a ferociously competitive industry. Now I feel differently. I hadn’t watched America’s Next Top Model since I was young, but like many, I recently watched Netflix’s excellent series, Reality Check: Inside America’s Next Top Model. It was the strangest sensation, rewatching episodes I hadn’t seen in more than two decades. At times I felt almost teleported back. How could I not find these scenes of models collapsing with hunger utterly abhorrent? I wondered what influence watching a show that celebrated eating disorders had on my own brain. I think it had an impact. I think the residual taint of it is still there. I can’t watch America’s Next Top Model any more, nor do I want to. Ironically, it’s all too ugly. Sirin Kale

Truly, has any show in the history of television had a worse legacy than The Apprentice? The main culprit is obviously the American original, for the way it legitimised Donald Trump, but the British version doesn’t exactly get away scot-free. In terms of values, it preaches the sort of idiocy that should have been torched after the financial crisis; competitive selfishness and relentless greed at all costs. It has also churned nimrod after nimrod out into the media landscape. Plus, it isn’t fun to sit through. Why are people still applying for this mess? Why are any of us still watching? I can’t believe I used to enjoy this show. Stuart Heritage

There are few less complicated joys for me than the writing of Terry Pratchett. In my early teens, I fell for it hard – until that point, I didn’t know books could be that silly, or surprisingly profound, while also featuring a magical orangutan. I spent years diving back into it whenever I needed something to make me smile. So when Prime Video’s adaptation of Pratchett and Neil Gaiman’s Good Omens came out, I was overjoyed. After years of ropey TV adaptations that failed to channel the way Pratchett’s writing balanced goofiness with seismic moments of drama, they’d finally got it right. David Tennant and Michael Sheen’s sparkling chemistry! Gaiman keeping things true to the book! Special effects that didn’t suck! For years, it was TV that I treasured. Until, that is, Gaiman became embroiled in sexual assault allegations, which he denies. I haven’t even seen the finale. This used to be TV that took me to my happy place. Now, not so much. Alexi Duggins

First things first: I still consider The Office to be a masterpiece. As a satire of reality TV, as a character study, as a gimlet-eyed portrait of turn-of-the-millennium Britain, it remains unmatched. And that’s precisely why it’s so difficult to enjoy a quarter of a century later: it recreates the relentless sexist banter of the era with the same nauseating accuracy it brings to everything else. The wink-wink misogyny might seem quaint compared to today’s manosphere, but to revisit the show in 2026 is to be reminded of a time when tedious yet still threatening jokes about women were part of the rhythm of everyday life. The Office was always uncomfortable – it’s pure cringe comedy – but now it feels deeply disconcerting. That’s not necessarily a bad thing: the best art never ages into a cosily banal comfort blanket. Even so, one rewatch should cure most cases of Y2K nostalgia. Rachel Aroesti

Looking for some light relief during lockdown in 2020, I started watching Married at First Sight Australia. The premise of the reality TV show is this: couples are matched by a panel of experts and meet for the first time at the altar. After they tie the knot, they go on a honeymoon, then move in together. Throughout the “experiment”, as it’s referred to, the group meet every week for dinner and a “commitment ceremony”, where each couple talk through how it’s going with the experts and decide if they want to stay or go. From sparks flying between couples to dramatic arguments at dinner, it makes for compelling reality TV. But earlier this year, a BBC Panorama investigation into Mafs UK revealed that there have been allegations of rape and sexual assault on the show, hearing hugely troubling accounts from three women. Meanwhile, female participants on Mafs Australia have spoken out about the vetting process, asking why men with past allegations of domestic violence and abuse have been allowed to take part. It’s another example of safeguarding failures in reality TV, and knowing what’s gone on behind the scenes, there’s no way I’d watch it now. Isabelle Aron

I was 17 when This Life sauntered on to our screens, all miniskirts, Marlboro Lights and wild shagging. A deeply foolish age, I should have reminded myself, when I also believed in cargo pants and New Labour. God knows why I thought Amy Jenkins’s landmark series would have aged well when the 1990s so bracingly have not. Still, I poured myself a (metaphorical) pint of Stella and geared up for a nostalgic rewatch. Would I still fancy Egg? And want to be Anna? (No, and God yes, I’m only human.) I managed about three episodes before I nearly died of casual sexism, homophobia and boredom. Never again. Chitra Ramaswamy

To be clear, it was only ever the guiltiest of pleasures. But for many years, I found I’m a Celebrity mindlessly enjoyable as a vicarious adventure holiday and a schadenfreude-laden Z-lister hazing ritual. Ant and Dec’s gentle but pointed teasing of the participants was inclusive: it felt as if we were all in on the joke. Everything changed in 2023, when Nigel Farage signed up. Suddenly, the joke was on us. Mainstream political figures were tiresomely tolerable. Farage, though, seemed a different kettle of witchetty grubs: a poisonous figure, trading on the electorate’s worst instincts and being allowed to massage his image in primetime. Clearly, I wasn’t going to watch that – and I never have again. Fortunately, The Celebrity Traitors has arrived now, offering a far more palatable version of challenge-based famous-people foolishness. Phil Harrison

after newsletter promotion

Bake Off was ruined for me like a cake left out in the rain when the rights to the show were dramatically bought from the BBC by Channel 4. After seven ad-less series on the BBC, negotiations over production costs saw the baking competition jump three doors down. In an act of solidarity, the show’s presenters Mel Giedroyc and Sue Perkins – along with its resident cake expert Mary Berry – decided not to follow the hit show. Bread baron Paul Hollywood, however, stayed, and a new cast of talent have endured his stoicism and personal brand of handshakes since. Not me, though. The betrayal soured my taste for village fete chumminess. The cutthroat affair was incongruous with the show’s image of wholesome Britain. It taught me that sometimes, under the layers of zingy fruit and flaky pastry, there’s a soggy bottom waiting. George Francis Lee

The male Sex and the City™ was kind of fun for a while back there in the 00s but Entourage has aged appallingly. Based on executive producer Mark Wahlberg’s life, it followed a movie star and his posse of hangers-on as they navigated Hollywood. This mainly involved chasing women around LA while fetishising cars and money. Potty-mouthed agent Ari Gold (Jeremy Piven) was a workplace bully whose treatment of his assistant Lloyd (Rex Lee) was racist and homophobic. Over eight seasons and a flop film sequel, it went from insider satire to douche-bro fantasy. I saw it pithily described online as “toxic masculinity – the TV show”. Creator Doug Ellin has accused HBO of burying the show due to “righteous PC culture”. Let’s not hug it out, actually. Michael Hogan

I’ve felt torn over watching the final season of Euphoria. On the one hand, I was up for Rue’s spiritual awakening and Maddy’s career as a perma-eye-rolling talent agent assistant – plus who wouldn’t want to watch Sydney Sweeney and Jacob Elordi get hitched? But I’m not the only one left disappointed by Rue’s evolution into a horny drug mule, Cassie’s cam-girl aspirations and the fact that Kat (Barbie Ferreira) was entirely MIA. It wasn’t the life I’d dreamed of for my favourite debauched TV teens – and the online discourse calling out Euphoria for its male-gaze misogyny and descent into “fetish slop” didn’t make watching any more fun. Did I enjoy Jules’s turn as a sugar baby? Sadly, no. Leah Harper

I first watched Coupling when it aired in 2000, I thought it was a riotous comedy that was bitingly honest about dating, sex and relationships. During a rewatch recently, I couldn’t get past the vacuous characterisation of many of the women – among the group of friends we have Jane, a manipulative stalker, and Sally, whose main focus in life is not getting wrinkles. What I remembered as edgy humour was in fact puerile “jokes” branding women who refuse to be dumped as “unflushables” and about how getting your mate’s porn collection when he dies is a bonus. Then there’s the episode where Patrick is revealed to have a cupboard full of sex tapes after recording his exes without their consent. It was like watching a sitcom written by Nuts magazine, and every bit as sexist and unfunny as that sounds. Ann Lee

House of Cards didn’t work when it tried to continue without Kevin Spacey as scheming politician Frank Underwood. But with Spacey now cast out, the earlier seasons are unwatchable too. That we liked Frank when we really shouldn’t have, because he was honest with us in his asides to camera – and because, dammit, he was good at lying and killing, and some of his victims deserved it – was a unique thrill, a forbidden suspension of our moral codes. The allegations about Spacey’s personal conduct make it impossible to keep that self-deception going. Jack Seale

Are baby products the secret to better skin? 15 toiletries worth trying

The Guardian Fri, 21 Aug 2026 12:00:33 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

With gentler formulas and lower prices, children’s toiletries can work just as well for adults. From nappy rash cream to nourishing bath milk, these are the products that have earned a place in my routine

There may be plenty of worrying headlines about children using adult beauty products from younger and younger ages, but what about the reverse?

I’ve been a beauty editor for more than a decade, but when I had my first child in 2020, I was immediately impressed with the body washes, bath products and moisturisers designed for babies, particularly as someone with eczema and sensitive skin. The products’ gentler, often fragrance-free formulas are easier on my skin, tend to cost less, and result in a less cluttered bathroom, since we can all use the same things. These are the ones I’m still using – on the entire family – five years on.

UK

US

Great for: eczema flare-ups

This was the only nappy cream I ever used on my children as babies, since it seemed to clear up any hint of a rash before it got bad. But it also works miracles when dabbed on my and my son’s eczema flare-ups (calendula is anti-inflammatory). The lanolin ingredient creates a barrier to lock in moisture, and the calendula and chamomile bring down redness quickly and effectively. It leaves a white cast, though, so avoid using it on your face.

Great for: removing makeup

Beyond nappy changes in the first couple of weeks with a newborn, I never found much use for cotton wool when caring for a baby. I did, however, discover that these extra-large, rectangular cotton wool pads are perfect for removing makeup. You only need one for your whole face, and they’re made from 100% Gots-certified organic cotton, meaning no dodgy chemicals.

UK

US

Great for: washing my own hair

I remember a cherry version of this shampoo, which smelled like marzipan, that my sister and I used when we were kids, so I bought this mainly for nostalgia. But it’s also a great shampoo – light, effective and delicious-smelling, leaving my hair silky and easy to comb through. (Although, as my son rightly points out, it actually smells more of peaches than mango.) I pack it for all of us when we go on holiday.

UK

US

Great for: a gentle pillow spray

No amount of lavender and chamomile would have lulled either of my children to sleep in their first years, so when I was given this pillow spray as a gift, I immediately adopted it for myself. I’m actually a pretty good sleeper (given the chance), but I find this helps me wind down when I’m feeling wired. I like that the scent – a delicate lavender with a hint of lemon balm – is subtler than most sleep sprays designed for adults.

UK

US

Great for: removing makeup

A French pharmacy favourite, the Mustela bébé range has long been available in the US but used to be difficult to find in the UK. Mercifully, it launched in Boots in 2024, when my youngest child was a year old. I quickly fell in love with the gentle avocado cleansing water, which I pump on to flannels to wipe away substances (jam and face paint) on my kids, but I also use it to remove my makeup every night.

Great for: a skin-soothing soak

Since my eldest son has eczema, bubble baths tend to be drying, leaving his skin tight and irritated. I bought this oat-based bath milk, which has colloidal oatmeal and oat oil – both great for eczema – as a substitute, and it left his skin so soft that I tried it myself. I now put some in my own baths, along with a slug of Aromatherapy Associates deep relax oil, and emerge with such silky-smooth skin I don’t even need to moisturise afterwards.

Great for: a non-greasy family sunscreen

During summer, at least one portable sun cream can be found rattling around in the bottom of my handbag at any given time. This broad-spectrum SPF50+ offers great protection and is free from ingredients that can cause harm to aquatic life, such as oxybenzone. It also isn’t greasy like some of the other kids’ sunscreens, so I’m happy to use it on the children and myself.

Great for: dry skin

The Aveeno baby range is great, especially for dry and sensitive skin, but the oat-based creams are my favourite. There’s an Aveeno baby dermexa range designed for eczema-prone skin, but the classic emollient cream works best for my son and me, keeping our skin hydrated and flare-ups at bay. I apply a layer over my body every morning, then top up in the evening if my skin feels dry.

Great for: a daily body wash

Even before having kids, I loved the La Roche-Posay brand for its no-nonsense skincare, sun protection and body care. But since my babies were born, we’ve all used this multipurpose body wash more or less daily. With glycerine and shea butter to protect the skin barrier, it’s hypoallergenic and gentle enough to use from birth, yet still cleans effectively. The large bottle means it can last for ages, even with four of us using it.

Great for: bites and scratches

It’s not exactly news that Sudocrem’s classic antiseptic healing cream is great, but it was only when I had kids that I truly understood its brilliance, and also discovered the infinitely more convenient My Little Sudocrem. Much better than a massive tub which goes out of date (and kids are destined to get their hands on and smear everywhere), this compact pot is now my go-to for the whole family’s insect bites, spots, cuts and grazes.

UK

US

Great for: removing sticky stuff and moisturising cuticles

I bought this oil when I did a baby massage course with my first son – it’s a fragrance-free blend of borage, sunflower and jojoba oils – and while it did the job perfectly well for that, its greatest use has been as a general sticky-stuff remover. I’ve found that nothing removes the residue left by plasters and dressings quite so well. It’s a small bottle, but a drop of oil goes a long way for our purposes. I also massage it into my nail beds between manicures, and it works just as well as expensive cuticle oils.

Great for: dry hands

With all the nappy changes, snack preparation and medicine dispensing, I have never washed my hands more than I do now that I have kids. When we started getting my eldest to wash his hands at the sink, I quickly realised I’d need a gentler product – our usual soap gave him red, itchy skin. I picked up a bottle of this mild Le Petit Marseillais soap on a trip to France and noticed an immediate, positive difference in the skin on my own hands too. I now stock up every time we’re on holiday.

Great for: cracked skin

Due to the aforementioned constant hand-washing, I have permanently dry skin on my knuckles and between my fingers, which sometimes cracks when the weather gets especially cold. A mum friend gave me this salve to use as a nappy cream, and while I’ve never used it for that (I love the Weleda one), it is one of the few things that soothes the dry skin on my hands.

Great for: a face exfoliator

Konjac sponges – natural sponges made from fibres of the konjac plant – are traditionally used in Japan to top-and-tail wash babies, as their naturally alkaline and mineral-rich fibres cleanse without the need for any product. I used them when my kids were newborns and still buy them for exfoliating my face in the shower. A word of warning: they’re biodegradable, so will start to naturally break down after a couple of months.

UK

US

Great for: a hydrating full-body cleanse

This incredible cleansing oil is a fairly recent discovery, but it may well give my beloved La Roche-Posay body wash a run for its money. Designed for the whole family, even newborns, its rich oil formula leaves skin hydrated, yet without a greasy residue, and is gentle enough to be used on the face as well as the body. Those without dry skin may even find it’s hydrating enough that they can skip moisturiser afterwards.

Lisa Niven-Phillips is a beauty journalist with more than a decade’s experience in covering everything from lipsticks to laser treatments, shampoo to skincare. With a good radar for snake oil, she prides herself on being able to see past fancy labels to discover the products that really work. A love of no-nonsense formulas, surprising beauty heroes, and anything that makes parents’ lives easier made this article a delight to work on

It’s Harry and Meghan in Finding Freedom 2: Back in Blighty

The Guardian Fri, 21 Aug 2026 11:42:32 GMT

Hard to fathom exactly why Megxit is over and the self-exiled wonder generators are leaving California. Luckily, the internet sleuths are on the case

Wednesday night brought an absolute cloudburst of psychic rain for our parched land, as it emerged that Prince Harry and Meghan were reversing their self-styled “freedom flight” to California and returning to live in the UK. Nature is healing! Is that … is that how the expression goes? Either way, all humans in Britain have taken the announcement brilliantly, while fatted calf prices climbed steeply at the news that the reverse Megxit is imminent, with only an adequate headline soubriquet yet to be found. Megain? Megraine?

Inevitably, thoughts turned swiftly to what it all meant. One of the funniest aspects of Meghan and Harry coverage is how their decisions are always analysed as though we were parsing the 4D chess moves of 19th-century master strategists. We are forever imagining we are dealing with a couple of Bismarcks or Clausewitzes, as opposed to a resting actor and the “chief impact officer” of a firm designed to offer tech-based solutions to men crying in their cars or something.

And so it is that motive is being obsessively pored over. There’s definitely some eye-catching speculation out there. Some feel that Meghan being willing to step so much as a toe on to our toxic shores can only be a way of telegraphing the unfortunate suggestion that the king’s days are numbered. Or maybe Harry just wants to spend more time with his £9.5m legal bill. Others have spicier takes. I saw a few horrified Sussex Squad Americans on social media suggesting that the only conceivable explanation is that Prince Harry is simply a world-beating god of sex. Allow me to expand. I’m sure the squad diehards won’t mind me projecting their own psychological projections on to Meghan, but the logic seemed comparable to someone saying: “Sorry, so the suggestion is that I move back to live on top of a live volcano, in a plague-ridden failed state, run by psychopathically violent warlords. Who’s asking?” 1990s-era Keanu Reeves. “BRB just calling the removal firm.”

Multiple other takes are of course available. In Hong Kong, they used to have an acronym for bankers who were too stupid to get the good jobs in London but were able to move out there and do very nicely: Filth (Failed in London, try Hong Kong). It’s not as good, acronym-wise, but I guess we could be looking at a Fimuk situation – Failed in Montecito, try UK. No doubt we’ve all forgotten the full ins and outs, but I believe Ellen DeGeneres has been on a similar journey. It’s possible that the Sussexes have just failed to keep pace with the elite fruit-spread makers of California, and that Meghan believes the waters of home counties jam-making will be much less competitive. I look forward to her conveying this judgment to the local Women’s Institute at her earliest convenience.

Or, look, possibly the real reason for this move is something in between all these things – but which of us wants to be wasting time on nuance right now?

What we do know is that it’s definitely on, and the couple’s children are enrolled in a school for September. Early thoughts? Mainly that someone’s class WhatsApp group just got an incredible new member. Speaking as a veteran of these digital abysses of passive aggression, may I state that the absolute last thing you need on one is someone whose stated life philosophy is to “create wonder in every moment”.

Seriously. You simply cannot run the risk of the following message materialising at Christmas/in high summer when you are limping towards the holidays. “Thinking about end-of-term presents, I thought it would be really magical to create a mirror where the frame is our children’s handprints. I can organise?” Really? Because I’ve been hurt before. But go on. “Literally all I would need from you ladies is a clay cast of your daughter’s hand with a pressed daisy picked by moonlight embedded in it. If anyone hasn’t pressed flowers before I would be very happy to offer a (fun!) tutorial at my place on Tuesday after drop-off.” Aaaaaaaaaaaagh. Please, I HAVE A JOB. I CAN’T DO ANY OF THIS. You know what everyone loves? John Lewis vouchers. Please. PLEASE. As for other events during the school year, might as well call the Vatican right now because I can assure you we have a nailed-on bake sale martyr on our hands right here.

Still, this is all very sad news for the country of the United States of America, and its now decimated entertainment industry, as Harry and Meghan leave behind them failed deals with Spotify and Netflix, among others. Then again, have they? Recent years have seen the Sussexes hamstrung by having exhaustively told the only story of theirs that anyone is remotely interested in. I can hardly believe I’m typing this, but it turned out no one wants to watch documentaries about global justice activism or polo. But this week’s news could easily reignite the only kind of content Netflix’s degraded first-look deal with Meghan would be extremely interested in having a first look at: the one where their life is made miserable by a toxic family in a toxic country with a toxic press. And then you make TV all about it.

It’s a bit like when there’s been a hugely successful movie with a crazy, high-concept situation, and the producers of the sequel just have to work out a way to get the characters back into the same crazy, high-concept situation, or at least a similar one, so they can go back to the money well for a second time. Having been on board a bus that can’t slow down, Speed 2 finds Sandra Bullock on a runaway cruise ship. Home Alone 2 sees Kevin once again left behind, this time in New York as opposed to Chicago, where the same burglars have somehow rematerialised. In Finding Freedom 2, it’ll probably work best for the Sussexes to embrace the absurdity with a cheeky one-liner. When Harry and Meghan are battling remorseless tabloid attention, poisonous family dynamics, and deranged public antipathy, let’s hope he turns to the Netflix cameras and quotes Bruce Willis in Die Hard 2: “How can the same shit happen to the same guy twice?” I don’t know, mate – but I assume you’re getting first-dollar gross on the box office.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

In the meantime, the shock news continues to spark an hourly carousel of #onlyinBritain questions. What’s going to happen on Remembrance Sunday? Will this mean “rival courts”? Hand on heart, it’s hard to escape the conclusion that there are, amazingly, a whole lot of people who are even more ridiculous and even more emotional than Harry and Meghan. And – also amazingly – they are not the population of the state of California.

Marina Hyde is a Guardian columnist

Digested week: So Harry and Meghan are moving back to the UK. Who cares?

The Guardian Fri, 21 Aug 2026 11:34:25 GMT

And as Diana’s brother announces a new book, what can possibly be left to say about the princess? Plus, the joys of car rental and Reform’s Whitehall farce

There are some days you never forget. It was about 6.30 in the morning the day after we had done a long drive back from hospital. Anna was five years old, Robbie just two and both were wide awake and had got me out of bed. I took them downstairs to plonk them in front of the TV to try and buy myself some time. I switched the TV on and didn’t turn it off for the rest of the day. Princess Diana had been killed in a car crash. I just stared and stared, not quite taking it in. Hard to believe that it all took place nearly 30 years ago, but Penguin has just announced that next month it will be publishing a biography of Diana written by her brother, Charles Spencer. “I want to speak on Diana’s behalf and do so in an openly positive way,” he has said, adding that she was “A one-off, dynamic character, full of love, charisma and self-doubt, who gave life a hell of a go, and left the world a far better place, despite exiting the stage while still so young.” Yup. Well it was hardly ever going to be a hatchet job, was it.

I can’t help wondering what more there can possibly be to say about Diana. Maybe we will be surprised. Maybe her brother has access to information that will completely reframe the way Diana is remembered. But somehow I doubt it. There again, I may not be the target market. I appear to be the only person who doesn’t give a toss that Harry and Meghan are returning to the UK. As far as I’m concerned, they can live where they like. Even so, I am sure I will still read the Diana offering.

Part One. After a wonderful week away with friends in France where we managed to relax, laugh and forget about cancer, there’s one thing that’s almost always guaranteed to bring you down to earth. A reminder that your holiday is well and truly over. That’s the moment when you take your car back to the car hire centre at Toulouse airport.

What a difference a week makes. On the way out, the staff at the car hire desk could not have been more helpful. How lovely to see you, he said. Then the inevitable hard sell. Would you like to buy the extra insurance that you thought you had already bought when you booked the car online? I could have sworn it had said it was fully inclusive but the sales rep with the golden smile insisted I was wrong. When it had said fully inclusive on the booking form, what it meant was that it was fully inclusive with exemptions. What I needed to know was that there was fully inclusive and fully fully inclusive and that I needed to take out further insurance if I wanted total peace of mind. Which I did, because I have memories in the past of winging it and getting stiffed for some invisible damage when I returned the car.

So I signed up, with my wife shaking her head and muttering that I had undoubtedly just been ripped off. Then the sales rep said that – because I was a valued customer or an easy mark, take your pick – he was also offering me another special deal. I could return the car without a full tank of petrol and be charged only €1.90 a litre for the missing fuel. This sounded like a deal. Unleaded is about €2.00 a litre and I know from past experience it’s a nightmare trying to find a garage near the airport on the way back. So I took that option, too, and was finally on my way.

Part Two. The car, to no one’s surprise, turned out to be a bit of a dud. The engine monitor light came on halfway through day two and never went off. I tried to ignore it but had this niggling worry throughout the holiday that the car was going to break down at our favourite lake where there is no network coverage to call for assistance. I also couldn’t stop thinking that the whole point of hiring a car was that you weren’t supposed to be worried about maintaining it. On day four the tyre pressure warning light also came on. A trip to the garage revealed the tyres to be at the correct pressure but the light stayed on.

Given all this, I’m not entirely sad to be shot of the car, us and it in one piece, at the airport. Only it turns out there is no one to check it in and complete the paperwork. Don’t worry, says the man at the desk. Just leave the keys with us and we will sort it. An hour later, after I’ve checked in, I get an email from the car hire place. A reconciliation notice. There was €350 of damage to the car. There really wasn’t. It was spotless. Not even a scratch. But because I had full insurance, I won’t be charged. Phew. Only I will be charged €35 for someone having to estimate the damage. On top of this, I will be charged another €100 for petrol, even though the car was two-thirds full and would take €30-worth at most. Moments later, the same car hire company sends me another email asking me to fill out a customer satisfaction survey. Bad timing.

We’re deep into the dog days of August when almost nothing is happening in Westminster. Kemi Badenoch and Ed Davey have gone to ground, presumably having family holidays. Only Andy Burnham has limited himself to just a week off and that’s because he’s only been prime minister for a month. So Burnham has been doing daily 90-second pool clips for the broadcasters, but no one is really paying that much attention. Yet there is still entertainment to be had, as Reform has chosen this summer to offer its own clown show. First we have had the Clacton byelection, which turned into a two-horse race between Nige and a man with a bin on his head. Rather sweetly, Richard Tice called Nige’s win “a triumph”. Nige has rather gone to ground. Dicky isn’t normally let out on his own and you can see why, as he has been enthusing about the benefits of climate change that he doesn’t believe is happening. We should all just enjoy the heat he says. Then there’s the infighting. Everyone in Reform seems to hate Zia Yusuf but isn’t allowed to say so because the only person with the authority to criticise a member of the inner circle is Nige and he rather enjoys Zia’s money. So Tim Montgomerie has been suspended for saying what everyone thinks. It’s a genuine Whitehall farce. A treat for those of us who can’t make it to the Edinburgh fringe.

Confession time. When the ultra low emission zone was introduced in London by Sadiq Khan in 2019, I had my doubts. I thought the claims about improving people’s health were probably overstated and its main purpose was as another revenue stream for the London mayor. It just felt like another area of state interference: back in 2011 we had bought a diesel car because in those days we had been told they were more environmentally friendly than petrol vehicles. Now we had to sell it at a rock bottom price, because no one in London wanted to buy a diesel, and fork out for a hybrid. I felt the same way about the 20mph signs that began to take over London. It seemed a deliberate, unnecessary attempt to annoy drivers further and to catch them out with speeding fines. I myself picked up a fine for doing 24mph in a 20 zone, just because I wasn’t paying enough attention. But time is a great healer and for the past few years I’ve rather got used to dawdling everywhere. I make my family mad by how slowly I drive. I’m rapidly turning into my dad. And now Sadiq has been completely vindicated. In what is genuinely a good news story, the first research is in and children’s lung capacity has improved significantly as a result of the imposition of Ulez. So huge respect to Sadiq for having the vision to stand up to the doubters like me. And what a legacy for the mayor. Not all politicians get to leave the country better than they found it.
