Women’s football shouldn’t have to copy a men’s game that isn’t working – just look at Ted Lasso

The Guardian Fri, 21 Aug 2026 09:00:31 GMT

The rapid professionalisation of woman’s football has brought money and status. But copying the structures and culture of the male game risks undermining what made it distinct

Karen Dobres is the author of Pitch Invasion: My Story as a Woman on a Football Club Board

The fourth season of the critically acclaimed football drama Ted Lasso has taken a surprising twist. The show’s writers have decided to have their hero coach AFC Richmond’s women’s team, testing whether Ted’s “Lasso way” can work in a very different footballing environment. We’re only three episodes in, but I’ve already found myself wondering if the series will showcase what makes the women’s game distinct, or just treat it as the same sport with different characters.

The early signs are promising: we’ve already seen the issue of substandard facilities, initial disinterest from the club’s fanbase and the flak that Coach Chilton gets for exhibiting the same qualities lauded in the men’s coach, Roy Kent.

Watching the show, I found myself thinking about real-life football and asking whether, in growing the women’s game, we can avoid reproducing systems and structures present in its male counterpart.

The classicist Mary Beard says in her book, Women & Power, “You cannot easily fit women into a structure that is already coded as male; you have to change the structure.” She was writing about women in public life, but her words could be easily applied to football, which remains stubbornly male-dominated.

The typical men’s football club is loss-making and more than half of fans feel that high ticket costs have made the game less enjoyable. Why copy that?

I discovered this reality when I (then an avowed football-disliker) visited Lewes FC in 2017, as this small club in East Sussex became the first in the world to equalise resources and facilities between its men’s and women’s teams. Its Equality FC campaign generated headlines around the world, and predictable criticism. Detractors said that the women’s squad didn’t attract the same crowds as the men’s, so why should they get the same resources?

I went to watch Lewes FC Women for the first time, because, as a feminist and local, I was drawn by its pioneering closure of football’s gender resource gap. In a safe, joyful, inclusive environment, I experienced an “a-ha moment”. Yes, this is sport, I thought, but it is also a social and political act of defiance and change.

Watching these women take up space, compete and play with such physical freedom made me feel like more than just a spectator at a game: I was watching women breaking free from patriarchy.

This was something I wanted to champion and I went on to manage Lewes’s Equality FC campaign. I knew that the solidarity I felt, and the festival-like culture I experienced could resonate with other women whom football had not yet made welcome.

The women’s game has a markedly different history to the men’s. In 1920, there were around 150 women’s teams and they frequently drew bigger crowds than men’s clubs, until the FA banned them from playing for 50 years. The women’s game has developed a rich culture of community, accessibility and inclusion – precisely because it had to survive outside the traditional structures of football.

This culture is now colliding with the fast-track “professionalisation” of women’s football, accelerated by big Premier League clubs subsidising their women’s teams. The women’s game is being rushed into copying and pasting the same structures as the men’s. Worse still, the financial chasm opening up at the top of the game – between the big four teams of WSL1 and all other women’s teams – is causing some owners to reasonably conclude that the cost of becoming competitive in women’s football is escalating faster than the revenues they can generate. In turn this leads to a fragile football pyramid.

Back in June, Durham, the only independent second-tier women’s club, were just days from being wound up (though they happily secured last-minute investment). This summer, nearly all of Plymouth Argyle’s women’s squad found out via email that they were going to be let go after the club decided that the venture was “unsustainable”. Forest Green Rovers have scrapped their women’s team for all of this season and Southampton have also cut their women’s team’s budget.

A female-centric future for the game hinges on players and fans no longer being treated as “small men”. That means reimagining facilities, medical support, childcare, sports science, kit, training and match-day experiences around female bodies and lives, rather than retrofitting a male model. This is happening, but sporadically. Despite money at the very top, the experience of most women’s teams is characterised by chronic underfunding.

after newsletter promotion

This isn’t about handouts, but a wider distribution of revenues from TV money and league sponsorships would enable development of the women’s game across a much wider base. Increased FA Cup prize money, shared more evenly to smaller clubs, would be – literally – a gamechanger.

Women’s football offers distinct audiences and values that should be highly attractive to sponsors. Think match-day experiences combining sport with music, food, art and community that would attract people who don’t see football as “for them”.

That is the approach I hope Ted Lasso will ultimately showcase. By switching to women’s football, the series can help raise the game’s profile more than any individual club ever could.

Women’s football, sidelined and kept humble for so long, may finally get some of the respect it deserves, on, and consequently off, screen. This game can change communities, it can change people’s lives, it can change the world.

But ultimately women’s football needs its own identity and ecosystem. And that requires radical thinking.

Karen Dobres is the author of Pitch Invasion: My Story as a Woman on a Football Club Board

Uefa and Concacaf discuss joint Nations League in latest challenge to Fifa

The Guardian Fri, 21 Aug 2026 09:00:30 GMT

Biennial tournament could launch as early as 2028

Confederations are seeking to oust Gianni Infantino

Uefa and Concacaf have begun talks about setting up a combined Nations League tournament featuring all 96 European and North and Central American and Caribbean countries, in another direct challenge to Fifa.

The Guardian has learned that having come together to push for Gianni Infantino’s removal in the light of the World Cup sell-off controversy, the two confederations are now working on creating their own biennial tournament, which could launch as early as 2028 after the next European Championship.

Although discussions are at an early stage, it is understood the new competition would mirror the current multi-league format used for the existing Nations Leagues by Europe’s governing body and Concacaf, the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football. It would be followed by a knockout phase, a final-four tournament to determine the champions.

League A would feature the top teams in Europe, including Spain, France, England and Germany, playing competitive league fixtures against the highest-ranked nations in Concacaf such as Mexico, the United States and Canada.

Uefa and Concacaf launched Nations League competitions in 2018, with the confederations staging fixtures in the same international windows, so the mechanics required to set up a joint tournament are already in place.

Under the draft plans the league phase would be played during the existing September, October and November international breaks, followed by knockout matches in March and finals in June.

As the fixtures would take place during international windows that have already been agreed, it is unclear whether the new tournament would need to be ratified by Fifa, although given the world governing body is in the midst of an existential crisis with Infantino facing a leadership challenge that may be a moot point.

With serious discussions having begun only in the past few weeks, the number of teams in each league has yet to be determined, but all 96 members of Uefa and Concacaf would be involved and much of the revenue pooled, generating significant additional income for smaller nations.

The commercial appeal of the bigger European teams playing regular competitive matches in North America and Canada would be considerable, while there would also be major benefits for Mexico, whose football federation (FMF) is known to be frustrated by what it sees as the financial limitations of playing within Concacaf.

The FMF has held initial discussions about leaving to join the South American confederation, Conmebol, in a move that would need to be ratified by Fifa, but the prospect of lucrative matches against European opposition could lead to a change of heart.

The proposed new format would replace rather than add to existing international fixtures, while games would be played in geographical blocks to reduce travel.

The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) is also understood to have expressed interest in joining a global Nations League at a future date, and the competition structure being discussed would be flexible enough to accommodate them. The AFC does not currently operate a Nations League, however, so that would be a more long-term aspiration.

Uefa and Concacaf have been working together for some time, but have become even more closely aligned since the World Cup sell-off plan emerged last month.

Both confederations have made it abundantly clear that they regard Infantino’s position as untenable as a result of his role in the Fifa Forward Enterprise proposal, and are working together to propose an alternative candidate to stand against him in the presidential election next March.

Uefa declined to comment, although one source with knowledge of the proposal confirmed discussions are under way.

Concacaf declined to comment directly, but highlighted the confederation’s longstanding commitment to collaboration, which has led to guest teams participating in the Concacaf Gold Cup.

A historically strong relationship with Conmebol has resulted in many South American teams taking part in the Gold Cup, as have South Africa, South Korea, Saudi Arabia and Qatar.

I put myself in the prime minister’s shoes – and learned some uncomfortable lessons

The Guardian Fri, 21 Aug 2026 07:00:28 GMT

On the political survival game everyone in Westminster’s playing, I discovered an unnerving reflection of our country’s atmosphere of mistrust

No 10: Full Confidence is the game all the lobby journalists and backbenchers are playing on their phones. Westminster hasn’t been so united by an app since the early 2010s, when everyone was trying to figure out what David Cameron saw in Angry Birds.

The game is quite engrossing: you are the prime minister, taking office, and your name is Yusuf Dunmore. Popularity starts high in all the important areas – cabinet, backbenchers, the media, the public. But from there, every decision you are called upon to make, from nominating a chancellor to your answers at PMQs, confronts you with an invidious choice between one crisis and another.

I was ready to resign in my third week – still technically the honeymoon period. The bad faith was all too overwhelming: an opposition that howled blue murder over things it didn’t even disagree with; a press that misconstrued for fun; a public with the aggregated emotional stability of a three-year-old who hadn’t had a nap. Marshalling all that while maintaining your own probity, when you had only intended to be 15% honest in the first place, seemed like more than any decent person could stand. None of this is to cast any shade on the game itself, which is very fun.

It’s always a useful corrective to put yourself in a prime minister’s shoes. Ten years ago, Peter Bull, a psychologist at York University, analysed the ways in which politicians avoid giving direct answers, and submitted that, at the time, Theresa May was our most evasive prime minister yet – in one interview, she answered a question straight only 14% of the time.

Bull was empathetic. Prime ministers have to protect their positive face (avoid making themselves look bad) at the same time as their negative face (avoid committing to anything, so they keep their freedom of action). The smart move in the immediate term is to say nothing of substance at all, but in the long term, that fosters an almost nihilistic alienation in the electorate. If you can’t trust someone to communicate something when they speak, what can you trust them with?

It’s only when you consider things from the politician’s perspective that you recognise we’re in a dynamic system of mutual distrust that spores and intensifies from one prime minister to the next: they’re evasive because they don’t trust our reactions; we lose trust because we can’t believe or make sense of their words. They then become ever more evasive, or alternatively, start to commit themselves wildly – to opinions, policies, values – in a bid for electoral popularity, which they then renege on.

It’s obvious, looking back, that May was simply the most evasive PM so far; you would definitely go to her for a straight answer before you’d go to Boris Johnson. Keir Starmer’s defenders always liked to point out, when his approval ratings tanked, that this wasn’t personal; this was politics – in the years since Brexit, every prime minister has faced severe unpopularity scores. We were meant to draw the conclusion that it wasn’t him, it was us, so we should just knuckle down and be governed; but the more devastating implication was that every time trust in a leader wanes, that lingers as a legacy for the next. In some recent cases, that was the prime minister’s only legacy (though, fair play to Liz Truss, my mortgage is also still incredibly high).

What a depressing thought, so let’s get back to your phone. The first decision to make as prime minister is who your chancellor should be, and never has the Brazilian philosopher Roberto Unger been more elegantly distilled: we think political ideas are realistic only to the extent that they match what we can already see, he argued. Your choice is between Reginald Forthwright, who the public loves and the markets hate, and Harriet Voss, ex-investment banker, who the markets love and the public has never heard of.

Forthwright’s actual economic policy, though, is a 3% flat tax on everything, and Voss has no policies at all. This reflects a truth even harsher than the mutual-suspicion doom loop, which is that we have absolutely lost the ability to conceive of the economic governance of the state, except in terms of the bond markets. Those who kowtow to them are realistic; those who don’t are living in a dream world, and the markets themselves are simultaneously omnipotent and labile – they don’t even know what they’re going to like until they see something they don’t – yet we must all, for the purposes of being grownups, surrender to them.

What pushed me over the edge as a new prime minister, though, was my “first howler” – in a press conference, I accidentally gave an answer that was the opposition’s policy, not my own. A gif had been made of my ensuing confusion before the event was over. In the 45 seconds I had to decide what to do next, I dwelt (unwisely, given the time constraints) on how the mistake would have come about. Either I was lukewarm about my policies and was only in the job because I thought I’d be good at it (Cameron-style). Or I was under so much pressure that my mouth was making noises without any input from my brain (could be May, Sunak, even Truss). Or perhaps I would literally just say anything to get out of a spot (a la Starmer).

After a few hours of playing, though, I was sure of one thing: the new normal that is reflected in this game – that was co-created by us, the unforgiving voters – is prime ministers without a communicable sense of self and purpose. Recovery will, likewise, be a group effort, but will have to start at the top.

Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

The Taliban have built a system for enslaving women in Afghanistan

The Guardian Fri, 21 Aug 2026 05:00:26 GMT

Five years on, the regime’s chokehold has left Afghan women with almost nothing, but many are still bravely fighting for their freedom

The Taliban did not just ban women from schools, impose the burqa and outlaw smartphones. The Taliban built a system that enslaves nearly half the country’s population, or according to outdated statistics: 21,701,532 women and girls.

In general, the Taliban’s system runs on laws that get changed, forgotten or scrapped as needed to oppress women, such as the abolition of the minimum marriage-age law, which made the only “legitimate” criterion for a girl’s marriage that she has reached puberty or in other words, that she is “fit for consummation”.

And so, the state/group encourages economically crushed families, impoverished by the Taliban, to sell their young daughters in exchange for a dowry that lets them support the rest of the family.

Or the law that legitimises domestic violence under the label of “corrective beating”, which gives a husband the right to beat his wife, as long as he does not cause fractures or serious injuries.

The Taliban also made sure to restrict the right to request divorce and shut down most shelters for abused women. If a girl or woman tries to escape this tragedy, the “morality police” pursue her.

This tightening chokehold has made Afghanistan one of the few countries in the world where women’s suicide rates exceed men’s (globally, they are almost twice as common among males), with 75% to 80% of recorded suicide cases and attempts being women and girls.

And if a woman survives an attempt to end her life, she usually cannot find treatment, because women are forbidden from being treated by male doctors.

At the same time, the number of female doctors keeps shrinking through emigration or retirement, and because girls are banned from studying.

So the only option left for many women is to wait for death in silence, because of course their voices are considered shameful to be heard. So what could a system like this be called, other than enslavement?

Despite all this, Afghan women are fighting for their freedom, opening secret schools for girls, documenting violations and publishing them online under pseudonyms, and even protesting.

In June, a very rare public demonstration took place, one of the few since the Taliban’s return to power in 2021, after the Americans withdrew. Women and men took to the streets of Herat demanding education, work and freedom, in the face of violent security crackdowns, arrests and a media blackout.

But despite the blackout, the problem was never that the “civilised” world does not know what is happening. It knows very well what happened and what was done in Afghanistan, but as usual, it chose to just watch.

Amanda Abou Abdallah, is the founder of Khateera, a women-led platform covering the Arab region

I’ll admit it: I’ve cycled through red lights. But Britain’s traffic laws are to blame, not me

The Guardian Fri, 21 Aug 2026 05:00:25 GMT

The essence of cycling is to keep moving, but London’s chaotic roads often make this difficult. My solution: fewer, not more rules

I plead guilty. I have loved and used the streets of London all my life, as a cyclist, driver and pedestrian. Touch wood, I have done so without accident, blemish or insurance claim. Yet now I find myself perpetually on the wrong side of the law. Regulation has become bureaucratic and chaotic.

When I try to drive at the authorised speed of 20mph on many through roads, I am hooted at and overtaken by vans, cars, coaches and buses. And when I sit dutifully on my bike at a traffic light, I am jostled by swarms of cyclists riding through on red, furious at being treated as if they were car drivers.

As for pedestrians, walking on many pavements is like taking a ride on the dodgems. Riders of ebikes and e-scooters ignore bans and expect everyone to move out of the way.

I normally approve of anarchy. There is too much regulation everywhere. The great Dutch traffic engineer Hans Monderman boldly advocated “shared space” in cities. He wanted kerbs, road markings and traffic signals minimised and replaced by “human discipline”. All road users should navigate urban space by watching out for each other all the time. Monderman is virtually unknown in Britain, but principles similar to his were trialled with success in London’s Exhibition Road and Seven Dials. His counterintuitive ideas have been applied with remarkable success across northern Europe, with accidents falling. In 2023, 45% of Copenhageners cycled to work or school.

As a lifelong cyclist I admit to finding a certain exhilaration in riding a bike. I avoid main thoroughfares but like snaking through streets crammed with traffic, finding shortcuts through alleys and mews. But the essence of cycling is to keep moving. Hence I have to admit to sometimes doing what many London cyclists do at red lights. That is, look carefully, follow Monderman and “share” any unoccupied road space ahead by riding on.

Traffic lights can now be rendered sensitive to queues waiting at them, and change sooner to green to allow buses through. Earlier this year, a policy director for the bike hire company Lime said he wanted lights to give priority to cyclists “to improve rider behaviour and encourage more people to cycle”. This makes sense. For the time being, at pedestrian crossings, cyclists should probably just get off at a red light and cross on foot.

Investment in London’s cycle network is enabling more people to travel by bike, with the strategic cycle network now 352km long, up from 90km in 2016. It is impressive that this network was created by the same London planning authority that, 50 years ago, thought the answer to traffic planning was to build a gigantic Motorway Box.

Certainly cycling in any city is risky. The only truly safe speed is zero. But all cyclists will have their own “risk thresholds” – and the risk is largely up to them. The Highway Code’s “rules” for cyclists are near hilarious. They boil down to two words: take care.

My argument is less true when applied to ebikes, I admit. These clearly do not work in shared space, whatever Monderman might have said. Electric Santander and Lime bikes may have transformed journey times: except for the simplest train ride, they can be the fastest means of travel across town. But this comes at a price. Ebikes litter public streets with tips of abandoned machines; convenience is the mother of shambles. It cannot go on and technology must ensure bikes are properly parked.

Ebikes now come in all shapes and speeds. It is astonishing that the sleek Freesky Alaska, with its 250W engine, can be treated as if it was just another manual pedal bike. To my mind, it is blatantly a motorbike. When a delivery driver on one careers past me in Hyde Park, I wonder if I took a wrong turning. These machines must be put on the roadway where they belong.

London used to be unique among great cities in being an enjoyable place to drive. It is no longer that. The bicycle has replaced that pleasure with a new freedom – but like all freedoms, it is one that craves intelligent regulation.

Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist

Trump Threatens Suit Over Report He Doesn’t Like, Aiming to Intimidate a Critic

The New York Times August 21, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

It was the latest example of President Trump’s bid to use the legal system against those who voice unflattering facts and opinions generally protected by the First Amendment.

By Alan Feuer

President Trump has opened a new front in his campaign to intimidate political foes, threatening a prominent liberal think tank with a $5 billion defamation lawsuit over a report concluding that his deployment of the National Guard to cities across the country has had little effect on reducing violent crime.

The threats against the think tank, the Center for American Progress, were Mr. Trump’s latest effort to use the legal system to punish critics for voicing unflattering facts and opinions generally protected by the First Amendment. And while it is unclear how far any suit the president might ultimately file will get in court, it could force the organization to spend money fighting it off and make it even more of a target of his allies and supporters.

On Monday, one of Mr. Trump’s personal lawyers, Alejandro Brito, wrote a letter to the center warning that he would file the suit if the group did not fully retract the report, which was published on its website on July 13. The letter, viewed by The New York Times, was addressed to the group’s president and chief executive, Neera Tanden, a longtime Democratic official who served as a senior adviser to President Joseph R. Biden Jr., and to several of its board members.

Mr. Brito claimed that the report about the National Guard was full of malicious and false statements. He gave Ms. Tanden and members of her board until 5 p. m. on Friday to retract it and apologize to Mr. Trump.

Ms. Tanden pushed back, saying in a statement that the center would “neither cower nor bend in the face” of legal action. She also defended the report, asserting that while its findings might have been “inconvenient to the Trump administration,” they were “grounded in rigorous, evidence-based research and analysis.”

“This threatened lawsuit’s attack on facts and evidence is baseless,” she added. “A fundamental protection of the First Amendment is to allow for the publication of facts and analysis that is contrary to the arguments and claims of any administration. A lawsuit is a transparent attempt to silence us.”

Mr. Trump has often lashed out at scholars and commentators for reproaching or critiquing him in the news media. And since winning re-election, he has filed a flurry of lawsuits against news organizations like the BBC and The Times, claiming they defamed him. He has even filed suit against the Des Moines Register, arguing that a poll the paper published before the 2024 election indicating that he would lose the vote in Iowa amounted to consumer fraud and election interference.

(The Times has filed its own suits against the administration, including two seeking increased access for its reporters at the Pentagon.)

The president has repeatedly claimed that his administration is the most transparent in American history. But he and his aides have used lawsuits and executive actions to go after law firms, universities and television networks. They have also used criminal tactics such as search warrants and grand jury subpoenas in an effort to pry loose sensitive information from reporters.

Many of these efforts have faltered once they reached court and faced judicial scrutiny. Mr. Brito himself has filed multiple failed suits on behalf of Mr. Trump. Last month, a federal judge in Florida referred Mr. Brito for potential disciplinary proceedings after ruling that a suit he filed for the president against the Internal Revenue Service amounted to an improper exercise in self-dealing.

The Center for American Progress report accused Mr. Trump of seeking to take credit for a nationwide decline in violent crime that began before he returned to the White House. The report determined that there was “no evidence” that the National Guard deployments had affected the crime rate, adding that they were poised to cost taxpayers more than $1.7 billion if they continued through the end of 2026.

The report asserted that the “primary goal” of the deployments was “never to stop crime.” Instead, it said they amounted to “a dangerous power grab by the Trump administration.”

The team that put the report together used an analysis based on homicide, violent crime and gun victimization data in cities where the National Guard was deployed — Washington, Los Angeles and Memphis — over the period from January 2023 to this February.

“This approach was employed to identify any statistical changes in crime trends associated with the deployment of the National Guard in specific cities,” its authors wrote.

Mr. Trump referred to the report on social media last week after watching a television segment about the report, which he described as “another Radical Left SCAM.” In the post, he threatened to sue the center and several of its funders, including the liberal financier George Soros, who has long served as a boogeyman for the administration.

A week later, Mr. Brito’s letter arrived at the center, saying that the president would sue if Ms. Tanden and her colleagues did not retract the report, issue an apology and give Mr. Trump unspecified financial compensation.

The letter ended with an all-caps salutation: “PLEASE GOVERN YOURSELVES ACCORDINGLY.”

On Friday, a lawyer for the center fired back in a letter of his own, deriding Mr. Trump’s accusations that he had been defamed.

“This is utterly absurd,” the lawyer, Kevin H. Metz, wrote to Mr. Brito. “Truth is not and cannot be defamation.”

Mr. Metz went on to say that the center welcomed the opportunity to make its case in court and receive more information on the National Guard deployments through the process of discovery.

Other think tanks of various political stripes have rallied to the center’s side.

“Independent organizations across the ideological spectrum must be free to express their analysis and opinions, and to challenge those in power without fear of political retaliation or legal intimidation,” said Peter Goettler, the president and chief executive of the libertarian Cato Institute. “Disagreements on matters of policy should be settled through open inquiry, evidence, and debate — not threats designed to silence criticism.”

Alan Feuer is a reporter for The Times who covers the effects President Trump has had on the courts, the Justice Department and the broader rule of law.

Elon Musk Is Expected to Point His Money Machine at Texas Politics

Wired August 19, 2026

Elon Musk is expected to spend big to boost Republicans in the midterms this November, according to Trump officials briefed on the matter.

The precise amount could change, but the officials expect Musk to spend around $100 million to $200 million with a focus on voter turnout in key races, including Texas, where the fate of Republican nominee Ken Paxton could determine which party controls the US Senate.

The planned cash injection—or any in-kind contribution relating to voter turnout—would be a boon for Paxton, who has been vastly outraised in contributions. According to the latest FEC filings, James Talarico had raised roughly $69 million compared to Paxton's $9 million.

While an endorsement from President Donald Trump carried him to victory, Paxton lagged behind in contributions throughout a bruising primary against Senator John Cornyn that resurfaced past scandals, and has fared little better since becoming the nominee.

To date, neither of the two largest national GOP entities have committed to spend on Paxton. The Senate Leadership Fund is run by allies of Senate Majority Leader John Thune, who supported Cornyn, while MAGA Inc has not released its spending plans.

Democrats in close races have generally outraised their Republican counterparts this cycle, so Paxton is not unique in being behind in fundraising. Numerous candidates are relying on national party committees and outside groups to make up the difference.

Musk’s projected spend adds to the Republican National Committee’s $128 million war chest, while the Democratic National Committee is $2 million in debt. The two main GOP super PACs for House and Senate races have $380 million, compared to Democrats’ $116 million. MAGA Inc has about $400 million on hand; there is no Democratic equivalent.

A spokesperson for America PAC declined to comment on the group’s spending plans. The New York Times earlier reported that Musk had authorized his PAC to spend at least $100 million for the 2026 midterms.

But Musk's track record in setting up voter turnout operations has been mixed.

In the 2024 election, the Trump campaign outsourced its field operations to America PAC, which paid third-party canvassing firms more than $46 million across several battleground states in an attempt to turn out “low propensity” voters, who like Trump but don’t always vote.

In the end, Trump swept all six battleground states, but Trump officials were unconvinced that was a result of America PAC’s work with paid canvassers (who often are not as enthusiastic as in-house canvassers and are known to pretend to hit doors to claim their paychecks), as opposed to Trump's celebrity appeal and ability to turn out his base.

The 2024 America PAC operation also faced complaints from workers who claimed that they had been tricked, and threatened with having to pay for their own lodging unless they hit massive quotas. (America PAC and Musk did not respond to requests for comment at the time.)

I Saw the Future of AI in a Robot That Can Learn on the Spot

Wired August 19, 2026

Last week, I ventured a whopping 15 minutes from my house to see robots do some mind-boggling, jaw-dropping stuff.

I visited the Cambridge, Massachusetts, offices of a startup called Generalist AI, where I watched robot arms perform simple chores like stacking cups, putting blocks into bowls, and the like. I was astonished by how quickly they figured things out—it was reminiscent of a flesh-and-blood person.

The arms mastered a range of tasks after ingesting a short, instructional video and, most impressively, no specific training for a given task. One of the most striking examples involved a robot that was instructed to sweep a block into a bowl using a dustpan and brush. When the brush was removed from the scene, the robot improvised by using the dustpan like a brush and flicking the block into the bowl.

In another case, a two-armed robot watched a videoclip of someone unzipping a purse before removing some banknotes. I watched—somewhat slack-jawed—as the robot unzipped a different kind of purse and carefully removed the notes. Most amazingly, when it couldn’t grab the money, it switched from using its right gripper to its left to get a better angle of attack. “Ha,” said one engineer standing nearby. “It never did that before.”

“This is exactly the kind of thing people were really excited about with GPT-3,” Generalist cofounder and CEO Pete Florence told me, in reference to OpenAI’s breakthrough large language model, released in 2020. “You could take that model and just prompt it to do a new task and it would have a real shot at doing it.”

Generalist appears to be focused on teaching its robots about the physics of the world, which seems inspired by the intuitive sense of physics humans exhibit from an early age. That may well contribute to the model’s ability to transfer what it has learned in one scenario to another. In fact, some of the company’s demos made me think of how children improvise and experiment when shown a task. The researchers have often been surprised by what the robot decides to do—one chose to sweep up items with a banana when it was placed in front of it, for example. This might seem trivial, but physical intelligence is something still largely lacking in machines, and the way babies learn so efficiently about their world may offer important insights for AI researchers.

I met Florence and Andrew Barry, cofounder and CTO, in a conference room overlooking teams of people doing robot training with special grippers on their hands. The company’s other cofounder and chief scientist is Andy Zeng. The trio have impressive backgrounds: They previously worked at Google DeepMind and Boston Dynamics on some of the most advanced hardware and robotic models around.

Traditionally, training an AI-powered robot to do different tasks has meant feeding thousands of examples into the model. This is a notoriously imperfect kind of learning, though, and a robot will struggle with the task if you change something as simple as the lighting.

Generalist and some other robotics startups are investing heavily in a general robotic model trained by humans. The company builds special gloves resembling robot pincers that have cameras attached to them, which people then use to perform different chores. I saw a crate piled high with several hundred of these grippers destined for workers in Mexico and elsewhere.

Florence and team are cagey about exactly what recipe they’re using to train the robots, but they say the company has already gathered a huge amount of high-quality training data. In contrast to some other companies chasing smarter robots, they have also built their AI models entirely from scratch rather than relying on an open-source language model.

Danfei Xu, a roboticist at Georgia Tech who is familiar with Generalist’s work, says that the startup stands out among companies chasing more general robot models. “They have pushed this to the extreme, and they’ve done a really good job executing,” Xu says. Besides gathering a huge amount of high-quality data, he says, “they are excellent roboticists, and they have done really good science.”

Xu also says that the stuff Generalist has demo’d so far suggests that they have an eye on deploying robots in real commercial settings. “They are the closest to something that's deployable,” he says.

“Generalist's data approach is collecting physical interaction data at large scale without tying it too closely to one particular robot,” says Karen Liu, a roboticist at Stanford University who also knows the company. “Their strongest results suggest that this bet may be working.”

That said, Generalist says the learning skills of its models are not yet all that reliable. A robot is only able to complete a task it has been shown about 59 percent of the time, on average; ideally, its success rate would be somewhere upwards of 99 percent. It also seems unclear how well these skills will generalize to every imaginable task or setting.

Even so, the potential for robots to quickly learn skills in, say, manufacturing seems huge. One of Generalist’s engineers seemed to discover this late one recent evening. A video that captured the episode shows the engineer stacking small cups on the table in front of a two-armed robot, just to see what the machine might do. The robot suddenly joined in, grabbing and stacking other cups with its two grippers. As the robot finished stacking the cups into one neat pile, the engineer began yelling to no one in particular, delighted by the maneuver.

This is an edition of Will Knight’s AI Lab newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

Coders Say They Already Found Workarounds to Claude’s Invisible Watermarks

Wired August 19, 2026

Within four hours of Anthropic confirming that Claude models would globally embed invisible, machine-readable watermarks into any AI-generated content, developer Guillaume Meyer had published his override.

His code to remove watermarks from Claude-generated text has since gone viral on GitHub, has been bookmarked more than 20,000 times on X, and has drawn more than 100 contributors, with many more incorporating the technology into their own projects. “Anthropic is embedding watermarks in its Claude texts … the issue is practically history just one day later,” wrote one AI specialist, accompanied by an image of Meyer breaking out of chains and standing on crumpled EU and Anthropic flags.

Meyer and others started investigating how watermarking works after Anthropic announced last week that Claude would adopt it in order to comply with the European Union’s AI Act.

Some are trying to evade the watermarking because they disagree with the idea that all AI-generated content should be labeled as such, Meyer told WIRED, while others, including himself, say they simply relish the technical challenge. Freelance content writers and social media creators have also contacted Meyer asking for assistance using the code, he says.

The new rules, which came in earlier this month, stipulate that model providers like Anthropic and OpenAI must label synthetic audio, image, video, or text so that this material can be detected by a machine as AI-generated—or face fines of up to 3 percent of annual turnover. While the rules say providers cannot market circumvention tools, there is no legal restriction on independent tools.

“I'm not against transparency, and I'm all for content attribution,” says Meyer. “I just think watermarking in itself is a really bad solution, because it has major drawbacks and risks.” He is concerned about the risk of false positives and that the watermarking might not distinguish between light or heavy AI use, especially since, as a native French speaker, he often uses Claude and other AI tools like Grammarly to edit his writing. Using the watermark as evidence–when even Anthropic admits it can only generate a probability that the text has been touched by Claude–could lead to employers unfairly rejecting candidates or overblown accusations of researchers using artificial intelligence just because the detector flags it, he says.

Anthropic watermarks text invisibly by leaving a pattern in Claude’s choice of words and phrases that is indiscernible to a human reader but would be detectable by a machine that knows how to look for it. Because this influences Claude’s output, some users are concerned this will degrade the quality of Claude’s responses, though Anthtropic insists this won’t be the case. The technique, called SynthID, was developed by Google, which has been using it to watermark its AI-generated content since 2023. Computer scientist Scott Aaronson proposed a similar method when working at OpenAI but says the firm never deployed it because the company was worried that watermarks would put customers off its product.

Meyer’s removal method uses a non-watermarking large language model to generate multiple rewrites, swapping in synonyms and slightly reorganizing content. Of course, this relies on using other large language models which do not insert watermarks—possibly not a safe bet since 190 organizations—providers OpenAI, Microsoft, and Meta among them—have signed the EU’s transparency code of practice. It remains to be seen how many of these laboratories are going to implement their watermarks, which must be included in all new models released from August and must be integrated into existing models by December.

While there’s no certainty this tool works until Anthropic releases the software it uses to detect a watermark, understanding the basic SynthID-text approach underpinning Claude’s watermarking makes them fairly sure the method works, says Wayne Pan, chief technology and cofounder at Silicon Valley–based sovereign AI startup Haimaker. He incorporated Meyer’s open-source tool into his platform because he similarly disliked the idea of Claude watermarking content even when it’s only been lightly edited and disagreed with the watermark being invisible to the user.

Other coders have developed their own removal tools: Software engineer Erik Hughes took 15 minutes to knock up a tool with Claude that removes invisible and look-alike characters, reorders sentences within paragraphs, and swaps several words for synonyms. Leon Chlon, a Visiting Fellow at the University of Oxford, says the watermarks can be removed by condensing Claude’s response, translating it into a dialect like Arabic, which has very different semantics compared to English, and then translating it back. Anthropic itself acknowledged that heavily edited, paraphrased, or translated content might not carry a watermark.

In a statement to WIRED, a spokesperson for Anthropic said: "We're adding marking to Claude's output to comply with the EU AI Act, and other labs are taking similar steps. It’s hard to identify AI-generated text, and this gives people better tools for identification. Text from supported Claude models, including output from Claude Code, will carry an invisible watermark, and it doesn't change the meaning, quality, or readability of Claude's responses. We also plan to ship a text-detection API so users can do more of this themselves.”

Anthropic says it’s working out how to implement watermark detection for text and plans to release a tool to do so soon—at which point developers will finally be able to see whether their methods are foolproof. It’s also continuing to work on improving the watermarking system. “I think they wanted to show that they're in good faith doing it,” says Pan, “but I don't think you can ever have a watermark that will withstand everything.”

Review: Google Pixel Watch 5

Wired August 19, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, when you buy something through our retail links, we may earn an affiliate commission.

8/10

The Google Pixel Watch has always been a gorgeous smartwatch (minus the Active Band, which we’ve complained about ad nauseam). With Google Health Premium and Google Health Coach now part of the experience, it’s also one of the few smartwatches that feels equally capable as a fitness tracker and an everyday companion.

The Pixel Watch 5 takes a repairable model we already love and fine-tunes it, with most of the meaningful changes coming to Google’s health and fitness tools. Like the Fitbit Air, it leans further into proactive health insights. Most of our complaints about the Pixel Watch 4 remain, except that Gemini now has (some) offline functionality.

Google says the Pixel Watch 5 is 20 percent faster than its predecessor, thanks to its upgraded Qualcomm Snapdragon W5 Gen 2 Accelerated chip. CPU performance gets a 12 percent boost, and there's double the RAM. I didn’t notice a dramatic difference in speed compared to the Watch 4, but I also had few complaints to begin with. Scrolling is smooth, apps load and update quickly, and Gemini responds to voice commands without much lag.

Google Pixel Watch 5

Rating: 8/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

The Pixel Watch maintains its domed design, which remains one of my favorite traits. The curved display makes information easy to glance at while giving the smartwatch a more approachable look. There were already plenty of watch faces to choose from, and Google has added two more, along with 11 complication styles.

You can also now use generative AI to create a custom face from a prompt. The customization is somewhat limited; you’re essentially choosing the font, but it was surprisingly responsive to my weirder requests. My Nickelodeon-themed prompt produced an orange face covered in slime, and brand-inspired prompts were decent at mimicking iconic fonts like Coca-Cola's. Still, I never landed on an AI-generated face I liked more than the defaults, so I went back to Digital Bold.

I tested the 45-mm model, and it’s the right choice if you want a larger display for readability and glanceability during workouts. But I previously used the 41-mm Watch 4, and I do prefer that size for my smaller wrists. Even with the smaller screen, notifications and workout stats are easy to read.

The Watch 5 features a larger battery than its predecessor, mainly to support new AI capabilities. For that reason, battery life remains similar, with Google estimating up to 40 hours. I get about 36 hours, which is still solid. What continues to impress me the most, though, is the fast charging, which delivers 15 hours of use in just 15 minutes. This is a game changer when I forget to charge it before heading out for a workout (which is often!). Google still hasn't introduced additional charging options or 3-in-1 or 2-in-1 docks for its Pixel portfolio (the Apple Watch has so many charging accessories), and we’re still patiently waiting.

It still comes with an Active Band (ugh), but there are new color options, including Fog, Canyon (exclusive to the 41-mm model), and Olive. Prices have also gone up, starting at $399 (41 mm) and $429 (45 mm). Similar to the Fitbit Air, there’s a Stephen Curry Special Edition, which comes with a water-repellent band for a total of $579.

Fitness tracking gets some of the biggest upgrades. The new Strength Training experience adds a workout builder, audio cues, rest timers, and the ability to track weights and reps. You can create a custom workout in the Google Health app, then have the watch guide you through each exercise and time your rest periods. You can also ask Google’s AI coach to build a workout based on a photo of your equipment.

Google Pixel Watch 5

Rating: 8/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Whether you’ll actually use all of this depends on your active lifestyle, but I can see it being particularly useful for someone new to the gym who wants a little structure that feels personal. I do appreciate that it syncs to the watch, so I can see rep counts and rest intervals without unlocking my phone.

Gemini is still one of Pixel Watch’s best features, and it can now tackle offline tasks, such as starting a workout, which is handy if you tend to leave your phone at home on runs. The dual-band GPS is the same, but Google says route tracking is now twice as accurate in urban environments. It now accounts for atmospheric interference and multipath errors, which should help it maintain more accurate positioning around tall buildings. So far, I’ve had zero issues with route mapping in Chicago, and I can say the same for the previous model. I’m curious whether people in New York City might notice a bigger difference.

The Watch 5 retains several health features from its predecessors, including Loss of Pulse detection, ECG, and skin temperature tracking. It also introduces four Health Guardian tools that have undergone clinical validation and will be available in September: Insulin Resistance Trends, Blood Pressure Trends, Breathing Emergency Detection, and Sleep Breathing Quality Trends.

Insulin Resistance Trends analyzes weeks of physiological data to identify shifts in metabolic health without requiring a blood draw. The watch can also passively track pulse and motion patterns throughout the month to estimate blood pressure trends without manual calibration. Breathing Emergency Detection monitors blood oxygen levels for potentially dangerous drops and, if you become unresponsive, can automatically contact emergency services.

Watch 5 sleep tracking.

Lastly, Sleep Breathing Quality uses minute-by-minute variations in blood oxygen levels to understand your breathing patterns better while you sleep. Every morning, you’ll see how much of the night you spent with optimal breathing, along with a monthly assessment to recognize longer-term trends. Most of these Health Guardian features, except for Breathing Emergency Detection, are more useful for identifying patterns and should not be used for diagnosis. I wasn’t able to evaluate Health Guardian during testing, considering many of these features aren't available yet and they require a month of data before establishing meaningful trends.

On the topic of slumber, sleep tracking gets a refresh, too. Google says the Pixel Watch 5 is 15 percent more accurate at tracking sleep than its predecessor. There’s now a dedicated Bedtime Mode that silences notifications, disables the always-on display, simplifies the watch face, and adds a red tint designed to be easier on your eyes in the dark. If you enable the setting, the watch can also automatically pause media when it detects that you’ve fallen asleep.

Smart Wake Alarms aim to wake you during a 30-minute window when you’re in your lightest stage of sleep. This is one of those features that will depend on your personal preference. I value every last minute of sleep, and I find that Smart Wake inevitably wakes me earlier than I want. It’s also worth remembering that sleep-stage tracking is better as a way to identify long-term patterns than as a precise measurement, which makes me a little skeptical of Smart Wake’s accuracy.

Google Pixel Watch 5

Rating: 8/10

Earlier this spring, Google launched the Fitbit Air, which was one of its first wearables built around Google Health Premium and Health Coach. The Pixel Watch 5 gets access to those same tools, too. Most of the insights are also locked behind the Premium subscription, so it really does feel like a necessary part of the experience. You do get three months free with the watch, at least.

The Watch 5 is Google’s best smartwatch, but many of the new software features will also be rolling out to the Watch 4. So if you need a smartwatch but you're feeling the pinch of the current economic crisis, you might be able to save some cash with last year's model.

Review: Google Pixel 11 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro XL

Wired August 19, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, when you buy something through our retail links, we may earn an affiliate commission.

7/10

There is one new feature on Google's Pixel 11 series that, I kid you not, caused my jaw to drop. It's an upgrade over one of my most-used Pixel features: voice-to-text.

I am a swipe typer, whizzing my finger across letters to form words instead of tapping each key individually. But I'm also heavily reliant on voice typing. Google's Pixel phones are far and away the best at it; more accurate at understanding my words than iPhones and Samsungs, not to mention sprinkling in punctuation at the right moments.

With the Pixel 11 devices, there's a new feature called Rambler—an upgraded, AI-powered voice-to-text feature—that is smarter than anything you've probably used before. Tap the microphone button on Gboard, and start talking. The Pixel will strip away the “ums” and “uhs,” and if you make a mistake and restate something, it won't bother to include that bit in your message, only keeping the parts it believes you want to convey. You can even ask it to add bullet points or an emoji to format your message, all in the same breath.

Rambler lives in Gboard, Google's keyboard app, on the Pixel 11 series. To access it, tap the microphone.

Google Pixel 11 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro XL

Rating: 7/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

The accuracy of the voice-to-text is incredible, especially as you see it understand the mistakes, pauses, or vocal fillers. But what really made my eyes widen was speaking in my mother tongue, Malayalam. Rambler did a surprisingly great job at romanizing my words into English—a way I sometimes type to my family because I can't read or write the language. It's something I've never been able to do with a smartphone's voice-to-text function. To top it off, I asked it to translate the transcribed sentence into Malayalam, and it did the job. I fired off the messages to my Mom, and she said, “Very good.” High praise indeed.

These are the kinds of features that make a Pixel phone feel joyous to use. Smart, helpful everyday capabilities that can make a genuine impact on your day. Call Screen is another one of them, a feature Google pioneered that filters spam and robocalls and is now a staple in competing devices. Google Recorder is another I use every day, turning what was once a basic recording app into a powerful on-device transcription service.

Rambler, exclusive to the entire Pixel 11 range, may end up coming to older Pixel devices—Google hasn't shared details yet. It's not even restricted to the Pro devices, which is what I've been testing the past week.

The Pixel 11 Pro XL (left) in Canyon, and the Pixel 11 Pro (right) in Olive.

The Pro Pixels this year are not a major leap over their predecessors. Many of the improvements are with the cameras—still a big reason to buy a Pixel—but there are some minor, welcome upgrades, like a scratch-resistant display coating, a brighter screen, more base storage, and faster charging. I quite like the all-glass camera bar, which looks especially elegant in the new colors (and most importantly, doesn't rock on a table).

Google Pixel 11 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro XL

Rating: 7/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

HiLight is one of the big new exclusive features—unavailable on the base Pixel 11—and I'm disappointed to say that you're not missing much. This LED glows when your phone is face down and when you activate Gemini, so you know the assistant is listening, much like Google's new smart speaker; it can light up a specific color when someone calls you, allowing you to stay somewhat connected. Except there are only five colors to choose from.

If I want to set a HiLight color for more than five people in my Contacts app, I'll have to reuse colors, rendering the feature useless—it's baffling that there's no color wheel. While Google says HiLight will support text message notifications in the future, it's bizarre that this simple capability isn't available at launch. I'm all for weird, quirky features on smartphones, but HiLight is too limited to be useful. Maybe, in a few Pixel generations, it will disappear, much like the temperature sensor from three Pixels ago.

For the vast majority of Pixel owners, you won't run into any performance issues with Google's new Tensor G6 chip. But for the sliver of folks who want to dip into high-end gaming—and why shouldn't they? These are flagship phones that cost $1,099 and $1,299, respectively—prepare to be bummed. Standard games like Tennis Clash and Pako Forever ran without a hitch, but demanding titles like Zenless Zone Zero struggled to run smoothly. Worse was Genshin Impact, which gave me a purple screen that was impossible to play.

Google has made some small tweaks to the design of the Pixel interface.

A Google spokesperson tells WIRED: “We are currently working with our partner HoYoverse to address this optimization issue on the Pixel 11. A fix is expected to be implemented in Genshin Impact's upcoming update.” In fairness, this graphical issue didn't happen in any other games I tried, even Zenless Zone Zero, another HoYoverse game.

Google Pixel 11 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro XL

Rating: 7/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Pixels have had this kind of suboptimal graphical performance for a long time, and it's becoming increasingly harder to ignore at these ever-increasing smartphone prices, especially when these issues aren't present on its peers. Will there ever be a Pixel with flagship-grade gaming performance?

Rambler is the breakout software feature for me this year, but Google is also highlighting Gemini Intelligence and “Proactive Assistance,” where Gemini will surface helpful actions. For example, my friend suggested getting dim sum this weekend, and when asked when to meet, a bubble popped up in the Messages app letting me quickly view my calendar without leaving the app. Then, when we settled on a time, another bubble popped up asking if I wanted to create the calendar event.

Gemini Intelligence's Proactive Assistance will surface these kinds of bubbles in select apps to complete actions on your behalf.

It all worked very smoothly, though Gemini struggled to understand that the restaurant's name was “Din Soup,” not Dim Sum. The bigger problem is that this kind of proactive assistance is largely available in the Messages app, which, unfortunately, is not my default messaging mode. When this becomes a system-wide capability that works in every app, I can see its utility.

Google has made some overall tweaks throughout the Pixel's interface that I think give it a stronger, more unique design language. I also do want to call out that these are still the only major Android phones with built-in Qi2 magnets—aka the magnetic back like MagSafe on the iPhone. I am all in on MagSafe accessories, whether that's my car dock or my mobile tripod, so it's indispensable to me.

Speaking of, battery life is rather unimpressive on both Pixel 11 Pro models. (The only difference between the pair is battery life and screen size.) I averaged four hours of screen-on time before the Pixel 11 Pro XL hit 20 percent, and roughly the same on the Pixel 11 Pro. Granted, I was downloading data over cellular, using Google Maps, and taking a lot of photos. I think average users will find it sufficient for a full day, but power users will undoubtedly need a top-up. Perhaps it's time for Google to consider denser batteries with silicon-carbon battery technology?

This is where I stood, in Brooklyn, at 1X camera zoom with the Pixel 11 Pro XL.

This is the photo I captured with 120X Pro Res Zoom. It's the top of the World Trade Center.

Do you really need 120X digital zoom? When you say it out loud, it sounds ridiculous, but then you look at the results, and it's hard not to be impressed. Yes, there are AI-generated pixels (anything past 30X zoom) filling in the gaps, which will be a nonstarter for many, but look how far away I am! It's actually quite a struggle to capture photos at that high level of zoom because the camera gets very shaky. Still, having access to this level of zoom means I am more comfortable zooming in to 30 or 50X, where the results are even better.

Google Pixel 11 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro XL

Rating: 7/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

The two big hardware changes to the camera system are the new 50-megapixel main sensor and a new 48-MP telephoto zoom with 30 percent better light sensitivity. But the Tensor G6 chip is also powering many imaging improvements that should result in stronger photos overall.

First of all, I am happy to report that Google seems to have finally fixed Portrait mode. For too long, the Pixel's Portrait mode has struggled with hair, causing weird glitches or artifacts with rogue strands of hair at the edges of a person's head. It's not perfect now, but it's significantly better at detecting individual strands of hair and figuring out the best way to blur everything behind them.

The Pixel 11 Pro XL's Portrait mode does a better job with hair than ever before.

The iPhone 17 Pro Max has a nice fall-off for the blur, but the scene is warmer than it was IRL.

Night Sight on these Pro devices is now Instant Night Sight, and is supposedly up to 4.5 times faster. I think Google may have jumped the gun on Instant because there's still a small pause when you hit the shutter button, and if you or your subject are moving slightly, it will still probably come out a little blurry. But it's certainly not as long of a pause as before, which makes low-light photography a smidge more forgiving to those kinds of smaller movements.

As someone who loves using the telephoto zoom on smartphone cameras, the 5X camera is excellent, delivering sharp, detailed images even at night. I took a handful of shots comparing these cameras with the iPhone 17 Pro, and I found Google did a better job replicating colors, though still slightly preferring cooler tones. The iPhone tended to make everything way warmer than it was in real life.

The nice thing is that Google finally gives you a little more control over how your photos look. Camera Looks, tucked away in the camera settings, lets you choose a different visual style. That might mean purposefully taking a worse photo, maybe with crushed highlights or lifted shadows, so your photos aren't this perfect slice of life, but imperfect and you. I seem to be gravitating to the Vanilla and Velvet looks the most.

Google Pixel 11 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro XL

Rating: 7/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Another one of those features that makes everyday life a little easier—if you tend to shoot videos for a living like me—is Creator Suite. This mode in the Video tab of the camera app enables handy tools, like an audio visualizer, so you know your wireless mic is picking up your voice. But what I love most is the built-in teleprompter. It understands the cadence of your voice and will progress to the next line as you speak. It worked perfectly in my test run, and I'm excited to use it at the next big event I cover soon.

Finally, there's Magic Capture. It's a dedicated mode next to Photo and Video that is designed to make it so that you can just hold the phone up and it'll capture several photos on your behalf. You'll even get a 1080p video clip (though you can boost it to 4K using Google's Video Boost technology). The idea is that if you're singing happy birthday to your kid, your face isn't buried behind a phone, instead looking at the scene in real life while you have the phone held next to you capturing the moment.

I didn't have a special occasion to use it for this past week, but I did hold up the phone while my dog was playing with other pooches at the dog park and also to shoot scenes of volleyball at the park, and it did a pretty good job capturing photos that would otherwise have required more focus on my part. I just wish Magic Capture could change the lenses itself because right now that's something you have to pick manually. This feature seems ripe for Google's upcoming pair of smart glasses, considering you won't have to hold anything up at all.

All in all, the Pixel 11 Pro models are yet another strong entry that deliver the camera prowess expected of a Pixel and the software smarts. There are still some areas where Google needs to catch up with its competitors, namely graphical performance and battery life, especially if it's going to charge this much.

But it's also worth noting that you do not need to spend this much if you want a good phone. Google brings many of these smart capabilities down to its cheaper A-series phone, which also still has a class-leading camera and performance for the money, or you can get a very similar experience with the slightly cheaper Pixel 11.

(And by the way, I've completely written these last few paragraphs using Rambler.)

Why Is It Absolute Hell to Buy a Movie Ticket Now?

Wired August 19, 2026

The conclusion to Denis Villeneuve’s epic Dune trilogy is still four months away, but the anticipation was palpable on Tuesday, the first day of ticket presales.

Theater chain apps suffered apparent outages as moviegoers waited in long virtual lines, hoping to finally glimpse a seat map with some empty spots left on it. In Manhattan, those who have grown mistrustful of this unreliable tech found time on a weekday morning to line up around the block at AMC Lincoln Square—hours before the box office opened. It was the third frenzied rush for blockbuster tickets in a few short weeks, following sky-high demand for Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey and Destin Daniel Cretton’s Spider-Man: Brand New Day.

Customers have been particularly keen to see these films on IMAX screens, with Dune: Part Three and The Odyssey also available in the even more exclusive IMAX 70mm format. Only 25 theaters in the US are capable of showing a film this way.

While directors and studios have embraced such premium screenings for tentpole releases (not least because those tickets are more expensive), the rarity of theaters equipped for them has contributed to a scarcity mindset. People are so bent on experiencing these movies in the “best” possible way, and, if not on opening night, as soon after as possible, that ticket resellers have attempted to auction them off for hundreds of dollars, while some cinephiles have embarked on Homeric journeys to IMAX theaters multiple states away.

As such, this week’s competition for Dune: Part Three tickets renewed a feeling of stress and weariness among fans of Hollywood spectacle. Why, some asked, does catching a movie now feel as difficult as scoring tickets to a red-hot concert tour?

Adam Aron, CEO of AMC Theatres, took to his X account to apologize for the latest cinematic frustrations. (Reached for comment, the company directed WIRED to his comments on the platform.) “We thought we were ready, but we weren’t,” he wrote of the Dune launch, noting that the traffic surge to AMC’s website and mobile app was about triple the volume they’d seen for the latest Spider-Man installment.

“It’s a high-class problem to have such staggering demand, but even so it is intolerable and inexcusable,” Aron wrote. He further announced that $2 million in IT costs had been approved in order to “fully address the issue.”

Fandango and Regal Cinemas, whose apps and websites also drew complaints amid ongoing glitches, did not immediately return requests for comment. A representative for IMAX, which is not involved in ticket sales, declined to comment on the record. IMAX currently has more than 1,800 locations worldwide; in a quarterly financial update earlier this year, CEO Rich Gelfond said they saw the potential to double their footprint.

This depends, however, on exhibitors actively investing in more IMAX venues, as well as the availability of new or retrofitted auditoriums big enough for the screens and the theater architecture that goes along with them.

In the meantime, customer exasperation is mounting. Internet film critics bemoaned the “concertification” of movies as they contended with the same overloaded apps and long lines as everyone else.

“I'm done with the shenanigans of trying to be ‘FIRST’ to see these blockbuster films,” Simone Cromer, once known for her “Club Chalamet” fan accounts devoted to Dune star Timothée Chalamet, wrote on X. “I'll watch it on a regular screen sometime that week, without having to travel too far.”

Barry Hertz, film editor and chief film writer at The Globe and Mail, posted on X that vendors were failing the filmgoing public. “If you're going to turn movie ticket-buying into a competitive sport, then you need to have the tech and UX to support that shift,” he wrote.

Hertz tells WIRED that “eventizing” a movie “feels like a lifeline for theaters coming out of the depths of the pandemic,” and that there’s nothing inherently wrong with them encouraging audiences to pursue “a movie in its most ideal format” as they fight to maintain their bottom line.

“What can't happen, though, is theater owners forgetting that the rest of the experience has to be as easy and painless as possible,” Hertz continues. In his view, they haven’t lived up to this responsibility. “Don't add layers of technical frustration on top of a leisure activity that is fighting for its life.”

Stephanie Wang, a professor of economics at the University of Pittsburgh who researches behavioral economics, suggests there are also significant social dimensions at play.

“Some consumers' desire for a ticket may be greater when they know both that many other people also want the ticket and cannot have it,” Wang tells WIRED. She points to an experiment published in The Review of Economic Studies in 2023 which found that “when some people are randomly excluded from being able to participate in an auction, the bids of those who are allowed to remain in the auction substantially increase.” Moreover, she adds, someone’s commitment to participating in the ultimate movie event can “signal to others, and sometimes to themselves as well, that they are true fans,” since it may “require you to give up time or sleep or something else of value.”

The potential solutions, alas, are not entirely obvious. Some members of the AMC Stubs A-List membership program this week suggested that they should have priority access to tickets at those theaters. But this ignores the economic reality of the subscription plan, which costs between $27.99 and $29.99 monthly and allows viewers to see up to four movies a week at no extra charge—including in formats like IMAX 70mm, a ticket which otherwise retails at $30 or more at AMC. In other words, outside of concessions, the chain isn’t making any additional money off A-Listers attending these premium screenings; the box-office take comes from the non-members paying full price.

“Of course, the classical economic question is, why don't the theaters just increase prices until supply equals demand and the market clears?” says Wang, identifying one theoretical way to cut down the secondary resale market. But, she says, theaters have reasons not to pull an audience that paid top dollar across the board. “They might want the fans who will give a rave review afterwards and spread the positive word in their social networks,” Wang explains, and those who sacrificed more for a ticket are more disposed to “believe that it's one of the best movies they have ever seen to justify the effort cost, which far exceeds the monetary cost.”

More likely, the chains and vendors will have to upgrade their tech, as AMC is already planning to do, and implement other guardrails to prevent a handful of users from snapping up as many tickets as they can to sell at a significant markup. Until they figure out those fixes, it seems that the battle for the best seats in the house will continue to be a bloodbath.
