Are Digital Wall Calendars Worth It?

Wired August 19, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

I won’t lie to you: I hated the first digital wall calendar I tried.

I tested it last year and was left unimpressed. It was expensive and massive, and my calendar details were slow to appear (if they appeared at all). The device felt more like clutter than a useful addition to my home. So, I wrote off the idea of using a digital wall calendar, but to my surprise, they have only picked up in popularity and options since then. After trying a few new models myself this year, I can now see why.

These gadgets work by taking your online calendar—whether your Google Calendar, the calendar app on your iPhone, or your corporate Microsoft calendar account—and putting it on a digital screen that you can mount on the wall or prop up on a countertop or table. They’re often more than just calendars, also functioning as chore charts, meal planners, and sometimes even digital photo frames. I usually have smart displays all over my home, especially in my kitchen and living area, but for the past two weeks, I’ve replaced them all with digital wall calendars. And you know what? I don't miss talking to those annoying AI-powered assistants.

Instead, as someone who already lives and breathes by her Google Calendar, I love being able to see it on a large display in the middle of the kitchen, without needing my phone—especially when it’s on a digital wall device that immediately reflects my most up-to-date calendar. My husband and I have also been using the extra features more often, particularly to guide my 4-year-old through his evening bedtime routine with the help of his own companion device. Here's everything you need to know about the best digital wall calendars and whether they're right for you.

Updated August 2026: I've added the Skylight Buddy as a kid-friendly tool that includes some features of these digital calendar devices. I’ve also ensured accuracy and up-to-date information throughout.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

Amazon

Amazon

Amazon (15.6-inch)

Skylight (With Plus Plan)

You might have heard these gadgets called by various names. Maybe “digital wall calendar” or “smart calendar device.” Maybe you've just heard the name Skylight Calendar, which is a notably popular model right now. No matter what you call them, these devices all do the same thing: replace a paper calendar with a digitized one that connects to the calendar tools you're already using, like Google Calendar or Apple Calendar. The devices let you see your entire family’s schedule in one view, with the ability to update or add to it without needing a phone or a separate account. It also erases issues like unreadable handwriting and forgetting to write down an event you've already scheduled digitally, and its color-coding system makes it easy to see who's on the hook for which activities.

While these are often called wall calendars, you can usually choose to place them on a tabletop. I preferred the models that included a tabletop stand, but I was still able to prop up the ones that only came with wall-mounting hardware during my testing.

These devices aren't just calendars; they’re also designed for larger family management. You'll find features to help you plan meals, track to-do lists for multiple people, and earn rewards on a digital chore chart. The Skylight Calendar 2 is a favorite of mine because it includes a photo screensaver, but you'll need to be a Plus subscriber to get that and some of the other bonus features. Basically, you can use these calendars to manage your family's full schedule, chores, meals, and more in a single device.

I didn't expect to feel this way, but having a physical version of my hyper-detailed Google Calendar in the center of my home has been a delight. My husband and I both check our calendar at a glance while we're chatting in the kitchen, and at the start of the week, we'll camp out in front of it for a few minutes to plan the week's dinners and grocery needs. My top pick, Skylight Calendar 2, actually prompts us to add items to our grocery list based on what meals we picked (if it's a stored recipe, that is).

My husband and I have found it so useful in part because we're both good about adding events to our individual calendars, so now this device can reflect that work. It lets us skip pulling out our phones when discussing plans for the next day or the upcoming weekend.

Skylight

Amazon

Skylight (With Plus Plan)

Skylight's calendar is the most popular for a reason. The brand is known for its digital photo frames, and now you can use the same Skylight app to operate any of its three digital calendars: The older 10-inch Calendar ($170), the newer Calendar 2 ($320), and the Calendar Max ($630). The main difference between these is size, but Calendar 2 is the newest model, with improved performance and interchangeable Snap Frames ($30 to $50) you can purchase to change the device's look.

What makes Skylight great is its software. It's easy to use, and it quickly imported my Google Calendar and the wide variety of calendars shared to it, so I could immediately add all of my family's schedules to the device. The left-side menu bar shows all the pages you can toggle between. Calendar, Lists, Tasks, Rewards, Meals, and Recipes are the main areas you'll use; you can also access the Photos, Sleep, and Settings pages from the same menu.

The app and device interface are clean and intuitive compared with other models, many of which feel like Android tablets with a fancy calendar mode added. I was able to easily assign calendars I created on the device to family members. For example, I assigned my husband's calendar to him without needing him to log in or import it, and I could have assigned any calendar I created to my son as well. I also liked that shared events only appear once on the Skylight, but with both of our designated colors added to show the event in question applied to both of us.

Lists and Tasks sound similar, but Tasks are meant to function as a chore chart, connecting back to the Rewards page to build habits and earn the reward you set after hitting a certain goal. The main audience for this is children who are old enough to check the calendar. Lists are for things like your groceries. If you add recipes to the Recipe tab and then add those to your meal plan for that week, Skylight will offer to put the corresponding ingredients on your shopping list.

The downside of Skylight is the paywall. To access some of the best features—meal planning, rewards, photo screensaver, and the in-app AI assistant tool Sidekick—you'll need to be a Plus subscriber for either $79 a year or $8 a month. Having this device double as a digital photo frame makes it worth the cost to me. I love getting to have my two favorite things nearby: photos of my family and instant access to our shared calendars.

Everblog

Amazon

Everblog

The Everblog HomeCal has an operating system that feels pleasantly similar to the Skylight. It has a bit of an Android undertone to it, but it doesn't feel like a giant tablet as much as the Apolosign or Cozyla calendars (both below). Setup was pretty seamless, but there was a delay for the device to update with my calendar invites. It would also take a while for the Everblog to reflect changes I made to my Google Calendar on another device. While it worked well for the most part during testing, I occasionally noticed events missing from my Everblog. It also turned each calendar email account I connected to the device into a separate profile, which was annoying. I could toggle off the extra emails when I was on pages outside of the calendar, though, so I didn't have three profiles for myself on my Chores page, for example.

The menu on the left-hand side is very similar to Skylight's, with options like Calendar, Chores, and Meal Plan. There isn't a recipe section, which I miss, but there is a Fridge section, which lets you track the groceries you already have. Part of why this exists is because Everblog also has a smaller, battery-powered version of this calendar that's designed to attach to your fridge, aptly named the FridgeCal ($249). Still, I prefer the Recipe tab on the Skylight. The Everblog also has a Chores tab, but no additional tab for tracking regular chores or other to-dos separately.

There's a free photo option, but the uploader tool in the app only lets you add one photo at a time. Painful, but I'm sure many would feel it's worth the free price tag. To use the feature, you'll need to go into the settings on the physical device to turn on photo slideshow as your screensaver. The Everblog defaults to pinging loudly at the start of any calendar event, which you can only change on the device, not in the app.

There's a button on the bottom right-hand corner of the screen that will take you to a homepage with an overview of the calendar and chores, and access to other applications like Spotify and Netflix, if you set up your accounts on this device for streaming content. It comes enabled for wall mounting, but you can purchase the Calendar Stand ($39) if you want to situate it on a tabletop, and there's a wooden frame ($99) you can buy to snap on to give it a nicer look.

Apolosign

Amazon (15.6-inch)

Walmart (15.6-inch)

Apolosign's digital calendar has three sizes: 15.7, 21.5, and 27 inches. It runs Google's Android OS, so it operates very similarly to an Android tablet and to Google's Pixel Tablet, if you've used either as a smart display, as I have. The Apolosign has two modes: Calendar and Android. Calendar mode worked similarly to Skylight. I seamlessly connected it to my Google Calendar, imported over most of my various shared calendars, and color-coded them.

The Calendar mode has a left-side menu bar (you'll have to tap to make it appear), with sections for Home, Calendar, Routines, To-Dos, Rewards, and Meals. The Home page has a two-column design, showing you the calendar on one side and your Routines and To-Dos on the other. You can then tap into any of these sections or check off items directly from the Home page. Apolosign also has baked-in notifications that chime to remind you about calendar events and to-dos, plus phone notifications to let you know how many items are on your calendar that day.

WIRED Reviewer Kat Merck also tested Apolosign, but used Android mode instead of Calendar mode. Android mode allows you to customize widgets and layout, so she opted for a monthly view. This mode also lets you use photos from Google Photos as a background and screensaver. She says it's nice to be able to customize the layout in this mode, but it struggles to sync with other programs, including Apolosign's own app.

I don't like the Apolosign experience quite as much as the Skylight or Everblog, and Kat agreed that this device is not very intuitive and takes a lot of patience to set up. But having no paywall is a huge plus, and many people will feel it's worth getting used to the more Android-style experience to not pay a monthly or yearly fee. But since it's essentially a large Android tablet, iPhone users have flagged on Reddit that they can't two-way sync between it and their iPhone devices. The Apolosign is often on sale for the same price, if not cheaper, than the Skylight.

Skylight

Skylight (With Plus Plan)

Skylight (Device Only)

If you want a version made for kids, Skylight has something along those lines called the Skylight Buddy (8/10, WIRED Recommends). It's not a digital calendar but rather a chore-and-routine display that helps kids visualize and check off their daily to-dos without needing to navigate an entire family calendar.

My 4-year-old loves his 7-inch Buddy, and it really does help get him to brush his teeth and put on his PJs in a timely (well, more timely) fashion now that it's in his room. It also has a night-light and sound machine, but the sounds are limited, and the night-light is pretty dim. So for those capabilities, I'm sticking to the Hatch Baby my son is used to and loves.

Ultimately, this is most useful if you already have and use a Skylight Calendar. That’s because the Buddy can sync to and show designated tasks already on the Skylight Calendar. But even if you don't have the Calendar and just want more of a routine tool or chore-tracker for your child, this is a really good option. There are subscription options to get more features—Buddy Plus is $39 a year, and Skylight Plus is $79 a year. Skylight Plus is what you should get if you have the Calendar, as it unlocks paywalled features for both devices. But I haven't needed any subscription-only capabilities to keep my son excited about and engaged in his bedtime routine.

Cozyla Calendar Plus 2 (15.6 Inches) for $350: This calendar is similar to Apolosign with an Android-based operating system, but it didn't import my shared calendars, meaning it took more work to set up. It was overall frustrating to navigate and didn't guide me through its tools as effectively as Skylight or Apolosign. While Cozyla doesn't have any subscription fees, its 15.6-inch size is more expensive than both Skylight's and Apolosign's.

Hearth Display for $699: This is another digital calendar and family tool that has a paywall with an affordable Family Membership ($6 a month) but a much higher initial price point. It's only available in a large, 27-inch size, and I found it was slow to load my calendar and also bulky compared to more affordable options.

How Do Digital Wall Calendars Work?

Digital wall calendars sync with your existing digital calendar app of choice, like Google Calendar, and display it on the physical screen. There are usually additional tools for recipes, to-do lists, and chores, but each digital wall calendar varies in how you import the information. You may have to manually import it or type the details into the device, but once you get used to the process, the function can be helpful for the whole family.

Will Changes to My Calendar Appear Instantly?

Changes you make on your native calendar app, like Google Calendar and Apple's Calendar, should reflect quickly onto the digital wall calendar device. But changes you make on the device aren't always backward compatible with the native calendar. It depends on the calendar's settings and how the information was shared; I can edit my primary personal calendar on the Skylight Calendar 2, for example, but I can’t edit my work calendar that I shared to the Skylight through my personal. There are also some syncing issues you may run into with the Apolosign, which doesn't two-way sync with an iPhone since the digital calendar runs on an Android operating system.

How Is a Digital Calendar Different From a Smart Display?

Many smart displays look similar to these devices but have an entirely different operating system. Sure, the Google Pixel Tablet has some overlap with the Apolosign and Cozyla, since they all run an Android operating system. But unlike smart displays, digital calendar devices are designed with specific tools to run your family and none of the clutter. You'll lose out on smart-home support, though Apolosign claims you can use Google Assistant on it (that hasn't worked for me so far). On most devices, you'll also compromise on extras like video streaming (you can, however, stream on Everblog). But as someone who uses a smart display regularly, I really didn’t miss it once I switched over to the digital calendar device. I do wish there were a weather-report page, as most digital wall calendars just show the current weather.

Does It Have to Go on the Wall?

No—in fact, most of these devices come with a table-stand option. I only tested in table-stand mode since I had multiple of these devices in my house at one time, but the wall-mounting option is nice, allowing you to keep your tabletops clear. The 15-inch models are great for tabletops, and you may want to consider larger sizes for the wall-mounting route.

Review: Google Pixel 11

Wired August 20, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, when you buy something through our retail links, we may earn an affiliate commission.

8/10

The hot pink Hibiscus color is dazzling, but is Google’s 11th-generation Pixel just another iterative upgrade, or does it dial things up to 11? Diving beneath the surface, we find a slightly better chipset and camera, faster wireless charging, a fresh batch of AI features, and not much else. Don’t get me wrong: This is a slick smartphone, perhaps the best Android phone for folks who are comfortable with Google and Gemini AI, but it’s only a very slight improvement over last year’s Pixel 10.

Although it lands alongside the Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL, the Pixel 11 shares more in common with the new Pro Fold (review coming soon). The Pro models' more powerful camera system, with the gimmicky, glowing HiLight LED, is what sets them apart. The base model storage has finally jumped up to a more practical 256 GB, but that means the starting price of the Pixel 11 is $100 more than the 10 at $899 (not technically a price bump since the 256 GB model of the Pixel 10 was the same price).

Refinement has been the pattern in smartphones for the last few years, and the Pixel 11 does nothing to buck that trend. If you’ve got a 3-year-old handset and you’re in the market for a new phone, the Pixel 11 should be in the conversation, but if you’re looking for a justification to upgrade from last year’s Pixel 10, you won’t find it here.

The instantly recognizable design has been slightly refined; most notably, the pill-shaped camera bump is thinner and all-glass. Stick a case on the Pixel 11, and it will lie flat on a desk. It sports the same satin finish on the recycled aluminum frame and gloss finish on the glass back as last year’s phone, but with some fun new colors.

Google Pixel 11

Rating: 8/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

I was delighted to get Hibiscus (otherwise known as hot pink), but there’s also a more subtle Pistachio (warm green), and the usual Frost (white) and Obsidian (black). I’m sad they cut Indigo (surely everyone’s favorite from last year). Like Apple, Google seems to save the fun colors for the regular Pixel, and the Pros look more muted.

Despite a 6.3-inch screen, this is what passes for a small phone nowadays. Switching from last year's Pixel 10 Pro XL, I really appreciated how easy it was to handle the Pixel 11 one-handed. It’s a little thick, but it feels good in hand and has almost the same profile as the Pro, so you can use cases interchangeably. And I do recommend snagging a Pixel 11 case; I already scuffed the paintwork when I dropped it on the beach.

The screen is the same as last year’s: an excellent 6.3-inch OLED display with a 1080 x 2424-pixel resolution and refresh rates of 60 or 120 Hz. It’s a shame Google didn’t upgrade to a variable refresh rate (1 to 120 Hz) since it can save battery life. It also defaults to 60 Hz, and you have to dip into the Display settings to toggle on the smoother 120 Hz. The display is plenty bright with a 3,000-nit peak brightness; I never found myself squinting. Side by side with the Pro, it’s not quite as bright or sharp, and it has larger bezels, but you have to look closely to see the difference.

The fingerprint unlock is as good as any, but Google’s Face Unlock still doesn't work in the dark, which will annoy any iPhone defectors. US buyers will also have to do without a SIM slot, as the Pixel 11 is eSIM-only stateside. Physical SIM cards make switching between phones more straightforward, but phone makers and carriers have made that process smoother with eSIMs than in the past. Sure, it’s much easier to pop a card in than to go through your carrier when traveling abroad, but setting up an international eSIM isn't that complex. Both have benefits, but with US phones and carriers embracing eSIM over the past couple of years, it's become a nonissue.

The new chip, Google’s Tensor G6, is supposed to deliver 20 percent gains in power efficiency, 25 percent faster browsing, and 15 percent faster app loading. The Pixel 11 has 12 GB of RAM and 256 or 512 GB of storage. For everyday use, it feels fast and responsive. I had no issues with loading apps or scrolling web pages, and the camera app feels a bit faster. Compared with my Pixel 10 Pro XL, I also noticed the Pixel 11 notified and loaded video from my Nest video doorbell a second or two faster.

I put it through its paces with the challenging mobile game Wuthering Waves. It was playable, but the action stuttered, and even on the Balanced (graphics and performance) setting, there were dropped frames aplenty during combat. After an hour, the Pixel 11 was warm, and the battery went from 40 to 26 percent. Less demanding games, like Mini Metro and Alto’s Odyssey, were fine, but dedicated gamers should still look elsewhere.

Google Pixel 11

Rating: 8/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

The 4,985-mAh battery is a disappointing 15-mAh jump over the Pixel 10, but Google claims battery life has improved 25 percent from 24 hours to 30 hours. I’m not sure it’s quite that much based on my first week of testing, but the Pixel 11 has seen me through very busy days without hitting empty, though I still think daily charging will be the norm for most folks.

The Pixel 11 charges at 30 watts wired (cable but no charger included), but support for Qi2 25W enables faster wireless charging. I recommend buying a Qi2 wireless charger. The magnetic Pixelsnap (Google's version of Apple's MagSafe on iPhones) feels a touch stronger than the one in the 10-series, and it’s such a handy feature that saves you from fumbling with cables. Google has also expanded the screensaver so you can have a multiple swipe function on the nightstand, including clock, weather, photos, charging status, and smart home controls.

Google has also switched to a MediaTek modem in the Pixel 11. I wouldn’t normally mention a modem, but the Samsung variant Google used in last year’s 10 series was prone to draining the battery and not holding a signal terribly well. Anecdotally, the Pixel 11 does better in a few spots where I’ve traditionally had trouble with my Pixel 10 Pro XL, which is great news for when you want to use your phone for calls. Your mileage may vary.

Google’s phones have always been about software over hardware, but the real-world value of AI features comes down to context. If I have to go digging or remember that a feature exists, I probably won’t get much value from it. This is why Google weaves its AI into everything, rather than applying it as a layer on top. The latest Gemini Intelligence features extend Google’s lead in this space.

Google Pixel 11

Rating: 8/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Rambler improves the Pixel’s voice-to-text, cutting ums and ahs and letting you draft messages conversationally. I didn’t like it as much as my colleague, but I’m not really a speech-to-text guy, and I have a Scottish accent that it sometimes picks up wrong. I use the Pixel’s Recorder app a lot and love it for instantly transcribing my interviews, but Rambler doesn’t show the text as you talk like Recorder does; everything pops up after you’re done, which I don’t like as much.

AI overviews pop up right there in the Messages app when someone texts with a meet-up request, and you can add it to your calendar, or if they have a restaurant suggestion, you can tap to open it directly in Maps. Gemini can also dig details like flight numbers out of your Gmail to share via Messages if you let it. This is quite handy.

Fans of Circle to Search will be glad to know you don’t even have to snap a photo anymore; you can open the camera app, hold down the nav bar, and circle anything in the viewfinder to get info on it. You can also get location-based suggestions on the lock and home screen, such as a shortcut to your loyalty card in Google Wallet when you’re in a relevant store or recommendations for what to order at a restaurant from Maps.

There’s nothing groundbreaking here, but features like Call Screen for screening spam calls and Now Playing for surfacing the name of the song you can hear are still there, and those are the kinds of things that I miss when I switch away from a Pixel phone.

AI is firmly embedded in Google’s apps, and there’s no switch to turn it off completely, but you can choose to turn off Gemini, cut its access to apps like Photos and Messages, and turn off features like Circle to Search. Most of the camera app AI options are exactly that: options. But if this all sounds gimmicky and the idea of an AI-infused phone gives you the creeps, the Pixel line is not for you.

The triple-lens rear camera is one of the top reasons to buy the Pixel 11. The camera feels faster, with less processing delay than the Pixel 10, and you can snap a shot and instantly load it into the gallery. Spec-wise, it’s almost identical, with a 48-megapixel main camera, 13-megapixel ultrawide, and 10.8-megapixel telephoto for 5x optical zoom. The main camera sensor is larger, enabling slightly better low-light performance, and the digital zoom capability is up from 20x to 30x. The 10.5-megapixel front-facing camera is the same.

Google Pixel 11

Rating: 8/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Everything works beautifully. Most people probably only ever use the main camera and the selfie camera, and reviewers can get too far into the weeds, but the bottom line is that you don’t need a particularly skilled hand or eye to snap great photos with the Pixel 11. I really appreciate the telephoto lens. I rarely have a use for the ultrawide, but the telephoto is great for zooming in from a distance, and though the 30x zoom is digitally enhanced by combining multiple images, there’s no generative AI at work, so you get a real image.

The camera app is feature-packed if you want to dive in. The most notable new features are the Camera Looks, which are like filters you select before you snap a shot. Phone cameras are typically tuned a certain way—Google’s phones tend to be punchy and high-contrast with realistic colors, while Samsung saturates colors and Apple prefers brighter images—but Camera Looks lets you tweak that to opt for warmer colors or dial up the shadows.

Magic Capture is a clever new feature that lets you hold your phone up at a party or event and record video and select still shots simultaneously, without having to watch through the viewfinder. It’s a nice way to be more in the moment, and a safer way to hand your phone off to Mum and maybe get decent photos back.

No one really needs to upgrade their phone every year or two. It’s only by skipping a few releases that you’ll feel a real difference, and this is especially true for Google's phones because so much of what makes them special is on the software side, and many of those features will make it onto older phones too, though they might take a while.

For slick software features and a camera that’s easy to get great results from, the Pixel 11 is tough to beat in this bracket. If you want performance, both the Samsung Galaxy S26 and the Apple iPhone 17 are superior. Unless you’re a keen photographer, I don’t see a compelling case for paying more to get a Pro model. The Pixel 11 is the value sweet spot in Google’s new lineup, at least until the A-series next year.

The Galaxy’s Fastest Star Could Reveal the Secrets of a Supermassive Black Hole

Wired August 20, 2026

A team of astronomers has just detected the fastest star in the galaxy. Its anomalous speed has a more unsettling explanation: It orbits Sagittarius A*, the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way, the mass of which is equivalent to four million times that of the sun.

S301, as astronomers have named the star, reaches 25,000 kilometers per second (km/s) at its maximum speed and takes 8.7 years to complete one orbit around Sagittarius A*. (By comparison, the sun orbits the center of the galaxy at about 230 km/s.) At its peak speed, S301 moves more than 100 times faster than our star, and reaches 8 percent of the speed of light.

The key to S301’s speed lies in how close it passes to the supermassive black hole. According to the European Southern Observatory (ESO), at its closest approach, the distance between the two is comparable to that between Saturn and the sun.

The enormous gravitational pull of Sagittarius A* accelerates the star as it approaches the black hole. S301, however, does not fall directly into it, but instead follows an extremely elongated orbit around it.

The shape of its orbit also explains why its speed varies so much. At its closest approach, it moves faster, while when it is farther away, it moves more slowly. Something similar happens in the solar system with some comets, such as Halley’s Comet.

S301 is the star with the highest-known orbital velocity in the Milky Way, and also the one that comes closest to Sagittarius A*. It likely did not form where we see it today, and may have lost a companion along the way.

“S301’s orbital properties, and the fact that stars cannot form so close to a massive black hole, indicate that the star was likely part of a binary pair that was torn apart by the tidal forces of Sagittarius A*. In the process, S301 became trapped by the black hole’s gravity while its companion star was kicked out with high velocity, most likely enough to leave the galaxy altogether,” explains the ESO.

Astronomers believe that within 10 years they will be able to determine the rotation of Sagittarius A*. Mass and rotation, or spin, are two of the fundamental properties that scientists use to describe a black hole astrophysically. So far, there are signs that Sagittarius A* is spinning, but it is not yet possible to determine precisely how much or in which direction it is spinning.

According to the theory of general relativity, a rotating black hole drags the spacetime around it along with it. That effect should slightly alter the orbit of S301. If astronomers are able to measure these small deviations over the next few years, they will be able to determine the spin of Sagittarius A*.

A black hole’s spin would warp the fabric of spacetime. Tracking S301 could provide more insight into this phenomenon.

Astronomers first detected S301 in 2023 using GRAVITY, an instrument on ESO’s VLTI in Chile. Since then, they have tracked its movement and, after identifying it, have been able to trace it backward through observations dating back to 2017. By combining this data, they reconstructed its orbit with greater precision and determined that the star passed its closest approach to Sagittarius A* in early 2023. It will approach the black hole again in 2031.

S301 is not the only known star orbiting close to Sagittarius A*. For decades, stars such as S2 have allowed astronomers to determine the black hole’s mass and test predictions of general relativity. The difference is that S301 passes so close to Sagittarius A* that it could allow them to directly measure its spin over the next decade—something that would require several more decades of observations with other stars.

This story originally appeared in WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

China Is Strapping ‘Digital Bombs’ to Civilian Infrastructure—Is the US Ready?

Wired August 20, 2026

Earlier this year, insurance executives gathered in a Times Square conference room to play out a scenario: A Chinese cyberattack knocks out 5,000 US water utilities at once. If you think that’s a far-fetched scenario, think again. WIRED’s Andy Greenberg got rare access to the closed-door war game and walked away with some disturbing conclusions. This week, Brian Barrett sits down to talk with Andy about Volt Typhoon, the Chinese state-sponsored hacking group that’s spent the past three years pre-positioning itself inside American infrastructure.

Specifically, the idea was to simulate a Chinese cyberattack that would knock out 5,000 water utilities in the US all at once and to do it under a countdown clock. WIRED senior correspondent Andy Greenberg got a rare invite to this closed-door war game; call it Dungeons & Dragons for a national security nightmare. It was designed by a former cybersecurity strategist to test what would happen if and when hackers linked to an infamous Chinese operation called Volt Typhoon finally decide to follow through on groundwork that they've been laying for three years.

Archival audio: This group that's known as Volt Typhoon, this is a state-sponsored Chinese hacking group.

Archival audio: China has secretly stepped up its electronic warfare, deploying what is being called the Volt Typhoon malware throughout the US ecosystem.

Brian Barrett: The result could include burst water mains, evacuated hospitals, and insulin shortages. Andy's here to tell us more about what he saw and heard, and why the scariest part might not quite be the hack itself, but what it revealed about who's actually in charge when the water stops. Andy Greenberg: Glad to do it, Brian.

It's the equivalent of the Allstates or the State Farms.

Andy Greenberg: Absolutely. The fact is, they were doing this internally for their own benefit. In fact, I was kind of sworn to secrecy in a sense; I'm not allowed to identify anybody in the room. You have to figure out how to deal with this on your own."

Andy Greenberg: Josh told me before it began, actually, that his entire goal with this was to, as he says, surface and shatter assumptions. He wants to shock people out of complacency about thinking that they might know how this is going to unfold and know how to deal with it. I think 5,000 water utilities is enough that that makes sense. I think that there are not enough incident responders in the country for all of those victims to get professionals in the room looking at their network. In fact, my table was already trying to brainstorm about, "Well, maybe we can get people from academia to help. Maybe we can beg for help from the US government. What the table I was sitting at came up with was, "Let's just say the biggest customers first." And Josh was like, "Well, biggest by what metric?" And the spokesperson for the table just off the cuff was like, "Well, biggest by revenue." And that I think was just their kind of knee-jerk insurance industry answer. It turned out to be, I think, a very unfortunately naive and probably quite disastrous response.

What are the repercussions of prioritizing revenue when you're dealing with a cybersecurity emergency like Volt Typhoon could cause?

Silicon Valley Doesn't Get Why You Hate AI

Wired August 20, 2026

Silicon Valley is trying to make sense of the growing backlash against artificial intelligence, but so far, it’s not going that well. The inconvenient truth is that a significant portion of the world is not optimistic about the technology they’re building. But recent attempts to diagnose the root of the problem by CEOs like Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei indicate they don’t understand what’s actually driving society’s disdain for AI.

The rest of popular culture, meanwhile, is finding ways to capitalize on AI hate. Just look at this new commercial for Liquid Death and Garage Beer. The two beverage brands teamed up with former Philadelphia Eagles football player and Taylor Swift brother-in-law Jason Kelce, who invited people to pee in bottles and send them to AI data centers. In an interview with Marketing Dive, Liquid Death’s creative lead said the data center backlash was “literally the one thing that unites all Americans right now.”

More than half of Americans under 30 say they are more concerned than excited about AI, a figure that’s grown 24 percent in the last five years, according to a Pew Research Center survey published earlier this week. More than 70 percent of people polled in all age groups say they believe AI will lead to fewer jobs.

But other recent polling data shows that people have broader anxieties about the technology that go far beyond jobs and the data center boom. Americans also think AI will harm young people’s ability to form meaningful relationships, that tech companies should be required to compensate creators whose works were used to train models, and that AI could harm the critical thinking skills of students.

The tech industry often chalks up the AI backlash to a communication and branding problem, but it’s much deeper than that. Hearing different messages around AI made little difference in people’s opinions on the technology’s societal impact, according to a recent survey from the Searchlight Institute.

While Silicon Valley is starting to grapple with growing negative public sentiment about AI, investors and executives I talk to have grown increasingly worried that the industry is failing to fully comprehend how big of a problem this could be for adoption of AI products.

Earlier this month, Zuckerberg published a 6,500-word essay painting his optimistic vision of an AI future. The Meta CEO described a world in which everyone has a personalized AI assistant that knows you intimately (presumably from all the personal information Meta’s apps have collected) and can help with your career, hobbies, and perhaps even raising your children. Of course, such a product doesn’t exist yet, but Zuckerberg is basically arguing that giving everyone unfettered access to highly capable AI is the best-case scenario for this technology.

I’m optimistic that AI will continue getting better and more helpful, but I’m skeptical that this will be enough to transform the way people feel about it. For people to even use the theoretical product Zuckerberg envisions, they will need to have a lot of trust in the companies that build it. Current polling suggests that the AI industry has yet to earn that trust.

The Meta CEO also made a not-so-subtle jab at Amodei, saying he was surprised that “discourse from many developing AI is so filled with doom.” On social media and during an appearance on the All-In podcast, tech investor Gavin Baker reiterated Zuckerberg’s points and went even further, writing that “Dario’s messaging has been massively helpful to efforts to ban data centers here in America.” White House AI adviser and All-In co-host David Sacks chimed in as well, writing that Anthropic’s “narratives have done more than anything to shape public fear.”

These comments prompted a rare public response from Amodei, who published a lengthy social media post in which he rejected the idea that his messaging was the culprit of the AI backlash.

“I think it is fundamentally a crisis of trust,” Amodei wrote. “I think that ordinary people don’t trust companies, governments, or the tech industry and always suspect that we are cooking up some new way to screw them over. The causes of this go back decades and AI is just the latest iteration of it.”

Amodei’s initial assertions ring closer to the truth, but he loses me later on. He went on to write that “the most accurate criticism of AI companies including Anthropic is that we haven’t yet delivered on our big promises to benefit the world.” One example he cites is the promise that AI will find a cure for cancer, a goal he’s previously said that people should reasonably expect the technology to achieve.

Amodei, and Silicon Valley broadly, may be missing the forest for the trees here. The AI backlash was not caused by scary warnings about the future from tech CEOs, or the fact that OpenAI and Anthropic have not yet cured cancer. It’s about the ways AI is already starting to change society, which many Americans fear is for the worse.

Tech companies have spent enormous effort making physical data centers more digestible to the public, with promises around responsible water usage, clean energy commitments, and investments in local communities. But unfortunately for them, there’s a lot of evidence suggesting that the data center buildout has simply become the physical manifestation of people’s hatred of AI and the ways tech companies engage with communities overall.

I often talk to rank-and-file employees at AI companies who understand these issues and hear about the backlash from their own families and friends across the country. But the leaders at the center of the AI boom still appear to be unprepared to address all the ways in which AI is changing the world. Silicon Valley will need to find a way to confront these issues more directly in the future if it wants people to fully embrace the products it’s building.

This is an edition of Maxwell Zeff’s Model Behavior newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

Review: Poolease X1 Pool Robot

Wired August 20, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, when you buy something through our retail links, we may earn an affiliate commission.

5/10

The market is stuffed to the gills with pool-scrubbing robots that cost thousands of dollars, and consumers are well justified in worrying whether that level of expense will ultimately be worthwhile. But there’s also a subset of pool robots that go the other way—much simpler devices that cost well under $500, sometimes much less.

It’s here where we find the Poolease X1, a pint-sized robot that can be yours for barely over 100 bucks. Can it possibly be any good?

I’ve tested robots along these lines in the past. All work under the same general principle. Stripped down to the basics, the tiny Poolease X1—just 9 pounds in weight and not much larger than a lunch box—has no spinning brushes or treads to propel it. Rather, the clearly Dyson-inspired robot is entirely powered by water jets, which send it on a largely random zigzag path around the pool while pulling debris up through the bottom of the device.

Because of this simple propulsion system, the X1 can’t clean walls or the waterline or even steps, nor can it “scrub” the way a robot with motorized rollers can. It’s strictly limited to the floor of the pool. Needless to say there are no wireless or mobile app features at this price level, either.

There’s also no debris basket on the X1, per se. Rather, the entire device splits into two, and leaves and other debris are simply captured inside it, with a simple filter screen serving to keep debris from passing through the device and back out though the propulsion system’s exhaust port. To clean the device, you snap open four clips surrounding the chassis to separate the halves, then spray the whole thing down with a hose.

Poolease X1 Robotic Pool Vacuum

Rating: 5/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

The unit arrives with some assembly required. The four caster-style wheels (in two sizes) must be snapped into place, along with two brushlike “scrapers” and two plastic plates that must be installed inside the device. None of this is difficult, but it feels awfully unnecessary for the consumer to have to complete the extra effort.

The X1’s charging port—a term I’ll use loosely—is located on the bottom of the robot, which means you need to flip it over to connect the power adapter, which risks scratching the device’s fetching purple paint job. This connection isn’t so much a port as it is two bare metal posts sitting in a narrow channel. It’s designed to be covered by a rubber stopper when in the water, though note that this stopper isn’t connected to the robot in any way and, I suspect, will be very easy to lose. (A spare cover is included in the box.) It’s also really tough to pry it out of place and to put it back.

The simple 1.8 amp charger will top up the 4300mAh battery in about three hours, giving it enough juice for a specified 90-minute running cycle.

While mini robots like this are clearly intended for above-ground and tiny pools, Poolease specs the robot to cover 861 square feet—the equivalent of a massive 30 x 30-foot pool that would be almost twice the size of my own. Nevertheless, I didn’t expect the X1 to do a spectacular job at cleaning it, and sure enough, it didn’t.

After powering it on by holding down a button located on the bottom of the device (naturally), the unit lazily careens back and forth around the floor of the pool, usually reversing only when it reaches a wall. There’s no intelligence to speak of under the hood here, which means any collected debris is largely a random race against time. The goal is to suck up all the leaves before the battery dies; in my testing, that was a bit longer than Poolease’s spec, approaching two hours of operation.

Poolease X1 Robotic Pool Vacuum

Rating: 5/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Results were not particularly impressive. With both organic and synthetic debris, the Poolease X1 was only typically able to collect 70 to 80 percent of leaves and other matter on the floor of my pool, leaving material scattered randomly all around. That’s better than I expected, but worse than it sounds. If your gardener left 20 percent of your lawn unmowed, you’d notice.

With minimal clearance between the bottom of the robot and the floor, I also noticed several times that the robot was prone to getting stuck, namely on the circular floor drain, which has less than an inch of rise over the floor surface. Apparently it’s the perfect size for the X1 to beach itself, so its wheels are just shy of touching the ground. The robot was successful in freeing itself eventually, but it spent several minutes doing so.

The X1 must be retrieved with a pole and hook (the hook is included) when it’s finished running. I described the simple cleanout process above. Here, debris regularly got stuck in a couple of narrow crannies inside the chassis, requiring me to either pick it out by hand or use the jet mode on my hose to blast it out (soaking me in the process). It’s also worth noting that the unit didn’t pick up any noticeable amount of dirt or silt; I suspect the suction system just isn’t strong enough to do much good on that front.

It’s clear that, despite specifications to the contrary, the Poolease X1 is not remotely powerful enough for my pool, and I suspect it may be too little for all but very small tank-style pools. Of course, the mere $110 price tag makes this a low-risk investment, which might be fine if you just want to keep it on hand for emergencies.

On the other hand, as they say, you get what you pay for. Imagine tasking your 5-year-old to clean up his room. I mean, they try, right?

Bumble Tried to Change Dating, but the Dating Market Forced It to Change Instead

Wired August 20, 2026

Not even 24 hours after dating app Bumble announced it was getting rid of its trademark feature that requires women to make the first move, Robin H.’s inbox was already attracting unwanted attention.

“This guy responded to my prompt, and he wasn’t a person I would have swiped on. I can’t believe some of these men think we’re a match,” the 53-year-old social worker in Orlando, Florida, tells WIRED. “Men will swipe on anybody and see what sticks. And with this change, they are just going to be reaching out to everybody.” (Citing privacy concerns, Robin asked that WIRED not publish her full last name.)

Bumble, which hit the market in December 2014, staked its brand on challenging traditional heterosexual dating dynamics. “Whitney Wolfe Is Bringing Feminism to Your Phone,” an Austin Woman headline exclaimed less than two years after launch. But the app’s sudden reversal last week suggests its women-first positioning has become a liability to the company’s sustainability.

Bumble’s policy update—which includes giving matches 72 hours to respond; previously it was 24—comes as Big Dating’s growth is lagging. Perhaps hinting at what was to come, in May, Bumble CEO Whitney Wolfe-Herd said in an interview with Axios that niche apps aren’t built for real longevity. The dilemma is emblematic of the volatility in the current dating market, where declining engagement and the introduction of AI are forcing companies to rethink how they should best appeal to singles.

These problems aren’t unique to Bumble. Match Group’s August 2026 results showed Tinder’s number of daily active users is down 4 percent from the previous year, while Hinge’s global monthly active users rose 13 percent during the same period. But even apps with sustained engagement struggle with brand perception issues.

Feeld, a niche kink app that championed polyamory and BDSM in its early days, has shifted its focus to attracting more vanilla users, resulting in a 200 percent spike in users in 2025, though people have described the new vibe as “normie hell.”

Likewise, Grindr has positioned itself as more than an app for hookups, expanding into a “gayborhood” that offers luxury travel experiences, medical prescriptions for GLP-1s and erectile dysfunction pills, musical artist activations, and AI matchmaking. To turn a profit, Grindr has essentially transformed into a digital gated community that now charges members $500 to hook up through its newest membership tier, Edge, while users who opt out are forced to navigate a platform drowning in ads and bots.

Bumble, which is publicly traded and reportedly exploring a sale, has taken a similar route: transforming a once-niche product into a for-everybody service that pay-gates basic features. The move has not settled well with users online, who have renamed it “Yellow Tinder”—a reference to the color of its logo—and complained that the changes will encourage harassment. “I’m not going to use an app that makes me feel like prey,” one user wrote on X.

“The change obviously goes against their whole thing,” says Emily Spence, a 28-year-old events producer in New York City who has used Bumble since 2015. “But the requirement for women to message first didn’t really prevent creeps from messaging you. Just because you say ‘hey’ first doesn’t mean a man isn’t gonna send you something crazy after. It was kind of like a false sense of protection.”

The new update may also reflect a desire for a return to more traditional courtship roles. In the announcement, the company noted that 66 percent of women surveyed on Bumble said they prefer men to send the first message, adding that it alleviates unnecessary pressure from the experience.

The company said that its testing of the new feature showed increased chat initiation, but it’s unclear if that will actually translate to more dates and higher user retention or just more unwanted messages. Bumble did not respond to a request for comment.

Stefanie Feldman, 41, appreciates the new direction of the app. “I like that it takes off the pressure. Sometimes I just want the men to do the work,” says the business manager in Los Angeles. “I’ve never considered myself a feminist. I want to be pursued. And just because someone reaches out to you doesn’t mean you have to say anything. So that is a feminine power in itself, learning to say no.”

Even before last week’s news, Bumble’s brand dilution seems to have been in the works for a while. In 2024, Bumble began tweaking its founding principle when it debuted the feature Opening Moves, which let men reply to a prompt on a user’s page. According to data the market intelligence firm Sensor Tower shared with WIRED, the app has also not featured its women-first social mission as part of its marketing in the US since 2023, with only a few limited branding spots reinforcing that women make the first move in 2022. As an alternative, Bumble “created more generic messaging on how the app has been successful for previous users and encouraged potential users to ‘get to know new people today,’” says Kara Lee, a senior analyst with the firm.

The reversal ultimately highlights the difficulty of building a dating app around a social mission and how the cost of doing business sometimes requires you to abandon your original ideals.

Riki Thompson, an associate professor of digital rhetoric at the University of Washington Tacoma who published a study on the app last year, adds that the shift away from mandatory first moves was the only way, in the interim, for Bumble to keep pace with its rivals.

“An app is only one small part of a much larger system, how people actually behave, what they expect from dating, and the norms they bring with them. You can design an app with great intentions, but you can’t fully control how people use it,” Thompson says in an email. “Bumble is still a business. It has to stay competitive and profitable in a marketplace where plenty of competitors aren’t built around any social mission at all.”

Update, August 20 at 1:30pm: This story was updated to correct an error about Bumble’s ownership. It is a publicly traded company.

The Best USB Car Chargers for Road Trips and Fast Charging

Wired August 20, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

A car charger is not a complicated device. The best USB car charger is the one that charges your phone quickly, does not overheat, allows multiple devices to charge, and remains compatible with whichever USB cable you (or your passengers) happen to have available. It is usually also a trusted brand, with certification to international standards—not a janky gas station charger that'll blow a fuse with an internal short or offer insufficient protection against dust and debris.

I put car chargers to the test with ammeters and phone apps, and on multi-hour road trips, to make sure each one lived up to its promises. The best car charger I've found is the three-port Anker 167.5W Nano ($38), which combines 100-watt fast-charging capability for auxiliary devices, plus dual-port USB-Cs, USB-A capability, and safety features that include overheat protection.

If you shun dangling cords, I offer the Anker 75W Fast Charger ($30) with slightly lower top amperage but a retractable cable. And for families whose kids can't live without constant tablets in the back seat, there's the DeWalt 72W Front and Back Seat Charger ($45).

For other power needs, check out WIRED's guides to the Best Portable Jump Starters, Best Power Banks, Best MagSafe/Qi2 Power Banks, and Best Laptop Power Banks or Best Portable Power Stations.

Anker

Amazon

This three-port charger from Anker offers pretty much everything I want from a USB car charger while remaining hearteningly compact and affordable. The 100W fast-charging USB-C port kicks out nearly 7 amps at top speeds, enough juice to charge my Macbook Air to 50 percent in about 25 minutes, before fast-charging slows down, and does the same for my iPhone. But especially, Anker's PowerIQ technology smartly assesses the differing voltage needs of various phones to avoid over- or under-voltage. I've never actually seen this Anker on sale on Amazon above $40.

It also doesn't hurt that Anker makes some of WIRED's most trusted portable power technology—tech whose reliability we've verified over years of real-world testing. You don't overwhelmingly want a janky cheap charger that blows a fuse. Good insulation and a tiny built-in fan effectively lower overheating versus other fast-chargers, though you'll still notice some heat when charging at 100 watts or above. USB-A capability is welcome for versatility, though my testing showed somewhat lower power than advertised on that port.

Either way, I was able to charge both my top-pick portable jump starter, the 4000A Wolfbox ($120), in a little over an hour while also keeping my phone topped off on a road trip—which is pretty much as high-demand as I get while also blasting AC and the radio, and this caused no problems with the 15-amp circuit on my older car. But note that while most modern cars run on 20-amp fuses, the max capacity for this charger when drawing from all three ports does run pretty close to the max load for an older-model car charger. The charger is able to draw quite close to the maximum amperage on a 15-amp fuse.

A similar budget pick: The lower overheating on my top-pick Anker bodes well for longevity, which means it might still be a cheaper option in the long haul. But note that a similar three-port fast-charger from Chinese brand Ugreen ($21) performed comparably on charging speeds. But it also got significantly hotter within 10 minutes of fast-charging.

Anker

Amazon

A retractable charging cable has the distinct merit of keeping your car tidy, without dangling charging cords to get tangled between your foot and the gas pedal. It also obviates the need to remember a cable at all. This Anker model offers a 2-foot cable that retracts quite easily back into its base after a quick tug on the cable, neat as you'd like. The cable's 45W fast-charging capability will max out the charging capability of most iPhones.

Anker is a brand I trust for charging technology. But it's worth noting that retractable cables introduce a couple failure points that could lower longevity. The cable can't be swapped out if it gets worn, and the retraction mechanism itself could wear out. Tidiness has a price, it seems. This said, the charger is not overly expensive, usually retailing closer to $20.

DeWalt

Amazon

The modern car family involves a nest of devices—parents in the front seat charging phones, children in the back with tablets, somehow watching the same thing over and over. And nothing ends the peace of a road trip quite like a tablet running out of juice halfway through an episode of Bluey.

This DeWalt is a good solution, offering decent (but not great) 30-watt charging on the USB-C port for front-seat parents, and a couple of auxiliary USB-A ports to keep maintenance charge on backseat devices. DeWalt is a power tool brand, of course, and so these ports were likely designed for a tool or two resting in the back seat. But kids have tools, too, and this'll serve their needs.

It's perhaps frustrating that the back seat chargers are USB-A. But I haven't found a good USB charger with a back-seat USB-C charging setup, assuming your car doesn't have a back seat charger of its own. And so while this DeWalt is a compromise, it's the best compromise I've found so far.

How I Selected and Tested USB Car Chargers

For this round of car-charger testing, I looked first for known quantities and trusted charging technology brands like Anker, Belkin, and Ugreen. I also ordered and tested devices that other credible sources had ranked as their favorite USB chargers, making sure that each charger is broadly available and easy to find. I only assessed chargers that meet international standards, and avoided dodgy-looking brands: Short circuits in cars aren't fun, for me or for you.

I then set about testing the claims for each car charger, using ammeters for each port on each charger, testing with an ammeter while pulling max loads. I additionally used the Ampere phone app to test the peak draw for a Motorola Razr and an iPhone 13, and also tested to see whether the charger heated up while pulling max draw—both using the phone app and an infrared thermometer.

I tested with each charger's included cord, where relevant, but also with a fast-charging cable on USB-C devices that advertise this capability. For my top contenders among 100-watt fast chargers, I also tested to see how long it took to charge a Macbook Air M4 and my top-pick jump starter, the 4000A Wolfbox.

As with every device tested by the WIRED Reviews team, I subjected my top-pick chargers to real-world road tests. I went on multi-hour road trips with devices plugged in. I charged portable jump starters or laptops while also charging phones. I tested durability in real-world conditions that may also involve grubby fingers. I assessed each device not just for brute speed, but for versatility in different use cases. For now, I favor chargers that offer both USB-C and USB-A capability, so as not to leave any devices out in the cold.

I also checked up on customer reviews for each of these chargers. If I saw any customer complaints, I tried my darndest to replicate them. I jammed chargers in and out of the ports, and wobbled the chargers around in their sockets. I acted the way people act when they're fumbling for a device charger they're not looking at while driving.

Are Cheap USB Chargers Unsafe?

I've put a bit of emphasis on trusted brands while testing USB chargers, and this isn't by accident. The world is full of dodgy gas station or Amazon chargers, and bad cables, with insufficient electrical insulation and inconsistent current delivery.

Bad USB-C cables and electrical insulation are known fire hazards in the worst cases, but inconsistent voltage is also just bad for your phone or laptop battery over time. Poorly made chargers, connectors, and cables can have higher resistance (leading to overheating), bad or inconsistent connections, and poor protections against shorts and surges. All of these things are bad. At worst, they can fry your device or lower your battery longevity.

As a rule of thumb, look for language that a product is “UL-Listed” or "UL-Certified" not merely "UL-Classified" or “Recognized.” The latter two mean that a product has been tested only against specific hazards or under specific conditions. Listed and Certified products have fully passed all tests within a given standard.

Scosche PowerVolt 60W Dual-Port Charger for $20: This dual-port USB-C charger from California car brand Scosche is the simplest thing imaginable. Two USB-C ports, each separately rated at 30 watts. Each charges quickly and is reliable. Though this Scosche doesn't offer a fast-charging option for laptops, it's perfectly optimized for a pair of phones—and admirably low-cost. If you're mostly just going to charge a phone, this is a tight runner-up to my top-pick Anker—especially if you're pretty sure you'll never need a USB-A charger in your car.

Anker 40W Two-Port Charger for $20: Like the Scosche, this Anker is a purpose-driven phone charger with two USB-C ports. It's a little lower-powered than the Scosche, with a little less juice than the newest generation of phones can support. But the price is right if you're willing to accept lower charging speeds.

Belkin BoostCharge 42W Dual-Port Charger for $24: This compact, well-insulated dual-port charger from California tech accessory brand Belkin is great as a budget option, with decently fast USB-C and USB-A charging. Just note that the tiny device might be a bit shallow for some deeper car chargers, and that when plugged in, the charger has a nonnegotiable and oddly bright LED light that stays on even when no device is charging. This won't bother you unless it bothers you.

Nekteck 45W Two-Port Car Charger for $32: This basic, bare-bones Neckteck charger is a decent compromise for those who need fast charging on a QC 3.0-compatible USB-A device. While a 45-watt max speed for USB-C charging isn't fast by modern standards, it's still faster than most phones. And the QC 3.0 USB-A charger is significantly faster than most USB-A chargers, for those with older devices.

Lisen 90W Charger With Cord for $20: This charger from Chinese car-tech company Lisen performed reasonably well in testing, though true fast-charging isn't available and the listed charge speeds are a little confusing and don't add up. The coiled cord is not able to be retracted or removed, making this charger a bit ungainly for daily use, but the option on a 60- or 90-inch cord does make this Lisen the rare device suitable for charging a USB-C phone or tablet in the back seat. This said, I tested a shorter cable, and longer USB-C cables are notoriously finicky for high amperage.

The six-port Ai Aikenuo back seat charging kit is useful for keeping a large number of devices charged up for work use or larger families, but it disappeared from Amazon right before this guide's publication. I'll monitor to see if this is a momentary glitch or whether it's been discontinued.

A MAGA County’s Top Election Official Wants to Hire Election Denial Superstar Tina Peters

Wired August 20, 2026

Last week, Clint Curtis, the top election official in Shasta County, California, publicly accused members of his own staff of bypassing security, which he later claimed was an attempt “to sabotage a federal election.”

Days later, Curtis announced plans to hire a new deputy: Tina Peters, the election denial superstar who was convicted of seven counts related to election interference in 2024 and sentenced to nine years in prison.

Peters, the former clerk of Mesa County, Colorado, has yet to publicly comment on the offer, but her lawyer Peter Ticktin tells WIRED she “is giving consideration to helping in the efforts in Shasta County, as there most definitely has been monkey business in the way the election was handled.”

Peters was convicted after she allowed Conan Hayes, a former pro surfer who later worked for pillow salesman turned election denier Mike Lindell, unauthorized access to election equipment in Mesa County as part of a scheme to prove that the 2020 presidential election had been stolen from Donald Trump. (Hayes was never charged for his role in the scheme). Colorado governor Jared Polis commuted Peters’ sentence in May after months of pressure from President Trump, who purported to have issued his own pardon even though Peters was convicted on state charges. Recently released court papers show how Trump and his advisers coordinated with federal agencies to cut federal funding and grants to Colorado as part of a pressure campaign to free Peters.

Curtis told The Guardian that Peters would not have access to the county’s voting system but refused to specify what her duties would include. Curtis did not respond to a request for comment.

Should Peters accept the role, she would likely feel right at home in Shasta County, a deep-red enclave in Northern California that has become ground zero for many of the election denial conspiracy theories promoted by Trump and his supporters over the past six years. And in Curtis, she would be working alongside a man who has a decades-long history of promoting many of the same election-related conspiracy theories she herself has championed.

“This should be stopped immediately: Shasta County Registrar Clint Curtis is trying to hire election-denier Tina Peters to collude with the Trump administration’s election mischief,” US senator Alex Padilla, a California Democrat, wrote on Facebook.

Curtis first came to national prominence more than two decades ago, when he claimed to have created a software program that could rig elections without election officials being able to notice anything amiss. Curtis, who testified before Congress about his program, said he did this at the behest of Florida state lawmaker Tom Feeney, who denied the claim.

In 2025, when the previous Registrar of Voters in Shasta County, Thomas Toller. retired midterm, Curtis put his name forward for the position, despite having no experience in running elections and spending most of his career working as a lawyer and a computer developer. He also lived in Florida at the time and had no ties to the area.

During the 2025 interview process for his current role, Curtis touted his associations with prominent figures in the election denial community, including Lindell, disgraced former national security adviser Mike Flynn, and former Trump adviser Steve Bannon.

Since his appointment, Curtis has faced a string of accusations about his behavior from members of his staff. An internal investigation concluded that he had physically threatened, verbally abused, and retaliated against staff at the Shasta County Elections Office, while an external investigation found he had retaliated against them. Among the specific allegations made by his colleagues were that Curtis threatened to have one employee dragged out by her hair and to “throat-punch” another. Curtis has consistently denied the allegations.

In June, Curtis lost his bid to keep his job past this year when Joanna Francescut, who worked in elections in Shasta County for 18 years, easily defeated him. Curtis had fired Francescut days after he took up his role.

The Board of Supervisors in Shasta County, having initially voted against censuring Curtis, last week voted 3-1 to censure him. However, Curtis responded to the public rebuke by making further allegations against his staff, including claims that they were bypassing security to tamper with elections. He subsequently invited the media back to his office to show them CCTV footage of one staff member opening a door without using a keycard.

When asked if he had asked the employee in question what he was doing, Curtis said he hadn’t.

"Shasta County has gone through a lot of controversy, division, and animosity related to elections, and based on the initial response from the public I’ve received already, recruiting Tina Peters would increase this and reduce trust in our elections," Matt Plummer, a member of the Shasta Board of Supervisors, tells WIRED, while acknowledging Curtis has the authority to make his own hiring decisions. The other members did not respond to a request for comment.

Plummer isn’t the only authority raising questions about the proposal. Stewart Buettell, the deputy CEO of the County of Shasta, tells WIRED, “There has been no formal process or application submitted to replace the current assistant registrar of voters,” adding that “any prospective employee would go through the same hiring process as anyone else seeking employment with the county.”

Brent Turner, the current assistant registrar of voters, told Shasta Scout on Tuesday that he was surprised to hear he may be replaced. “I believe I’m the assistant registrar. And if anything changes I will certainly let you know,” said Turner.

Curtis told the Redding Record Searchlight that he would be hiring Peters as a consultant as a way of circumventing what he predicted would be the county’s efforts to block the appointment. He said that as a consultant, she would be able to continue to work in Colorado and Washington, DC while also at times supervising onsite in Shasta County.

Buettell said that if Peters was hired as a consultant that would “typically require a contract for services, consistent with Shasta County policy, which has not been initiated.”

While there has been strong criticism of the effort to employ Peters, some election experts believe mechanisms are in place to prevent it from actually happening.

"This announcement seems to be nothing more than performance art by the current and outgoing clerk, who was rejected by voters in the primary,” David Becker, the head of the Center for Election Innovation and Research and a former Justice Department lawyer, tells WIRED. “It’s highly questionable that county officials could spend any taxpayer dollars on this or give any authority to a convicted and unrepentant felon like Ms. Peters.”

Despite her parole conditions barring her from travelling outside Colorado without permission, Peters has spent the months since her release appearing in-person at multiple MAGA events as well as numerous interviews with right-wing podcasters, continuing to promote election denial conspiracy theories. She has also met with Trump in the Oval Office and has claimed to have met the head of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and presented her plan to secure elections.

If Peters does decide to take up the role in Shasta County, which Curtis told Action News Now would begin on September 4, it will allow her time to fulfil one more public engagement, when she is scheduled to speak at the Destroying the Whore of Babylon conference later this month.
